..0.General Information
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

   ..Course Description 
         -This course takes a systems-level approach to neuroscience, studying the structures and connections of the nervous system, with a focus on how these systems are integrated for the control of movement. Course work involves using research evidence that highlights the neural basis of movement and its application to clinical practice. Physical therapists, across practice settings, play a critical role in helping people function as independently as possible. The content presented in this course provides the foundation for students to make accurate movement system diagnoses, establish appropriate goals, and implement optimal interventions to achieve the best outcomes for all patients.

   ..Course Outcomes 
         On completion of this course, students will be able to:
               -Identify specific information concerning the structure and currently recognized functions of the nervous system. 
               -Explain general concepts of global organization and basic functions of the normal, intact nervous system; and theoretical explanations of the nervous system including less well understood neural mechanisms. 
               -Explain the neuroanatomical and neurophysiological mechanisms being evaluated in neurological examinations, and the evaluation of motor control in health, disease, and injury. 
               -Relate the clinical manifestations of neural dysfunction and probable sites of lesions and use your knowledge to evaluate and assess clinical pathology. 
               -Explain the neural basis of specific interventions to promote optimal motor control for individual clients.

   ..Announcements
      Welcome to PT 2060 Introduction to Neuroscience course. Hope you all had a restful winter break and are gearing up to begin the Spring 2025 semester next week.

      For our first live sync session of the course, we will meet next week on Wednesday, January 8 at 2:00 pm EST for Group A and at 3:45 pm EST for Group B. Please check that you are always using your Pitt account to log into to the Zoom links. The course syllabus and schedule are available for your access on Canvas. Ensure to review them before our first live sync session. I will also briefly go over the syllabus on Wednesday.

      Every Wednesday once the live sync session for both the group ends, I will have an open office hour for the entire class from 5:30 pm to 6:30 pm EST on the same weekly Wednesday zoom link. This open office hour is optional for you. In addition to this you are always welcome to schedule a 1:1 appointment for office hour with the course faculty as and when needed. Along with me in this course you’ll also meet Dr. Dunlap and Dr. Edwards who will be teaching in the course.

      All modules of the course are published for your access ahead of time, so that you can begin studying at your pace. Though you are only expected to review the weekly asynchronous content in preparation of our weekly live sync sessions in order to actively participate in the learning activities. For the purpose of having focused discussion of topics at each live sync session, each module's asynchronous content is arranged in two parts; only the content that is placed before Wednesday live sync session will be discussed on Wednesday and the content that is placed after Wednesday session and before Friday live sync session will be discussed on Friday. For example: For the upcoming Wednesday, Jan 8 live sync session you are only expected to review the video lectures posted on page 1.2 General Organization and Division of the Nervous System, related background readings and the Wednesday live sync session worksheet posted under Wednesday live sync session page. Though you are always welcome to review the entire module content ahead of time, if you like. 

      At the end of every week, you'll have a graded discussion post submission due on Sundays at 11:59 pm EST which is essentially your reflection on the week's content that you have learned. In addition to proctored Midterm and Final Exam, you will also have weekly proctored quizzes in this course to regularly test your content knowledge, starting with Quiz 1 on Module 1 on Wednesday, January 15 at 1 pm EST.

      You are expected to have access to the required reading textbooks of the course and the Pitt Library links to those textbooks are posted in the syllabus. For your effective learning and retention of the content knowledge, the course content will require multiple review on your part, so I will encourage you to start early. You will take away from this course as much as you will put into it.

      In this course you’ll gain foundational knowledge of Neuroscience and Neuroanatomy on which you will continue to build your content knowledge of Neurologic Physical Therapy as you move forward in the program through Neuromuscular course sequence. The Neuro faculty team is looking forward to facilitating your learning experience in this course and throughout the Neuromuscular course sequence in the program.

      When you have any questions or concerns always remember that we are just an email away from you.

      P.S. Please note the important Proctorio updates:
         As of December 26, 2024, the Proctorio Chrome extension has been renamed "Secure Exam Proctor." The previous version, called "Proctorio," will no longer be supported. To ensure smooth proctoring for upcoming assessments of this course, you should verify that you have the correct extension installed ahead of the quizzes and exams. You can do this by visiting ('https://getproctorio.com')

..Group Tutoring Information / Assigned Group Information: Tutoring Groups
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

      .In order to effectively facilitate your learning experience in the course, weekly group tutoring support is provided to you. Your small group tutors are Pitt DPT students who have taken this course in the past and have successfully passed the course. Hence, these tutors will be a great resource for you to tap into throughout the course. You may find your assigned group assignment by reviewing the Assigned Group Information: Tutoring Groups page.  
      You are highly encouraged to attend weekly tutoring sessions across the entire course but it's optional for you, unless otherwise made mandatory by the course faculty under the following circumstances:
            -Weekly tutoring is mandatory for students who are on academic probation.
            -Weekly tutoring will be made mandatory for you if your grades on Quiz 1 are 70% or less and if the grades continue to stay the same on subsequent exams.
      Your tutors are paid by our department to provide students with study strategies, guidance on how to problem solve, and provide general encouragement. Tutoring sessions are not lectures or regurgitation of Canvas content. You are expected to come prepared to tutoring sessions with questions and demonstrating your effort in how you understand a concept.

      .Instructions
            -Contact your tutor to schedule a time to meet with them in their small group sessions.
            -Tutors have limited time to meet with their assigned groups, therefore, only meet with your assigned tutor.
            -Learners are NOT allowed to request tests from previous classes. If this occurs, the learner and tutor will be penalized according to the University of Pittsburgh's policy on Academic Integrity (refer to syllabus).

                  Introduction
                        -This Neuroscience handbook was developed for students to use as a self-study guide throughout the Neuroscience course as well as the Neuromuscular Physical Therapy course series in the DPT program. It provides study prompts covering all the content that you will be expected to know throughout the duration of this course. This handbook is most effective when used in conjunction with asynchronous lectures, live session discussions, and required textbook readings. Use this guide to take notes and create your own study materials as you progress through the course and program.

                  Module 1
                        Nervous System Organization Lecture
                              -Introduction to Nervous System
                              -Describe the divisions of the Nervous system
                              -Describe the general parts of the brain
                              -Describe the general parts of the spinal cord
                              -Describe the divisions of the peripheral nervous system

                        Embryology and Nervous System Development Lecture
                              -Describe the three developmental stages in utero
                              -Explain the Pre-Embryonic Stage
                              -Explain the Embryonic Stage
                              -Explain the Fetal Stage
                              -Define ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm

                        Neural Tube Formation Lecture
                              -Describe the formation of neural tube
                              -Describe the formation other developing structures in relation to neural tube
                              -Explain the Neurodevelopmental disorders

                        Brain Formation Lecture
                              -Describe the primary brain vesicles
                              -Describe the secondary brain vesicles
                              -Explain the differentiation of Telencephalon and Diencephalon
                              -Explain the differentiation of Midbrain
                              -Explain the differentiation of Hindbrain
                              -Explain the differential of Spinal Cord
                              -Associate the developmental regions of forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain with their respective structures in the adult brain

                        Neuroimaging Lecture
                              -Describe the following Neuroimaging Techniques:
                                    -Computed Tomography (CT)
                                    -Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
                                    -Positron Emission Tomography (PET)
                                    -Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) 
                                    -Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI)
                              -Compare and contrast the advantages and disadvantages of different neuroimaging techniques

                  Module 2
                        Neuron Structure Lecture
                              -Define a neuron
                              -Describe the parts of a neuron
                              -Define the types of neurons

                        Neuron Communication Lecture
                              -Describe neuronal communication
                              -Define Resting Membrane Potential
                              -Define Local Potential
                              -Define Action Potential
                              -Describe the propagation of Action Potential
                              -Explain the factors that influence the Action Potential
                              -Explain the difference between convergence and divergence of neuronal input

                        Synapse Lecture
                              -Describe the structure of synapse
                              -Describe the types of synapses
                              -Describe the synaptic transmission 
                              -Explain the regulation of synaptic transmission
                              -Explain the post synaptic potential
                              -Explain the presynaptic facilitation and inhibition

                        Neuromessengers Lecture
                              -Define neurotransmitter
                              -Define neuromodulator
                              -Describe the site of action, effect of binding and associated disorder related to neurotransmitters and neuromodulators 

                        Supporting Cells Lecture
                              -Define Glia
                              -Explain the functions of glia
                              -Describe Astrocytes and their functions
                              -Describe Oligodendrocytes and their functions
                              -Describe Schwann cells and their functions
                              -Explain the functions of microglia
                              -Explain the clinical application of role of glia in neuroinflammation
                              -Explain the clinical application of demyelination in CNS and PNS

                        Neuroplasticity Lecture
                              -Define Neuroplasticity 
                              -Explain the purpose of neuroplasticity
                              -Describe Habituation 
                              -Describe Experience Dependent Plasticity and its mechanisms:
                                    -Long Term Potentiation
                                    -Long Term Depression

                        Neuroplasticity: Cellular Recovery Lecture
                              -Describe the role of neuroplasticity in cellular recovery
                              -Describe Axonal Injury and recovery in CNS
                              -Describe Axonal Injury and recovery in PNS
                              -Explain the difference between the axon recovery in CNS Vs PNS
                              -Explain the role of neuroplasticity in rehabilitation

                  Module 3
                        External Morphology of the Brain – Lateral View, Inferior, and Medial View Lectures
                              -Identify the primary and association areas in the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes of the cerebral cortex and their respective functions.
                              -Identify Brodmann areas for primary sensory and motor cortices.
                              -Describe the structures and functions of the limbic lobe.
                              -Identify the structures at the levels of diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon, and myelencephalon.

                        Supportive Brain Structures Lecture
                              -Describe the layers of the meninges and the spaces associated with them.
                              -Identify the dural reflections and the components of the brain that they support.
                              -Identify and describe the flow of the major dural venous sinuses.
                              -Identify the ventricles and the flow of CSF throughout the ventricular system.

                        Cerebral Blood Supply Lecture
                              -Identify the components of the anterior intracranial circulation and posterior intracranial circulation.
                              -Describe the purpose of arterial anastomoses.
                              -Identify the structures that are supplied by the anterior cerebral artery, middle cerebral artery, posterior cerebral artery, vertebral artery, anterior inferior cerebellar artery, posterior inferior cerebellar artery, and branches of the basilar artery.
                              -Given a lesion to an artery listed above, describe the resulting deficits.

                        Internal Morphology of the Brain Lecture
                              -Identify the ventricles, major white matter structures, and structures of the basal ganglia in horizontal and coronal brain sections.
                              -Identify brainstem structures such as the red nucleus, substantia nigra, basilar pons, and pyramids in coronal sections.

                        Brainstem and Cerebellum Lecture
                              -Identify major structures on the ventral aspect of the brainstem at the levels of diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon, and myelencephalon.
                              -Identify major structures on the dorsal aspect of the brainstem at the levels of diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon, and myelencephalon.
                              -Describe the 3 major functional roles of the cerebellum.
                              -Identify the functional divisions of the cerebellum, and functions.
                              -Identify the deep cerebellar nuclei and their associated functional divisions.

                        Brainstem Cross-Sections Lecture
                              -Identify and describe the information transmitted via the major ascending and descending pathways using brainstem cross-sections.
                              -Identify the cranial nerves and cranial nerve nuclei (and recall functions) using brainstem cross-sections.
                              -Identify cerebellar peduncles and tracts using brainstem cross sections.
                              -If an area of the brainstem is lesioned, describe the resulting deficits.

                        Spinal Cord Lecture
                              -Describe the general blood supply of the spinal cord.
                              -Identify the major ascending and descending tracts using spinal cord cross sections.
                              -Describe the divisions of dorsal roots and the sensory information carried in each.

                  Introduction

                  This handbook will serve as your guide to the neuroanatomy components of Neuroscience. This handbook includes all the structures that you will be expected to know and identify. Please refer to this handbook to help you identify the structures using your Netter Anatomy Atlas and Haines Neuroanatomy Atlas and to correctly determine the function of each structure. The information included here will also be covered in asynchronous videos and live sessions, as well as in your immersion labs. Please feel free to make your own notes within the handbook as you move through each module and to use this as a study guide for quizzes and exams.
                   
                  Neuroanatomy

                  External Morphology of Cerebral Cortex (Haines Atlas Chapter 2)

                  Structural Organization 
                  Sulci (grooves)   
                  Gyri (convolutions)

                  Major Anatomical Subdivisions
                  Two hemispheres (right and left) 
                  o      divided by the longitudinal fissure
                  Four lobes to each hemisphere 
                  o     Frontal, Parietal, Temporal, Occipital
                  Insula: deep to temporal lobe (retract lateral sulcus to observe)
                  Limbic lobe: not a true lobe but rather a “functional” lobe; a ring of structures surrounding the corpus callosum

                  Major Functional Subdivisions
                  Primary Areas (10% of cortex):
                  o      Motor
                  o      Somatosensory 
                  o     Visual
                  o     Auditory 
                  o     Broca’s Area (motor speech) 
                  o     Wernicke’s Area (speech perception)
                  Association Areas (90% of cortex): 
                  o     Frontal Association Area (Premotor, Prefrontal)
                  o     Supplemental Motor 
                  o     Parietal Association Areas (Posterior Parietal, Inferior Parietal) 
                  o     Occipitotemporal Area

                  Frontal Lobe (lateral view)
                  Posterior border is the central sulcus, which divides the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe
                  Inferior border is the lateral sulcus, which divides the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes
                  Major functions include movement planning, programming movement, executive function, personality, desire, consequences of action, motor aspects of speech, attention/awareness, and voluntary conjugate eye movements

                  STRUCTURE   BRODMANN’S
                  AREA  FUNCTIONAL AREA   FUNCTION(S)
                  Precentral gyrus  4     Primary motor cortex    Execution of movement
                  Superior Frontal gyrus        Lateral pre-motor area (posterior region of gyrus anterior to area 4)   Motor programming, sensory guidance of limb movements, initiation and sequencing of movement
                  Middle Frontal gyrus          Frontal Eye Fields (posterior region of middle & posterior superior frontal gyrus)  Voluntary eye movements and conjugate gaze
                  Inferior Frontal gyrus
                  Pars Opercularis & Pars Triangularis      44
                  45    Broca’s Area      Motor aspects of speech
                  Prefrontal area               Executive function, motor planning


                  Parietal Lobe (lateral view)
                  Anterior border is the central sulcus
                  Posterior border is the parietal-occipital line (imaginary line drawn between the preoccipital notch and the superior aspect of the parietal-occipital sulcus from the medial surface of the brain)
                  Major functions include somatosensation, higher perceptions (integration) related to external sensory inputs (mainly from somatic, visual, and hearing areas)

                  STRUCTURE   BRODMANN’S
                  AREA  FUNCTIONAL AREA   FUNCTION(S)
                  Postcentral gyrus 3,1,2 Primary somatosensory area    Primary somatosensory area

                  Superior Parietal Lobule      5,7   Sensory association area      Integrates sensory and motor functions and aids in programming complex motor functions (with premotor cortex)
                  Inferior Parietal lobule
                     Supramarginal gyrus
                   
                  Angular gyrus     
                  40
                  39          Receive input from auditory and visual cortices and perform higher complex perceptions and spatial relations; dominant in left hemisphere

                  Occipital Lobe (lateral view)
                  Anterior border is parietal-occipital line
                  Major functions include primary visual cortex and visual association areas

                  STRUCTURE   BRODMANN’S
                  AREA  FUNCTIONAL AREA   FUNCTION(S)
                  Lateral Occipital gyri  17
                  18,19 Primary visual cortex (distal tip of lobe)
                  Visual Association areas (anterior portion of lobe)   
                  Vision; organize/integrate visual stimuli

                  Temporal Lobe (lateral view)
                  Inferior to the lateral sulcus
                  Major functions include hearing, understanding speech, language, perception of moving objects and recognition of faces

                  STRUCTURE   BRODMANN’S
                  AREA  FUNCTIONAL AREA   FUNCTION(S)
                  Superior Temporal gyrus 22    Wernicke’s Area (posterior portion of gyrus)    Associated with understanding speech (perception)
                  Transverse Temporal gyri of Heschl  41
                  42    Primary auditory cortex 
                  Auditory Association area     Hearing
                  Speech and language comprehension
                  Middle Temporal gyrus               Associated with perception of moving objects in the visual field, memory
                  Inferior Temporal gyrus             Recognition of faces, memory

                  Inferior View Brain Structures 

                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION(S)
                  Olfactory tract and bulb      Relays information related to sense of smell
                  Orbital gyri      Prefrontal areas associated with limbic lobe
                  Parahippocampal gyrus   Plays large role in memory and learning
                  Occipitotemporal gyri   Assists with processing of color information, face/body recognition, word recognition
                  Uncus Landmark for the amygdala – role in behavior in context
                  Longitudinal fissure    Divides the cerebral hemispheres


                  Medial View Brain Structures (Haines Atlas Chapter 2)

                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION(S)
                  Paracentral lobule      Primary motor and somatosensory for lower extremities (Les); bisected by central sulcus; most anterior aspect is supplemental motor area
                  Superior Frontal gyrus  Supplemental Motor Area (SMA) – involving motor programming
                  Cingulate sulcus  Separates superior frontal gyrus from cingulate gyrus
                  Cingulate gyrus   Emotions and “drive”
                  Precuneus   Sensory association area; Marginal branch of cingulate sulcus is the anterior border and the Parieto-occipital sulcus is the posterior border
                  Cuneus      Vision; upper and lower banks of the calcarine sulcus are primary vision (striate cortex); on either side of primary vision is vision association area (extrastriate cortex)

                  Limbic “lobe” (medial view)
                  Functional lobe made up of a number of functionally related structures
                  Involved in emotions, memory, behavior
                  Found in the area that surrounds the cingulate gyrus

                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION(S)
                  Cingulate gyrus   Emotions and “drive”
                  Parahippocampal gyrus (hippocampus) Deep to the gyrus is the hippocampus; Memory
                  Uncus (amygdala)  Deep to the uncus is the amygdala; emotional memories and behavior; structure can herniate through tentorial notch with high intracranial pressure
                  Subcallosal area/Paraolfactory gyri Part of functional limbic lobe

                  Diencephalon
                  Region surrounding/or in proximity to the thalamus (medial view)

                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION(S)
                  Thalamus    Multifunctional - Relays sensory/motor information, sensory processing, regulation of sleep and wakefulness, consciousness, mood                                                       
                  Hypothalamus      Activities related to autonomic nervous system, metabolic processes, pituitary function
                  Mammillary body   Aspects of memory
                  Anterior commissure     Shares information (olfactory) between hemispheres
                  Fornix (body and columns)     Connects mammillary body to hippocampus
                  Pineal body Role in modulating sleep, pain modulation, stress, learning
                  Posterior commissure    Shares information (pupillary reflexes) between hemispheres
                  Corpus callosum (rostrum, genu, body, splenium) Large white matter structure which shares info between hemispheres
                  Septum pellucidum Thin membrane separating anterior horns of the lateral ventricles

                  Mesencephalon (Midbrain)
                  Region in proximity to cerebral aqueduct (medial view)
                   NOTE:  In the following regions of the posterior fossa brainstem (midbrain, pons and medulla) two general terms are often used to describe the ‘roof’ or tectum and ‘floor’ or tegmentum of the region.  For example, the tectum of the midbrain, is the roof in the midbrain.   You will identify specific structures in the tectum of the midbrain.  

                  Text in italics indicates structures or parts of structures that are difficult to identify from the medial view, but we will explore in more detail in future labs


                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION/OTHER INFORMATION
                  Tectum (corpora quadrigemina) “roof” over cerebral aqueduct
                     Superior Colliculus  Associated with Vision
                     Inferior colliculus  Associated with Audition
                  Midbrain tegmentum (externally= cerebral peduncles/crus cerebri)  “floor” of midbrain, pathway to/from cortex and brainstem
                  Interpeduncular fossa   Space between the two cerebral peduncles

                  Metencephalon (Pons)
                  Region within proximity to the pons (medial view)

                  STRUCTURE   FUNTION/OTHER INFORMATION
                  Basilar pons      Ventral to floor of 4th ventricle
                  Floor of 4th ventricle (Pontine tegmentum)      
                  Roof of 4th ventricle (Pontine tectum)    Cerebellar structures

                  Myelencephalon (Medulla)
                  Region within proximity to the medulla

                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION/OTHER INFORMATION
                  Pyramids (ventral),  (medullary olives)   Descending path for motor function to body
                  Pyramidal decussation   Crossing of descending motor fibers near the junction of the medulla and the spinal cord
                  Sensory fibers (gracile/cuneate fasciculus) (dorsal)  Ascending sensory fibers from LE/UE

                  Supportive Structures of the Brain

                  Meninges 
                  Support and protect the central nervous system (CNS); comprised of 3 layers
                  Layers: from external to internal
                  o     Dura mater (periosteal and meningeal layers): tough, outermost layer
                  o     Arachnoid: highly vascular
                  o     Pia mater: adheres to brain tissue

                  Spaces associated with the meninges
                  Epidural space: between inner table of the skull and dura mater
                  Subdural space: between dura mater and arachnoid
                  Subarachnoid space: between the arachnoid and pia mater, location of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)

                  Dural Reflections 
                  Reflections formed by meningeal layer of dura mater reflecting away from periosteal layer, pulling with it the other 2 layers of the meninges (arachnoid and pia mater) to form a 6-layered dural reflection.
                  Falx cerebri: dural reflection that provides support between the right and left cerebral hemispheres
                  o     Anterior attachment at the crista galli, additionally attached along the superior and posterior aspects of the  skull
                  Tentorium cerebelli: dural reflection positioned like a ‘roof over the posterior fossa’, and supports the cerebral hemispheres from below (lies above of the cerebellum)
                  o     Anterior attachment at anterior clinoid process and posterior aspect of sella turcica; posterior attachment along the groove for transverse sinus
                  o     Tentorial notch: opening in the tentorium cerebelli that allows for the brainstem to freely pass through dural reflection into the posterior cranial fossa
                  Falx cerebelli: dural reflection that lies between and supports the smaller cerebellar hemispheres

                  Dural Venous Sinuses
                  System for draining blood from brain, sinuses formed in the borders of the dural reflections, returns deoxygenated blood back to the heart
                  Venous sinuses: superior sagittal sinus, inferior sagittal sinus, straight sinus, transverse sinuses, sigmoid sinuses, cavernous sinus
                   Venous drainage pathways of the brain ultimately to internal jugular vein to leave the brain:
                  o     superior sagittal sinus → right transverse sinus → right sigmoid sinus → right internal jugular vein
                  o     inferior sagittal sinus → straight sinus → left transverse sinus → left sigmoid sinus → left internal jugular vein
                  o     deep cerebral structures → great cerebral vein of Galen → straight sinus → left transverse sinus → left sigmoid sinus → left internal jugular vein
                  Ventricular System 
                  Located within the cerebral hemispheres and brainstem
                  ‘Floats and bathes the brain’ and provides nutrients to brain
                  Closed space within the center of brain tissue, continuous with the subarachnoid space
                  Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is made in the roof of the ventricles, circulates and is reabsorbed into the venous blood through specializations of the arachnoid (arachnoid villi) into the superior sagittal sinus.
                  Ventricles of the brain (4):
                  o     Lateral ventricles (2): “C-shaped” ventricle that underlies each cerebral hemisphere; communicates with third ventricle via the interventricular foramen 
                  o     Third ventricle: midline, central ventricle between the right and left sides of thalamus
                  o     Cerebral aqueduct: underlies the midbrain; passageway for CSF from third to fourth ventricle
                  o     Fourth ventricle: triangular shaped ventricle overlies the pons and medulla and under the cerebellum
                  o     Lateral apertures (2): lateral exits for CSF from 4th ventricle, surrounds hemispheres
                  o     Median aperture: single midline exit for CSF to circulate around the spinal cord
                  o     Lumbar cistern: expanded subarachnoid space below the tip of the spinal canal

                  Relationship of ventricles to regions of the brain/brainstem where they are located:

                  Ventricular System Structure  Associated Brain Region
                  Lateral ventricles      cerebral hemispheres
                  Third ventricle   thalamus and hypothalamus
                  Cerebral aqueduct midbrain
                  Fourth ventricle  pons/cerebellum/medulla

                  Intracranial Circulation (Haines Atlas Chapter 2)

                  Arterial Anastomoses
                  Sharing of blood supply between arterial systems
                  1.    Circle of Willis: communication of anterior to posterior circulation systems
                  2.    Corticomeningeal (leptomeningeal) Anastomosis: overlap of ACA, MCA, and PCA on superior/lateral cerebral hemispheres; referred to as the “watershed” area

                  Anterior Intracranial Circulation
                  Stems from the internal carotid artery system       

                  Internal carotid artery
                  Branches:

                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION/OTHER INFORMATION
                  Anterior cerebral artery (ACA)      Supplies the medial brain surface (frontal/parietal lobes)
                  Anterior communicating artery       Joins the two ACA’s
                  Middle cerebral artery (MCA)  Supplies the lateral brain surface (frontal/parietal/upper temporal)
                  Posterior communicating artery      Connects anterior circulation to the posterior circulation via Posterior cerebral artery

                  Posterior Intracranial Circulation
                  Stems from the vertebrobasilar system

                  Vertebral arteries (right and left)
                  Gives rise to branches (below) but also supplies lateral regions medulla

                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION/OTHER INFORMATION
                  Anterior spinal artery  Supplies ventral two-thirds of spinal cord and ventral caudal medulla
                  Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)     Blood supply to inferior cerebellum and dorsolateral medulla

                  Basilar artery
                  Gives rise to branches below but also supplies medial pons via paramedian basilar branches, and serves the lateral aspects of the pons via short and long circumferential basilar branches

                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION/OTHER INFORMATION
                  Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA)      Supplies ventral cerebellum and dorsolateral mid-lower pons
                  Pontine arteries  Blood supply to pons via paramedian (medial) and short and long circumferential (lateral) basilar branches
                  Superior cerebellar artery    Supplies superior cerebellum, midbrain structures, superior & middle cerebellar peduncles
                  Posterior cerebral artery (PCA)     Blood supply to midbrain, hypothalamus, thalamus, occipital lobe (visual cortex)/inferior temporal gyrus


                  Ventral View of Brainstem (Haines Atlas page 22)

                  Diencephalon
                  Find the optic nerve, chiasm, and tract – this helps to identify the diencephalon region

                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION/OTHER INFORMATION
                  Mammillary body   Connected to hippocampus via fornix, role in memory
                  Infundibular stalk      Communicates info from hypothalamus to pituitary gland
                  Optic Nerve (CN II)     Communicates visual information from the eye
                  Optic chiasm      Crossing axons of the optic nerve from both eyes
                  Optic tracts      Carries axons of optic nerve to the lateral geniculate nucleus (after the chiasm)
                  Olfactory tract   Associated with sense of smell

                  Mesencephalon (Midbrain)
                  The “space” below the optic chiasm is the interpeduncular fossa, which represents the midbrain region
                  On either side of the “space”, identify the cerebral peduncles
                  This structure is a main white matter “highway” for ascending and descending information to pass to/from the brainstem from/to the cerebral hemispheres

                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION/OTHER INFORMATION
                  Cerebral peduncles      Major white matter pathway for descending from cerebral hemisphere to brain stem
                  Interpeduncular fossa   Space between cerebral peduncles; exit for CN3
                  Oculomotor nerve (CN III)     Extra-ocular eye movements (up, down, in, up/in) 
                  Trochlear nerve (CN IV) Exits brainstem dorsally, eye movement (down/in)

                  Metencephalon (Pons)
                  The ventral aspect of the pons is the basilar pons (the basilar artery runs vertically up the surface of this portion of the pons)
                  From this aspect of the pons, many cranial nerves can be identified on its superior, lateral, and inferior borders

                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION/OTHER INFORMATION
                  Middle cerebellar peduncle    Communicates info from cerebrum to cerebellum via pontine nuclei and fibers
                  Trigeminal nerve (CN V) Sensation to face, muscles of mastication
                  Abducens nerve (CN VI)  Eye movement (laterally)
                  Facial nerve (CN VII)   Facial muscles (expression) and taste
                  Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)   Hearing/Balance (position in space)
                  Cerebellopontine angle  Aspects of the cerebellum, pons, and medulla converge; region of CN’s VII, VIII

                  Myelencephalon (Medulla)
                  Sitting directly beneath the basilar pons is the ventral aspect of the medulla
                  Ventrally, the medulla has two “bumps” that sit superior-laterally – these are the olives of the medulla
                  Cranial nerves 9-12 will exit either in-front (pre-olivary) of or behind (retro-olivary) the olives

                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION/OTHER INFORMATION
                  Pyramids/ Pyramidal decussation     Ventral descending motor pathway/ crossing of pathway
                  Olive Gives rise to climbing fibers to cerebellum
                  Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)    Located in front of olive, tongue movements
                  Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)      Sensory information for pharynx, taste
                  Vagus nerve (CN X)      Swallowing, vocal cords, breathing, cardiac information, gag reflex
                  Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)      Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles

                   
                  Dorsal View of Brainstem (Haines Atlas page 30)

                  The dorsal brainstem is identified by looking for the corpora quadrigemina, or the opened section of the 4th ventricle

                  Diencephalon
                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION/OTHER INFORMATION
                  Lateral geniculate nucleus    Associated with vision & superior colliculus
                  Medial geniculate nucleus     Associated with audition & inferior colliculus

                  Mesencephalon (Midbrain)
                  STRUCTURE   FUNCTION/OTHER INFORMATION
                  Tectum: superior and inferior colliculus  Forms “roof” over the cerebral aqueduct; assoc. vision/hearing respectively
                  Brachium of superior and inferior colliculi     Pathways connecting colliculi to geniculate nuclei
                  Trochlear nerve (exit toward ventral brainstem) Eye movement (down/in)
                  Cerebral peduncles      Major white matter pathway for descending from cerebral hemisphere to brain stem

                  Cerebellar Structures (Haines Atlas pages 34-35)

                  3 Major Functional Roles
                  Coordination of movement (timing/pattern of muscle activation during movement)
                  Maintenance of equilibrium (inputs from vestibular system)
                  Regulation of muscle tone (oversees spinal cord/brainstem postural control structures)

                  Major Structures
                  Cortex: Grey matter (periphery)
                  Medullary Center: White matter (nerve fibers to cortex, from cortex to deep nuclei, from one cortical area to another
                  Deep Nuclei: 4 pairs:  1) Fastigial nucleus, 2) Globose nucleus, 3) Emboliform nucleus (2 & 3 together referred to as Interposed nucleus), and 4) Dentate nucleus
                  Peduncles: afferent and efferent white matter pathways (nerve fibers) to and from various brainstem regions
                  o     Superior Cerebellar peduncle – Midbrain 
                  o     Middle Cerebellar Peduncle – Pons 
                  o     Inferior Cerebellar Peduncle – Medulla

                  Cerebellar Lobes (3 Lobes)
                  Anterior lobe: smaller lobe located superiorly
                  Posterior lobe: larger lobe 
                  Flocculonodular Lobe: consists of two structures, the left and right flocculus and the nodulus (midline) of the cerebellum
                  Primary fissure: separates smaller anterior lobe from larger posterior cerebellar lobe

                  Structure   Information NOTES
                  Anterior Lobe     Smaller lobe (superior) 
                  Posterior Lobe    Larger lobe       
                  Primary Fissure   Separates anterior lobe from posterior lobe     
                  Vermis (vermal region)  Midline, 1 vermal region      Postural control, coordination during activity, proximal limb and trunk control
                  Paravermis (paravermal region)      Sits on either side of the vermis, 2 paravermal regions     Postural control, coordination during activity, distal limb control
                  Lateral Cerebellar Hemispheres      Sits on either side of the paravermis, 2 hemispheres  Refining voluntary movement, motor planning, limbs
                  Flocculus (2)     Part of flocculonodular lobe, associated with balance and vestibular related information  Balance adjustments, eye movements in response to vestibular inputs
                  Nodulus (1) Part of flocculonodular lobe, associated with balance and vestibular related information  Balance adjustments, eye movements in response to vestibular inputs
                  Tonsil (2)  most posterior, caudal aspect of cerebellum     Can herniate thru foramen magnum with increased intracranial pressure
                  Superior Cerebellar peduncle (2)    Primarily outgoing information      To midbrain, and onto cortex
                  Middle Cerebellar peduncle (2)      Primarily incoming information      From cortex to pons to lateral cerebellar hemispheres
                  Inferior Cerebellar peduncle (2)    Primarily incoming information from spinal cord From spinal cord to vermal and paravermal cerebellum

                  Corpus callosum   Large white matter structure that shares information between hemispheres

                  In charge of voluntary emotional expression and cognition processing

                  Ascending/Descending Pathways

                  Overview of Spinal Cord Anatomy

                  Anatomic Organization of the Spinal Cord
                  31 pairs of spinal nerves
                  8 cervical
                  12 thoracic
                  5 lumbar
                  5 sacral
                  1 coccygeal
                  Conus medullaris: tapered end of the spinal cord, L1-2 level
                  Cauda equina: bundle of spinal nerves which exit the conus
                  Central canal: obex serves as beginning of central canal, continuous with 4th ventricle

                  Grey Matter: consists of cell bodies and synapses
                  Cervical and lumbar enlargements of the ventral horn of grey matter due to serving limbs
                  Thoracic: prominent intermediate grey 
                  o     lateral horns: intermediolateral cell column of pre-ganglionic sympathetic fibers

                  White matter: consists of axons (pathways relaying information)
                  White matter regions: Dorsal columns, Lateral columns, Ventral Columns
                  Lumbar has less white matter than grey, thoracic primarily white matter, cervical has less grey
                  matter compared to white matter (all information from lower body/trunk passes through
                  cervical level)

                  Blood supply
                  Anterior spinal artery (1): supplies anterior 2/3 of spinal cord, and medial medulla
                  Posterior spinal arteries (2): each supply posterior 1/6 of spinal cord, dorsal medulla
                  Rami of segmental arteries: pierce dura to run to the spinal cord

                  Meninges: same as those covering the brain and continuous with peripheral nerve coverings

                  Divisions of Dorsal Root Fibers
                  Medial division fibers
                  Enter the posterior-medial white matter of dorsal spinal cord
                  Fiber characteristics: large fiber afferents and heavily myelinated
                  Fibers relay sensory information such as vibration, joint position sense, discriminative touch, as well as non-conscious sensory information from the body to the brainstem and cerebellum
                  Lateral division fibers
                  Enter the small white matter tract of Lissauer’s (immediately prior to the dorsal horn gray matter), ascends/descend 1-2 levels and then enters and synapses in the dorsal horn gray matter of the spinal cord
                  Fiber characteristics: small fiber afferents and are lightly or non-myelinated 
                  Fibers relay sensory information related to pain/temperature from the body to the brainstem

                  Propriospinal Tracts:  interneurons forming a white matter pathway surrounding the perimeter of the ventral horn, which relay/shares information across a few (short) or many (long) spinal segments in both directions
                  o     Propriospinal neurons have a cell body in one spinal segment and an axon terminating in another spinal segment
                  o     Short propriospinal tract neurons: connect neighboring segments; travel dorsolaterally and tend to communicate between lateral motor neurons (info from descending dorsolateral tracts)
                  o     Long propriospinal tract neurons: travel longer distances to more remote spinal segments; travel ventromedially and tend to communicate between medial motor neurons

                  Ascending 3-Neuron Sensory Tracts
                  Ascending 3-Neuron pathways to the cortex. These tracts contain three neurons from beginning to end of tract.

                  Dorsal Column Medial Lemniscus (DCML) Tract (Haines Atlas pages 192-195): carries ascending somatosensory information regarding vibration, joint position and discriminative touch from the body to the cerebral cortex.

                  Ordered neuron    Origin      Division of
                  Dorsal Root Enters SC   Travels     Synapses/
                  Terminates
                  1st   Periphery, sensory receptors (Merkel disc, Pacinian &  Meissner corpuscles)   Medial      Dorsal white
                  matter      Ascends via dorsal columns (gracile/cuneate fasciculi); LE is medial and UE lateral Synapses in Dorsal column nuclei (gracile/cuneate tubercles) in caudal medulla
                  2nd   Dorsal column nuclei (gracile/cuneate tubercles)      N/A   N/A   Crosses at level of nuclei and ascends as a combined bundle of white matter fibers (Medial Lemniscus) to the thalamus   Synapses in the Ventral Posterior Lateral (VPL) nucleus of thalamus
                  3rd   VPL of thalamus   N/A   N/A   Exits the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus, enters Post. Limb of Internal Capsule, travels to cerebral white matter   Terminates in Cerebral cortex, post-central gyrus (areas 3, 1, 2)

                  SOMETHING TO NOTE: Right-sided body sensory information ascends to the right dorsal column nuclei, crosses out of the nuclei to the left side of the brainstem and ultimately terminates in the left post-central gyrus.  So, if your patient had a right-sided spinal cord lesion, what side of the body would their sensory deficit be located?  What if they had a lesion to the left pons?

                  Spinothalamic (SPTH) Tract Component of Anterolateral System (ALS) (Haines Atlas pages 196-199): spinothalamic tract carries ascending sensory information regarding pain and temperature from the body to the cerebral cortex

                  Ordered neuron    Origin      Division of
                  Dorsal Root Enters SC   Travels     Synapses/
                  Terminates
                  1st   Peripheral sensory receptors (nociceptors)      Lateral     Lissauer’s tract, ascends 1-2 levels, then synapses in gray matter of dorsal horn of SC   Ascends 1-2 levels within Lissauer’s tract before entering spinal cord gray matter to synapse.  Synapses in gray matter of dorsal horn of spinal cord
                  2nd   Dorsal horn gray matter of spinal cord    N/A   N/A   Crosses spinal cord via the ventral white commissure to join the contralateral white matter bundle (ALS/SPTH), and then ascends to the VPL of the thalamus  Synapses in VPL of thalamus
                  3rd   VPL of the thalamus     N/A   N/A   Exits the VPL of thalamus and enters the Post. Limb of Internal capsule, ascends to cerebral white matter   Terminates in cerebral cortex, post-central gyrus (sensory) and widespread cortical areas
                  SOMETHING TO NOTE: Second order neurons of ALS (not SPTH tract fibers) also deliver information to other brainstem centers:
                  Spinoreticular tract fibers- reticular formation nuclei (pain modulation)
                  Spinomesencephalic tract fibers- tectum of the midbrain (pain modulation, limbic, eye movement in response to pain)

                  Ascending 2-Neuron Pathways to the Cerebellum (Haines Atlas pages 242-243)
                  These tracts contain 2 neurons from beginning to end.  All three Spinocerebellar tracts carry information regarding unconscious (non-conscious) proprioception information from muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs to the cerebellum, thus they do not terminate in the cerebral hemispheres, and therefore not “perceived” as sensation by the individual (unlike previous 2 pathways).

                  Three Spinocerebellar Tracts
                  Dorsal Spinocerebellar Tract 
                  o     Muscle spindle info about LE (individual/groups of muscles) 

                  Dorsal Spinocerebellar (DSCT): non-conscious information from LE/trunk (below C8)
                  Ordered neuron    Origin      Division of
                  Dorsal Root Enters SC   Travels     Synapses/
                  Terminates
                  1st   Muscle spindles of trunk/LE   Medial      Dorsal white matter of the spinal cord    Travels ventrally towards the  intermediate gray of the spinal cord, Clarke’s nucleus (T1-L3 segments)      Synapses in Clarke’s nucleus in the intermediate gray of SC
                  2nd   Clarke’s nucleus  N/A   N/A   Exits nucleus and moves laterally to the dorsolateral perimeter of ipsilateral spinal cord white matter to ascends as a fiber bundle called the DSCT, ascends to inferior cerebellar peduncle   Enters ICP to terminate in ipsilateral cerebellum

                  Cuneocerebellar Tract
                  o     Muscle spindle info about UE (individual/groups of muscles)

                  Cuneocerebellar tract: non-conscious information from UE’s & trunk (C8 and above)
                  Ordered neuron    Origin      Division of
                  Dorsal Root Enters SC   Travels     Synapses/
                  Terminates
                  1st   Muscle spindles of UE/upper trunk   Medial      Dorsal white matter of spinal cord  Enters the lateral aspect of SC and immediately ascends as a white matter bundle lateral to the cuneate fasciculus, ascends to lower medulla and enters the Accessory Cuneate Nucleus     Synapses in Accessory Cuneate Nucleus (ipsilateral)
                  2nd   Accessory cuneate nucleus     N/A   N/A   Exits nucleus and ascends to the inferior cerebellar peduncle     Terminates in ipsilateral cerebellum

                  Ventral Spinocerebellar Tract
                  o     Golgi organ LE and UE (whole limb movement & postural adjustment)

                  Ventral Spinocerebellar (VSCT) tract: nonconscious information whole limb/body
                  Ordered neuron    Origin      Division of
                  Dorsal Root Enters SC   Travels     Synapses/
                  Terminates
                  1st   Golgi tendon organ UE/LE      Medial      Dorsal white matter of SC     Travels ventrally to spinal border neurons in the lateral region of intermediate gray of SC     Synapses on spinal border neurons
                  2nd   Spinal border neurons of intermediate gray      N/A   N/A   Crosses via ventral white commissure to contralateral white matter perimeter pathway (VSCT), ascends to level of superior cerebellar peduncle, crosses again to enter cerebellum    Terminates in the cerebellum (on the side from where the first order neuron originated)


                  Ascending sensory information for the face (Haines Atlas pages 202-205)
                  3-order Neuron pathway of the Trigeminothalamic Tract:  sensation from the face travels in a different pathway to the cortex
                  o     Provides somatosensory inputs from anterior two thirds of the head via 2 distinct sub-pathways: (1) pain & temperature, and (2) touch, pressure, vibration, and position sense that eventually combine to make up the trigeminothalamic tract which terminates in the inferior-lateral post-central gyrus.

                  Sub-Pathway 1
                  Pain & Temperature pathway of the trigeminothalamic tract:
                  Ordered neuron    Origin      Location of cell body for 1st order neuron      Enters brainstem  Travels     Synapses/
                  Terminates
                  1st   Sensory receptors of the face Trigeminal ganglion near mid/upper Pons   Via Trigeminal nerve (CN5)    Enters pons and descends within the spinal trigeminal tract to enter the spinal trigeminal nucleus    Synapses in spinal trigeminal nucleus (which runs from mid-pons to upper SC)
                  2nd   Spinal trigeminal nucleus     N/A   N/A   Crosses out of nucleus and ascends in the trigeminothalamic tract to the VPM of the thalamus    Synapses in  VPM of the thalamus
                  3rd   VPM of thalamus   N/A   N/A   Exits the VPM to enter the Post. Limb of Internal capsule, and ascends thru cerebral white matter     Terminates in the inferior-lateral aspect of post-central gyrus
                  SOMETHING TO NOTE: Right-sided sensory information from the face enters the right Trigeminal nerve and descends to the spinal trigeminal nucleus of V, synapses and then crosses to the left side of the brainstem to ascend as the trigeminothalamic tract to the VPM of the thalamus, and eventually the left post central gyrus.  So if a patient had a right CN 5 lesion, what side of the face would the sensory deficit be found?  What if they had a left midbrain lesion? 

                  Sub-Pathway 2 
                  Vibration, position-sense, and discriminative touch pathway of trigeminothalamic tract
                  Ordered neuron    Origin      Location of cell body for 1st order neuron      Enters Brainstem  Travels     Synapses/
                  Terminates
                  1st   Sensory receptors in the face Trigeminal ganglion near mid/upper Pons   Via Trigeminal nerve    Enters pons and slightly ascends to enter the ipsilateral Chief sensory nucleus of V      Synapses in ipsilateral Chief/Sensory nucleus of V
                  2nd   Chief /Sensory nucleus of V   N/A   N/A   Exits the nucleus and crosses to join  the trigeminothalamic tract, ascends to the VPM of the thalamus      Synapses in the VPM of the thalamus
                  3rd   VPM of thalamus   N/A   N/A   Exits VPM to enter Post. Limb of internal capsule, ascends thru cerebral white matter     Terminates in the inferior-lateral post-central gyrus
                  SOMETHING TO NOTE: The lower aspects (spinal cord through mid-pons) of the crossed trigeminothalamic tract carries ONLY pain/temperature information.  Not until you get to the level of the mid-to-upper pons, does the other sensory information join the tract.  

                  The descending motor component of trigeminal nerve serves motor function for muscles of mastication, part of descending corticobulbar fibers and is discussed in more detail with descending tracts.


                  Descending Tracts

                  Spinal cord targets

                  Ventral horn gray matter: Lateral and Medial motorneurons (MNs) and internerons (INs)
                  Each descending group of pathways (dorsolateral or ventromedial) will terminate on one of two targets in the ventral gray matter:
                  Dorsolateral spinal cord pathways: terminate and synapse on lateral MNs and INs serving single
                  limb movements
                  Ventromedial spinal cord pathways: terminate and synapse on the medial MNs and INs serving
                  axial and proximal limb girdle muscles

                  Dorsolateral Pathways
                  All tracts terminate on lateral motor neurons (MNs) and interneurons (INs) in the ventral horn gray matter of the spinal cord and serve single limb movements
                  Lateral Corticospinal tract (CST) (Haines Atlas pages 210-213): begins in the motor cortex and terminates on contralateral lateral motor neurons and interneurons located in the ventral horn of the spinal cord
                       Serves limb muscles and enables fractionation of movement (fine motor control/coordinated movement) of the fingers and hand and modulates sensory information

                  Neuron      Origin      Projections Crossing    Termination
                  1st   Pre-central gyrus (motor/pre-motor: 60%; post-central gyrus: 40%) as Corticospinal tract (CST)  Cerebral white matter, Internal capsule, cerebral peduncles, through ventral pons and medulla as the “pyramids”   Pyramidal decussation of lower medulla (90% of fibers cross to become Lateral CST in SC)  Lateral MN & IN’s of ventral horn of spinal cord; some to dorsal horn neurons and intermediate gray; connects to outgoing alpha motor neuron
                  SOMETHING TO NOTE: 10% of fibers do NOT cross at the pyramidal decussation but stay ipsilateral to become the ventral corticospinal tract (VCST), which synapse on medial MNs and INs (which shares information with MN/IN’s on contralateral side); serves bilateral axial/trunk muscles.

                  Rubrospinal tract (Haines Atlas pages 220-223): Primary action is to facilitate motor neurons that innervate large muscle movements, primarily serves cervical regions (greater influence on muscle flexors and inhibits extensors)
                       The red nucleus receives major input from primary and pre-motor area.  Rubrospinal tract is thought of as “a sister” to Lateral CST

                  Neuron      Origin      Projections Crossing    Termination
                  1st   Arises from Red nucleus
                  Located in the midbrain Passes through contralateral midbrain, pons, and medulla on its way to cervical levels of SC    Fibers cross immediately
                  upon exiting the Red nucleus  Terminates on lateral MN’s and IN’s of the ventral horn at primarily cervical spinal levels

                  Ventromedial Spinal Cord Pathways (Haines Atlas pages 220-223) 
                  Terminate and synapse on the medial motor neurons and interneurons serving axial and proximal limb girdle muscles
                  Vestibulospinal tracts: convey impulses from the vestibular labyrinth and is comprised of 2 tracts:
                  o     Medial Vestibulospinal Tract: arising from the medial vestibular nucleus and terminates on medial motor neurons and interneurons at the cervical level; associated with the spinal accessory nerve for rotation/lifting of head and shoulder blade for orientation of individual during altered posture and balance

                  Neuron      Origin      Projections Crossing    Termination
                  1st   Medial Vestibular nucleus     Exits nucleus and descends in white matter pathway, the medial longitudinal fasciculus  (MLF)   Primary tract does NOT cross  Terminates on ipsilateral Medial MN’s and IN’s of ventral horn primarily at cervical levels

                  o     Lateral Vestibulospinal Tract: arising from the lateral vestibular nucleus and terminates on medial motor neurons and interneurons at all levels; important for maintenance of upright posture and balance via excitation of antigravity/extensor muscles (mainly of trunk and ipsilateral limb girdle muscles)

                  Neuron      Origin      Projections Crossing    Termination
                  1st   Lateral Vestibular nucleus    Exits nucleus and descends in white matter pathway    Primary tract does NOT cross  Terminates on ipsilateral Medial MN’s and IN’s of ventral horn primarily at ALL spinal levels
                  SOMETHING TO NOTE: Lateral Vestibular Nucleus is modulated by activation of vestibular apparatus (excitation) or cerebellar (inhibition) inputs

                  Other Descending Pathways
                  Corticobulbar (corticonuclear) tract (Haines Atlas pages 214-217): collectively refers to any descending cranial nerve-related motor axons from cerebral cortex traveling to the respective contralateral nuclei (or bilateral) which in turn give rise to the respective cranial nerve (serves as upper motor neuron to the cranial nerve nuclei onto which they synapse). All descending fibers travel together and are collectively referred to as the corticobulbar tract.
                  o     Pathway: lateral aspect of motor cortex (pre-central gyrus) and association areas (pre-motor, etc.) to cranial nerve nuclei in contralateral brainstem areas
                  o     Examples: facial nerve, trigeminal nerve (motor component), hypoglossal nerve, etc.
                  o     Control of facial muscles, muscles of mastication, tongue movement, sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, larynx and pharynx, and eye movements

      .Welcome to Module 1.
            -In this module you will learn about the general organization of the human nervous system, overview of structures of the nervous system, embryology and development of nervous system from conception to birth and different neuroimaging techniques that are commonly use in the clinical practice to identify lesions in the nervous system.

      .Learning Objectives
            Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to: 
                  Describe the divisions of the Nervous system 
                  Describe the three developmental stages of nervous system in utero 
                  Describe the formation of neural tube 
                  Describe the formation of Brain and Spinal Cord 
                  Describe the following Neuroimaging Techniques: 
                  Computed Tomography (CT) 
                  Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)

            Nervous System Organization

            .Objectives
            • Introduction to Nervous System
            • Describe the divisions of the Nervous system
            • Describe the general parts of the brain
            • Describe the general parts of the spinal cord
            • Describe the divisions of the Peripheral nervous system

            .Introduction to Nervous System 
            • Many people live with functional limitations related to nervous system dysfunction
            • Coping with brain injury, spinal cord injury, birth defects, or neurologic conditions
            • Sitting, standing, walking, getting dressed, and remembering a name may become 
            challenging
            • Physical therapy play a crucial role in helping people regain their ability to move and function 
            as independently as possible after nervous system dysfunction
            • This knowledge is essential to make accurate diagnoses, establish appropriate goals, and 
            develop and implement optimal interventions to promote the best outcomes for people with 
            neurologic conditions

            Embryonic

            Pre-Embryonic Stage


            Pre-Embryonic Stage
            Duration: From conception to approximately day 14.
            A.Fertilized Ovum, a single cell
            B.Four-cell stage
            C.Solid sphere of cells
            D.Hollow sphere of cells. The inner cell mass will become the 
            embryonic disk
            E.The two-layered embryonic disk, shown in cross section (left) and 
            from above (right).
            • The upper layer of the disk is the ectoderm, and 
            • The lower layer is the endoderm


            Embryonic Stage


            Embryonic Stage
            Duration: From day 15 to the end of the eighth week.

            • Develops into sensory organs, epidermis, and the 
            Ectoderm nervous system

            • Develops into dermis, muscles, skeleton, and the 
            Mesoderm excretory and circulatory systems

            • Differentiates to become the gut, liver pancreas, and 
            Endoderm respiratory system


            Embryonic Stage
            A.Longitudinal thickening of the ectoderm, 
            called the neural plate (day 16)
            B.The midline section of the neural plate 
            moves toward the interior of the embryo, 
            creating the neural groove (day 18) 
            C.The folds of the neural plate meet, forming 
            the neural tube. The neural crest 
            separates from the tube and from the 
            remaining ectoderm (day 21) ¦Es un pato (2) amb cresta (1)
            D.The open ends of the neural tube are 
            neuropores. The neural tube differentiates 
            into an inner and an outer layer


            Fetal Stage


            Fetal Stage
            Duration: End of eight week until birth ¦8 = cagallons caigent = Fètid (fetal)
            • Nervous system develops more fully, and myelination begins

            • Occurs during the embryonic stage and consists of 2 phases:
            • Phase 1: Tissues that will become nervous system merges to form a tube running 
            along the back of the embryo
            • Phase 2: When the ends of the tube closes, the formation of brain begins
            • Formation of the Neural Tube (Days 18 to 26)
            • Relationship of the Neural Tube to Other Developing Structures
            • Brain Formation (Begins Day 28) ¦18-26-28 Dos 8s, un 8 rencat en mig (6), i "1,2,2"
            • Continued Development During Fetal Stage

      .('03 PT2060_Mod1_Neural Tube Formation.pdf') Neural Tube Formation
            Neural Tube Formation

            Objectives
            • Describe the formation of neural tube
            • Describe the formation of other developing structures in relation to neural tube
            • Neurodevelopmental disorders 


            Formation of 
            Neural Tube


            Formation of the Neural Tube
            • Formation of the Neural Tube (Days 18 to 26)
            • Nervous system begins as a longitudinal thickening of the ectoderm, called the neural plate


            Formation of the Neural Tube
            • The plate forms on the surface of the embryo, extending from the head to the tail region, in 
            contact with amniotic fluid
            • The edges of the plate fold to create the neural groove, and the folds grow toward each other


            Formation of the Neural Tube
            • When the folds touch (day 21), the neural tube is formed.


            Formation of Neural Tube
            • The neural tube closes first in the future cervical 
            region.
            • Then the groove rapidly zips closed rostrally and 
            caudally, leaving open ends called neuropores
            • The overlying ectoderm (destined to become the 
            epidermal layer of skin) closes over the tube and 
            the neural crest
            • The superior neuropore closes by day 27, and the 
            inferior neuropore closes approximately 3 days 
            later


            Formation of Neural Tube
            • By day 26 the tube differentiates into two concentric 
            rings. The inner layer contains somas and will 
            become gray matter ¦6 = anell = rings
            • The outer layer contains processes of cells whose 
            somas are located in the inner layer. The outer 
            layer develops into white matter, consisting of 
            axons and glial cells
            • The neural tube develops by the end of the fourth 
            week. 
            • The brain and spinal cord develop entirely from the 
            neural tube


            Neural Tube and 
            Other Developing 
            Structures


            Neural Tube and other Developing Structures
            • As the neural tube closes, the adjacent mesoderm 
            divides into spherical cell clusters called somites
            • Developing somites cause bulges to appear on the 
            surface of the embryo
            • The somites first appear in the future occipital region, 
            and new somites are added caudally. 


            Neural Tube and other Developing Structures
            • The anteromedial part of a somite, the 
            sclerotome, becomes the vertebrae and the 
            skull. 
            • The posteromedial part of the somite, the 
            myotome, becomes skeletal muscle. 
            • The lateral part of the somite, the 
            dermatome, becomes dermis.


            Neural Tube and other Developing Structures
            • Grooves form on each side of the neural tube, separates the 
            tube into ventral and dorsal sections
            • The ventral section is the motor plate. Axons from somas 
            located in the motor plate grow out from the tube to 
            innervate the myotome region of the somite, leading  to the 
            formation of a myotome – a group of muscles derived from 
            one somite and innervated by a single spinal nerve
            • After embryonic stage: Myotome means a group of muscles 
            innervated by a segmental spinal nerve


            Neural Tube and other Developing Structures
            • Neurons whose somas are in the motor plate become 
            lower motor neurons, which innervate skeletal muscle, 
            and interneurons. 
            • Axons of upper motor neurons descend from the brain 
            through the spinal cord to synapse with the lower motor 
            neurons
            • In the mature spinal cord, the gray matter derived from 
            the motor plate is called the ventral horn.


            Neural Tube and other Developing Structures
            • The dorsal section of the neural tube is the association 
            plate (also called the alar plate). In the spinal cord, 
            these neurons proliferate and form interneurons and 
            projection neurons. 
            • In the mature spinal cord, the gray matter derived from 
            the association plate is called the dorsal horn
            • Neurons in the dorsal region of the neural tube process 
            sensory information. 
            • Neurons with somas in the ventral region innervate 
            skeletal muscle.


            Neural Tube and other Developing Structures
            • The neural crest separates into two columns, one 
            on each side of the neural tube
            • The columns break up into segments that 
            correspond to the dermal areas of the somites. 
            • Neural crest cells form peripheral sensory 
            neurons, myelin cells, autonomic neurons, and 
            endocrine organs
            • The cells that become peripheral sensory 
            neurons grow two processes; one connects to the 
            spinal cord, and the other innervates the region of 
            the somite that will become dermis. 
            • After the embryonic stage: Dermatome is the area 
            of the dermis innervated by a single spinal nerve

            .Neurodevelopmental Disorders (See 'Q&A doc::Explain each neurodevelopmental disorder')
                  1. Neural Tube Formation  
                     - Peak Time of Occurrence: In utero weeks 3–4  
                     - Disorders Secondary to Interference:  
                       - Anencephaly  
                       - Arnold-Chiari malformation  
                       - Spina bifida occulta  
                       - Meningocele  
                       - Myelomeningocele  
                       - Myeloschisis  

                  2. Cellular Proliferation  
                     - Peak Time of Occurrence: In utero months 3–4  
                     - Disorders Secondary to Interference:  
                       - Fetal alcohol syndrome  
                       - Cocaine-affected nervous system  

                  3. Neuronal Migration  
                     - Peak Time of Occurrence: In utero months 3–5  
                     - Disorders Secondary to Interference:  
                       - Heterotopia  
                       - Seizures  
                       - Autism  

                  4. Organization  
                     - Processes Involved:  
                       - Differentiation  
                       - Growth of axons and dendrites  
                       - Synapse formation  
                       - Selective neuron death  
                       - Retraction of axons  
                     - Peak Time of Occurrence: In utero month 5–early childhood  
                     - Disorders Secondary to Interference:  
                       - Intellectual disability  
                       - Trisomy 21  
                       - Cerebral palsy  
                       - Autism  

                  5. Myelination  
                     - Peak Time of Occurrence: Birth–3 years  
                     - Disorders Secondary to Interference: Unknown                                                         |

            Key Take Aways
            • Describe the formation of neural tube
            • Describe the formation other developing structures in relation to neural tube
            • Neurodevelopmental disorders
