            Neuromessengers

            .Objectives
                  • Define neurotransmitter
                  • Define neuromodulator
                  • Describe the site of action, effect of binding and associated disorder related to 
                  neurotransmitters and neuromodulators 

            .Neuromessengers
                  The chemicals that convey information among neurons

                  .Neurotransmitters
                        • Released at presynaptic neuron 
                        and acts directly on postsynaptic 
                        neuron
                        • Excitatory or Inhibitory 
                        • Effects are brief, lasting 
                        milliseconds to minutes

                  .Neuromodulators
                        • Released into extracellular fluid and 
                        adjust activity of many neurons
                        • Act at distance away from the 
                        synaptic cleft
                        • Changes gene expression 
                        • Effects manifest slowly, lasting for 
                        minutes to days

            .Common Neurotransmitters/neuromodulators
                  | Category     | Transmitter                          | Action on Postsynaptic Membrane                          |
                  |--------------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
                  | Cholinergic  | Acetylcholine (ACh)                  | Usually excitatory                                       |
                  | Amino acid   | γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA)           | Inhibitory                                               |
                  |              | Glutamate (Glu)                      | Excitatory                                               |
                  |              | Glycine (Gly)                        | Inhibitory or excitatory, depending upon receptor        |
                  | Amine        | Dopamine (DA)                        | Inhibitory or excitatory, depending upon receptor        |
                  |              | Histamine                            | Usually inhibitory                                       |
                  |              | Norepinephrine (NE)                  | Inhibitory or excitatory, depending upon receptor        |
                  |              | Serotonin (5-HT)                     | Usually inhibitory                                       |
                  | Peptide      | Endorphins                           | Usually inhibitory                                       |
                  |              | Enkephalins                          | Usually inhibitory                                       |
                  |              | Substance P                          | Usually excitatory                                       |
                  |              | Calcitonin gene-related peptide      | Excitatory                                               |
                  | Gas          | Nitric oxide                         | Excitatory                                               |

            .GABA Inhibition
                  • GABA is extremely important to control excitability
                  • 10-20% of all the inter neurons are GABA.
                  • Although excitatory neurons outnumber these, GABA is important and plays a crucial role in preventing seizures (hyper excitability)

            .Acetylcholine (ACh) (!!)(Falta Mnemo)
                  TABLE - ACETYLCHOLINE (ACh) SUMMARY  
                        1.Site of Action: Skeletal muscle membrane  
                              Effect of Binding: Initiates skeletal muscle contraction  
                              Disorders: Myasthenia gravis destroys ACh receptors  
                        2.Site of Action: Autonomic nervous system  
                              -Effect of Binding: Slows heart rate, constricts pupils, increases digestive secretions and smooth muscle contraction  
                              -Disorders: (No specific disorders listed)  
                        3.Site of Action: Brain  
                              Effect of Binding:  
                                   Arousal, pleasure, feelings of reward
                                          Disorders:  
                                               Tobacco smoking
                                   Cognitive function  
                                          Disorders:    
                                               Alzheimer’s disease                           

            .Amino Acid (!!)(Falta Mnemo)
                  TABLE - Amino Acid Transmitter Summary 
                        1. Site of Action: Glutamate: brain  
                           - Effect of Binding: Usually excitation; learning and memory  
                           - Disorders: Excess: epileptic seizures, excitotoxicity, chronic pain, Parkinson’s disease, schizophrenia  
                        2. Site of Action: Glycine: spinal cord  
                           - Effect of Binding: Excitation (NMDA) or Inhibition (glycine receptors)  
                           - Disorders:  
                             - Low in spinal cord: unwanted skeletal muscle contractions  
                             - Low in brain: impaired learning and memory  
                        3. Site of Action: GABA: CNS  
                           - Effect of Binding: Inhibition; sedation, antianxiety, antiseizure, and sleep inducing  
                           - Disorders: Low: seizures, unwanted skeletal muscle contraction, anxiety  
                        Note:  
                        - CNS: Central nervous system  
                        - GABA: γ-aminobutyric acid  
                        - NMDA: N-methyl-D-aspartate  

            .Amine (!!)(Falta Mnemo)
                  TABLE - AMINE NEUROTRANSMITTER SUMMARY  
                        1. Dopamine: emotion/motivation system  
                           - Effect of Binding: Feeling of wanting a reward  
                           - Disorders: Low: depression, drug addiction  
                        2. Dopamine: basal ganglia  
                           - Effect of Binding: Control of movement, attention, decision making, goal-directed behavior  
                           - Disorders: Low: Parkinson’s disease; ADHD  
                        3. Dopamine: frontal lobe  
                           - Effect of Binding: Thinking, planning  
                           - Disorders: Excess: schizophrenia  
                        4. NE: adrenal medulla and sympathetic nervous system  
                           - Effect of Binding: Increased heart rate and force of contraction; dilation of bronchioles, inhibition of peristalsis  
                           - Disorders: --  
                        5. NE: emotion system and some areas of cerebral cortex  
                           - Effect of Binding: Control of mood, increased attention to sensory information  
                           - Disorders: Excess: feeling fearful, panic disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder  
                        6. Serotonin: CNS  
                           - Effect of Binding: Regulates sleep, appetite, arousal, mood  
                           - Disorders:  
                             - Low: depression, anxiety  
                             - Excess: obsessive-compulsive disorder, schizophrenia  
                        7. Histamine: brain  
                           - Effect of Binding: Regulates wakefulness, attention, and vomiting  
                           - Disorders: --  
                        Note:  
                        - ADHD: Attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder  
                        - CNS: Central nervous system  
                        - LSD: lysergic acid diethylamide  
                        - NE: norepinephrine  

            .Peptide (!!)(Falta Mnemo)
                  TABLE - Peptide Neuromessenger Summary Outline
                        Site of Action:
                        1. Opioid peptides: peripheral sensory neurons and central nervous system
                           - Effect of Binding: Inhibit signals interpreted as painful.
                           - Disorders: Excess: anxiety.
                        2. Substance P: nerve endings in skin, muscles, joints
                           - Effect of Binding: Transmits signals from damaged or threatened tissue.
                        3. Substance P: brain
                           - Effect of Binding: Respiratory and cardiovascular control; mood regulation; signals interpreted as pain.
                           - Disorders: Excess: some pathologic pain conditions.
                        4. Calcitonin gene–related peptide: brain
                           - Effect of Binding: Vasodilation; long-term neural changes in migraine.
                           - Disorders: Excess: migraine.

            .Key Take Aways
                  • Define neurotransmitter
                  • Define neuromodulator
                  • Describe the site of action, effect of binding and associated disorder related to 
                  neurotransmitters and neuromodulators

..2.5. Supporting Cells and Neuroplasticity

      -learn about supporting cells of the nervous system, neuroplasticity and its role in cellular recovery and rehabilitation. These videos will provide an overview of the supporting cells and their functions and clinical application, mechanism of neuroplasticity and role of neuroplasticity in cellular recovery and rehabilitation  [14:48],  [15:04],  [15:04]

      .('10 PT2060_Mod2_Supporting Cells - Glia.pdf')
            Supporting Cells: Glia

            (See 'Mini Menú Supporting Cells' en Q&A doc)

            .Objectives
            • Define Glia
            • Explain the functions of glia
            • Understand the types of glia
            • Describe Astrocytes and their functions
            • Describe Oligodendrocytes and their functions
            • Describe Schwann cells and their functions
            • Explain the functions of microglia
            • Explain the clinical application of role of glia in neuroinflammation
            • Explain the clinical application of demyelination in CNS and PNS

            .Supporting Cells: Glia
            • Glia means “glue”
            • Glial cells form a critical support network for neurons 
            • They provide structure for neuron network
            • They also transmit information and strongly affect neural signaling at synaptic and extra 
            synaptic sites
            • They are actively involved in the pathogenesis of disorders such as Alzheimer’s Disease & 
            Multiple Sclerosis

            .Functions of Glia
            • Glia have three core functions:
            oMyelinating the axon of neuron
            oSignaling/cleaning/nourishing the neuron and neuron network
            oDefending the neuron network and nervous system against pathogens

            .Types of Glia
            • Glia are classified based on size and function
            • There two types of glia:
            • Macroglia
            oAstrocytes
            oOligodendrocytes
            oSchwann cells
            • Microglia

            .Astrocytes
                  • Astrocytes are Star-shaped cells
                  • Present in Central Nervous System (CNS)

                  Functions:
                  • Clean up potassium ions from the extracellular space & neurotransmitters 
                  from synaptic cleft, and debris from extracellular space
                  • Supply nutrition to nerve cells
                  • Part of blood-brain barrier which helps to protect the CNS
                  • A liaison that fills the communication gap between the neuron and vasculature
                  • During nervous system development and recovery, they form pathway for 
                  migrating neurons in the CNS
                  • Release neurotransmitter but they do not generate Action Potential

            .Oligodendrocytes and Schwann Cells 1
            • Oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells form myelin
            • Myelin is the protective covering of lipids and proteins that 
            insulates axons
            • Myelin prevents the dissipation of electrical currents within the 
            axon, allowing fast and efficient transmission of neural signals

            .Oligodendrocytes and Schwann Cells 2
            • Oligodendrocytes:
            oFound in the central nervous system (CNS)
            oThey myelinate parts of several axons from different neuron
            • Schwann Cells:
            oFound in the peripheral nervous system (PNS)
            oMyelinate only one axon at a time
            oWhen peripheral nerves are inflamed, Schwann cells act as 
            phagocytes 
            oAfter injury, Schwann cells provide trophic factors for repair 
            of axons

            .Microglial Cells
            • Microglial cells normally function as phagocytes
            • Microglia act as the immune system of the CNS and clean the neural environment
            • In the healthy nervous system, microglia continually sample the extracellular environment for 
            indicators of damage
            • They are activated during nervous system development and following injury, infection, or 
            disease
            • The microglia clean up and remove debris from the dying cells. 
            • This essential for normal healing following a stroke, traumatic brain injury, or CNS infection
            • Abnormal microglial activity contributes to neural damage in certain diseases, causing 
            imbalance between protective and destructive roles:
            • Alzheimer’s disease, HIV, Parkinson’s Disease, Stroke and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis 
            (ALS)

            .Brain Glymphatic System
            • Recent research has proposed the presence of a glymphatic system in the brain
            • A system that is analogous to the lymphatic system in the rest of the body
            • It’s called glymphatic because it involves glial cells
            • Astrocytes appear to play a critical role in this newly identified system
            • Brain flushes the toxins efficiently only when we are in deep asleep. Hence, sleep is 
            important!
            • The glia and the astrocytes shrink when we are in deep sleep and the intercellular space 
            increases
            • The CSF collects the toxins and flushes it out of the body via venules

            .Clinical Application: Neuroinflammation
            • Neuroinflammation is the response of the CNS to infection, disease, and injury mediated by 
            reactive microglia and astrocytes
            • These cells are beneficial when they remove debris, produce neurotrophic factors that support 
            axonal regeneration and remyelination, and mobilize astrocytes to reseal the blood-brain barrier 
            and provide trophic support
            • Excessive neuroinflammation can lead to infiltration of immune cells into the brain, increased 
            permeability of the blood-brain barrier, edema, death of neurons and oligodendrocytes, and 
            inhibition of neural regeneration
            • In Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, MS, ALS, microglia and astrocytes become 
            excessively activated, losing their physiologic buffering function and releasing toxic compounds 
            into the neuronal environment

            .Clinical Application: Demyelination in CNS
            Central Nervous System Demyelination: 
            • Involves damage to the myelin sheaths in the brain and spinal cord
            • Multiple Sclerosis (MS) occurs when the immune system produces antibodies that primarily 
            attack oligodendrocytes
            • Destruction of the oligodendrocytes in MS produces patches of demyelination, called 
            plaques, in the white matter of the CNS 
            • Slowed or blocked transmission of neural signals

            .Clinical Application: Demyelination in PNS
            Peripheral Nervous System Demyelination:
            • Peripheral neuropathy is any pathologic change involving peripheral nerves and it affect 
            axons or myelin
            • Involves destruction of the myelin surrounding the sensory and motor fibers, 
            • Results in disrupted proprioception (awareness of limb position), pain, numbness, lack of 
            coordination, and weakness
            • Autoimmune disorders, metabolic abnormalities, viruses, trauma, and toxic chemicals can 
            cause peripheral demyelination
            • Guillain-Barré syndrome is an autoimmune disease that involves acute inflammation and 
            demyelination of peripheral sensory and motor fibers

            .Key Take Aways
            • Define Glia
            • Explain the functions of glia
            • Understand the types of glia
            • Describe Astrocytes and their functions
            • Describe Oligodendrocytes and their functions
            • Describe Schwann cells and their functions
            • Explain the functions of microglia
            • Explain the clinical application of neuroinflammation
            • Explain the clinical application of demyelination in CNS and PNS

      .('11 PT2060_Mod2_Neuroplasticity.pdf')
            Neuroplasticity

            .Objectives
            • Define Neuroplasticity 
            • Explain the purpose of neuroplasticity
            • Describe Habituation 
            • Describe Experience Dependent Plasticity and its mechanisms:
            • Long Term Potentiation
            • Long Term Depression

            .Neuroplasticity 1
            Ability of neurons to change their functions, chemical profile or structure

            .Neuroplasticity 2
            Required for:
            • Learning
            • Creation of new memories
            • Recovery from damage to the CNS

            .Neuroplasticity 3
            Includes:
            • Habituation
            • Experience-dependent plasticity: Learning and memory
            • Cellular recovery after injury

            .Mechanism
            • Involves ionotropic Receptors (AMPA and NMDA)
            • Induce Long-Term Potentiation (LTP), a form of synaptic plasticity
            • Involves metabotropic receptors that induce metabolic changes in cells
            • Involves calcium potentials that has role in altering signals within the nervous 
            system

            .Habituation
            • Decrease in response to a repeated, benign stimulus
            • Simplest form of neuroplasticity
            • Non-associative learning
            • Decrease in the release of excitatory neurotransmitters
            • Decrease in free intracellular Ca2+
            • Rest with no stimulus – habituation no longer present/partially resolved
            • Prolonged repeated stimulus – Permanent structural changes occur
            • Allows other types of learning to occur

            .Experience-Dependent Plasticity 1
            • Also called as use-dependent or activity-dependent plasticity
            • Required for Learning and Memory
            • Complex process than habituation
            • Persistent, long-lasting changes in the strength of synapses 
            • Synthesis of new proteins
            • Growth of new synapses
            • Modification of existing synapses
            • Especially at dendritic spines
            • Essential for neural recovery following an injury or insult
            • Harmful – Contribution to development of chronic pain syndromes

            .Experience-Dependent Plasticity 2
            • Learning a new task: Numerous brain regions
            • Skill: Fewer & distinct area of brain with increased but focal activity
            • Long term practice: Enlargement of brain area representation with skills
            • Example: Playing musical instruments or Driving

            .Experience-Dependent Plasticity 3
            Mechanisms:
            • Plasticity of intrinsic excitability of neurons by functional changes in ion 
            channels
            • Plasticity at inhibitory GABAergic synapses
            • Homeostatic plasticity to stabilize neural circuits
            • Long-term potentiation (LTP)
            • Long-term depression (LTD)

            .Experience-Dependent Plasticity
            • Glutamate - excitatory neurotransmitter in brain, learning and memory
            • LTP and LTD of excitatory glutamatergic synapses
            • Best known plasticity in learning and memory formation
            • Presynaptic occurrence – Changes in neurotransmitter release
            • Postsynaptic occurrence – Changes in receptor density and efficiency
            • Genetic alterations must occur in the cell during learning process to change the 
            structure of a neuron
            • Calcium is a predominant regulator of gene activity
            • Nucleus contains Ca2+ ion channels
            • Occur in motor, somatosensory, visual and auditory cortices and cerebellum

            .Long-Term Potentiation (LTP)
            • Conversion of silent synapses to active synapses
            • Silent synapses lack functional glutamate (AMPA) receptors & are inactive
            • Highly correlated presynaptic and postsynaptic firing can activate them
            • Set of mobile AMPA receptors cycles between the cytoplasm and the synaptic 
            membrane
            • LTP is initiated by activity of NMDA receptors – Increased cations 
            • Insertion of mobile AMPA receptors into the synaptic membrane causes binding 
            of glutamate to exposed receptors
            • Continuous stimulation, postsynaptic membrane generates new dendritic spine
            • Structural changes occur and new synapse is produced

            .Long-Term Potentiation (LTP) ('')

            .Long-Term Potentiation (LTP) ('')

            .Functions of NMDA Receptor 
            • NMDA receptors are special receptors involved in synaptic plasticity
            • They require a certain level of depolarization to become activated
            • During LTP, the depolarization caused by repetitive activation removes 
            magnesium ions from NMDA receptors, allowing them to function more 
            effectively
            • As LTP progresses, the interactions become more intense

            .Long-Term Depression (LTD)
            • Conversion of active synapse to silent synapse
            • Removal of AMPA receptors from the membrane into the cytoplasm
            • Postsynaptic membrane less likely to get depolarized on release of glutamate 
            from presynaptic neuron.

            .Key Take Aways
            • Define Neuroplasticity 
            • Explain the purpose of neuroplasticity
            • Describe Habituation 
            • Describe Experience Dependent Plasticity and its mechanisms:
            • Long Term Potentiation
            • Long Term Depression

            Neuroplasticity: Cellular Recovery

            .Objectives
            • Understand the role of neuroplasticity in cellular recovery
            • Describe Axonal Injury and recovery in CNS
            • Describe Axonal Injury and recovery in PNS
            • Explain the difference between the axon recovery in CNS Vs PNS
            • Explain the role of neuroplasticity in rehabilitation

            .Neuroplasticity
            • Axonal Injury
            o Degeneration 
            o May or may not cause cell death
            o Regeneration of axon possible with some neurons
            • Cell body Injury
            o Cell death
            o Recovery is promoted by:
            ▪ Altering specific synapses
            ▪ Functional reorganization of CNS
            ▪ Changing neurotransmitter release

            .Axonal Injury
            Axon severed or stretched (CNS or PNS):
            • Proximal and distal segments
            • Cytoplasm leaks out of cut ends
            • Segments retract away from each other
            • Wallerian degeneration of distal segment
            • Myelin sheath pulls away 
            • Axon swells & break down
            • Death of distal segment
            • Glial cells scavenge and clean debris
            • Central chromatolysis – Occasional cell death

            .Axonal Injury and Recovery in PNS 1
            Sprouting: Growth of a new branch of an intact axon or the regrowth of damaged axons
            A. Collateral Sprouting
            • Denervated target is reinnervated by branches of intact axons
            B. Regenerative Sprouting
            • Axon and target are damaged
            • Injured axon sends outside sprouts to new target

            .Axonal Injury and Recovery in PNS 2
            • Functional regeneration of axons - PNS > CNS because:
            • Production of Nerve Growth Factor (NGF) by Schwann cells 
            • Effective clearance of debris
            • Formation of bands of Bungner – guides axonal regrowth to the target
            • Slow recovery
            • Approximately 1 mm growth/ day or 1” recovery/month
            • Exercise begun after 5 days of peripheral nerve lesion increases axonal regeneration and 
            reinnervation of muscle
            • Sprouting onto inappropriate target can cause problem
            • Example: Synkinesis- Motor axon innervates different muscle

            .Axonal Injury in CNS
            • Most of the damage evolves hours /days post injury due to cascade of cellular events 
            • Damage to white fiber tracts after Spinal cord injury or Traumatic Brain Injury lead to:
            • Increased permeability of axons
            • Disturbance of Na+/Ca+ channels
            • Influx of Ca+
            • Disruption of axonal transport with accumulation of intra axonal components
            • Axon swelling and breaking down
            • Axon retraction
            • Central chromatolysis
            • Wallerian Degeneration

            .Axonal Injury and Recovery in CNS 3
            • Functional axon regeneration does not occur in CNS axons:
            o Lack of Nerve Growth Factor (NGF)
            o Glial scar formation by astrocytes and microglia:
            ▪ Blocks axonal regeneration
            ▪ Release growth inhibiting factors 
            • Neurite outgrowth inhibitor – NOGO
            • NOGO Inhibitor and Stem cells – May help to promote regeneration of CNS

            .Axonal Injury and Recovery in CNS 4
                  A. Recovery of synaptic effectiveness
                        Edema, Edema resolved

            .Axonal Injury and Recovery in CNS 5
                  B. Denervation hypersensitivity
                        Before injury to presynaptic neuron
                        After death of presynaptic cell

            .Axonal Injury and Recovery in CNS 6
                  C. Synaptic
                        After loss of some presynaptic terminals
                        Before injury to presynaptic cell

            .Axonal Injury and Recovery in CNS 7
                  D. Unmasking of a silent synapse
                        Active synapse
                        Silent synapse

            .Rehabilitation and Neuroplasticity
            • Plasticity allows for recovery from nervous system injury
            • Active movement is crucial for optimizing motor recovery
            • Recovery of neuronal function is influenced by:
            o The dose of rehabilitation – frequency, duration and intensity
            o Amount of time between injury and initiation of rehab
            • Early rehabilitation is the key to improved recovery
            • Delay may reduce the impact of therapy
            • Task specific training:
            o Essential for motor learning
            o Long lasting cortical reorganization in the activated brain area 
            o Example: Constrain-induce movement therapy (CIMT) for Stroke

            .Key Take Aways
            • Understand the role of neuroplasticity in cellular recovery
            • Describe Axonal Injury and recovery in CNS
            • Describe Axonal Injury and recovery in PNS
            • Explain the difference between the axon recovery in CNS Vs PNS
            • Explain the role of neuroplasticity in rehabilitation

            1.Neuroplasticity concepts in application: Watch the YouTube video called: Theory of CIMT. Professionals and discuss the following questions with your instructor

                  ('Theory of CIMT. Professionals.mp4')
                        Constraint-induced movement therapy is a form of rehabilitation for the upper limb that
                        0:04
                        links the two theories of neuroplasticity and cortical reorganisation.
                        0:08
                        CIMT was developed by Dr Edward Taub and his team in the USA. They worked with adults recovering
                        0:15
                        from stroke with hemiplegia, who had limited use of their affected side in activities of
                        0:19
                        daily living. Dr Taub’s team found that by restraining the stronger side and using
                        0:24
                        the weaker side as much as possible alongside specific intensive exercises, they could make
                        0:29
                        significant improvements in the amount and quality of movement of the upper limb over
                        0:33
                        a short period of time. These results have been repeated in numerous studies including
                        0:39
                        large multi-site randomised controlled trials, and similar results have since been demonstrated
                        0:45
                        for children and adults with other neurological conditions.
                        0:49
                        The two theories underpinning CIMT are learned non-use and cortical reorganisation.
                        0:55
                        Dr Taub theorised that when trying to use an affected upper limb the patient experiences
                        0:59
                        negative feedback in the form of pain or failure at the task. They learn to compensate with
                        1:05
                        their unaffected side instead and begin to develop a pattern of compensatory behaviour.
                        1:11
                        Even when the initial central nervous system depression subsides and some motor recovery
                        1:15
                        is possible, the patient continues to follow this new compensatory behaviour and fails
                        1:20
                        to involve their affected upper limb -therefore they “learn” not to use it.
                        1:25
                        The second theory of CIMT links in with theories of “use-dependent cortical reorganisation”,
                        1:30
                        where the representational size of body parts on the cortex is explicitly linked with the
                        1:36
                        amount the body part is used. In cases of learned non-use or developmental disregard
                        1:41
                        in children, researchers have found the representation of the affected limb has decreased on the
                        1:46
                        cortex.
                        1:48
                        Several studies have now shown that following a full CIMT programme the affected side has
                        1:53
                        increased its representation on the cortex, and this increase remains on a 6 month follow
                        1:57
                        up. This has been demonstrated in adults following stroke, and in children with hemiplegia.
                        2:04
                        So CIMT does not just affect the ability and the strength of the upper limb, but it affects
                        2:08
                        plasticity and reorganisation in the brain. It's a combination of everything that makes
                        2:13
                        the treatment so powerful, and can have lasting changes for weeks, months and years after
                        2:18
                        treatment.

            5.Case Study: Read the case study and discussion the questions that follow:
            I.D., a 19-year-old man, suffered severe flu symptoms, requiring him to stay home from work. About a week later, I.D. noted tingling and numbness in his fingers, and he was unable to stand and could not use his hands. After being taken to the hospital, he experienced respiratory weakness and was placed on a ventilator. He had near total paralysis of voluntary muscles, including facial and swallowing muscles, requiring tube feeding. Nerve conduction studies for both motor and sensory pathways were conducted. (To test peripheral sensory nerve pathways, an electrical stimulus is given to the skin at a distal point over a nerve and is recorded with surface electrodes at a more proximal point over the same nerve. The time required to transmit the signal between the two points indicates the conduction velocity. Peripheral motor conduction studies are similar, except that the electrical stimulus is given proximally over the nerve and is recorded from the skin over an associated muscle.) For I.D., studies indicated that peripheral sensory and motor conduction times were significantly prolonged bilaterally.  I.D. had suffered peripheral nerve demyelination, presumably due to an autoimmune response to viral infection.  
                  a.The disease was confirmed to involve the peripheral nervous system. Did the loss of myelin involve oligodendrocytes or Schwann cells?
                  b.How does loss of myelin along peripheral sensory fibers affect the propagation of action potentials in the affected axons? In your answer, explain what myelin is and what it function in an intact neuron/axon. 
                  c.Would loss of myelin in afferent sensory neuron fibers impair the generation of local receptor potentials or the propagation of action potentials? Explain.

      .('Module 2 Top 3 Muddiest Points Explained.docx')
            Top 3 muddiest points identified by the class based on discussion board participation:
                  1.Neuromodulator Mechanisms: 
                        -Same chemical can act as a neurotransmitter or neuromodulator based on whether the chemical is released only at specific synapse or is released into the extracellular space.
                              Simple video explaining the role of neuromodulator: https://youtu.be/yW94KF1y_IY?si=MIC4OtE3VDzlcmmT (!!)
                              Biochemical details of neuromodulator activity: https://youtu.be/Dc0p73gGIqU?si=Rm9K0zGim4sU1poh (!!)

                  2.Denervation Hypersensitivity: 
                        -Denervation hypersensitivity occurs in postsynaptic neuron when presynaptic axon terminals are destroyed. This leads to a compensatory chemical mechanism inside the post synaptic neuron leading to development of new receptor sites on the postsynaptic membrane in response to the reduction in neurotransmitter released from the presynaptic neuron. These changes occur in post synaptic membrane with the intention to continue to make connection with other neighboring neurons. When neurotransmitters are released from other nearby axons, an increased or hypersensitive response occurs owing to the additional receptor sites on the postsynaptic membrane

                  3.NMDA Receptors in Plasticity: 
                        -Visualization of cellular level biochemical mechanisms can be challenging. Hence, review these videos to better understand the cellular level mechanisms:
                              Detailed video explaining the role of NMDA receptors: https://youtu.be/4-DuvwoH2zQ?si=LwUnvcZhArdkxoLf (!!) 
                                    -LTP and memory formation animation video: https://youtu.be/4Hm08ksPtMo?si=bY0PBHHnpktfmdXq (!!)
                                    -LTP video animation: https://youtu.be/-mHgPfXHzJE?si=I14Ai7xCqMBx318g (!!)

..Module 3: Neuroanatomy

//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
..3.0. Module Introduction
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

      -This module will review the neuroanatomy of the brain and supportive structures, including the venous sinuses and dural reflections, the external and internal morphology of the cerebral hemispheres, the cerebral blood supply, brainstem, and cerebellum. This will provide you with the foundational knowledge to recognize structures and areas of the brain that may be involved in common diagnoses physical therapists treat in the clinic.

      .Learning Objectives
            Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to: 
                  Explain the principles of general nervous system organization and function
                  Identify the external morphology of the brain including the cerebral hemispheres, the supportive systems of the meninges, the ventricles and cerebrospinal fluid
                  Relate the clinical manifestations of neural dysfunction or injury and probable sites of lesions
                  Identify the external and internal morphology of the medial cortex, the brainstem, cranial nerves and cerebellum
                  Identify the structure and function of the anterior and posterior circulatory systems

      .('15 PT2060_Supportive Brain Structures.pdf')
            Supportive Brain Structures

            .Meninges and Dural Reflections/Infoldings - I
            • Meninges: support and 
            protect the CNS; comprised 
            of 3 layers (from external to 
            internal)
            o Dura mater (periosteal 
            and meningeal layers): 
            tough, outermost layer
            o Arachnoid: highly 
            vascular
            o Pia mater: adheres to 
            brain tissue


            .Meninges and Dural Reflections/Infoldings - II
            • Dural reflections are formed by 
            meningeal layer of dura mater 
            reflecting away from periosteal 
            layer, dragging the other layers of 
            the meninges with it to form a 6 
            meningeal layers in 
            the dural reflection


            .Meninges and Dural Reflections/Infoldings - III
            • Spaces associated 
            with the meninges
            • Epidural space: between 
            inner table of the skull 
            and dura mater
            • Subdural space: 
            between dura mater and 
            arachnoid
            • Subarachnoid space: 
            between the arachnoid 
            and pia mater, location 
            of cerebrospinal fluid 
            (CSF)


            .Dural Reflections

            Tentorium cerebelli


            .Dural Venous Sinuses - I
            • A system for draining blood from the brain; formed in the borders of 
            the dural reflections; returns deoxygenated blood back to the heart


            .Dural Venous Sinuses - II


            .Ventricular System - I
            • Ventricular system:
            o Floats and bathes the brain and 
            provides nutrients
            o Closed space within the center 
            of brain tissue, continuous with 
            the subarachnoid space
            o Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) made 
            in the roof of the 
            ventricles in choroid plexus, 
            circulates and is reabsorbed 
            into the venous blood through 
            specializations of the arachnoid 
            (arachnoid villi) into the superior 
            sagittal sinus

            Ventricular System


            .Ventricular System - II

            Lateral ventricle

      .('16 PT2060_Cerebral Blood Supply.pdf')
            Cerebral Blood Supply

            .Major Circulatory Systems for the Brain
            • Anterior intracranial circulation stems from the internal carotid arteries
            • Posterior intracranial circulation stems from the vertebrobasilar system


            .Arterial Anastomoses
            • Sharing of blood supply between arterial systems
            • Circle of Willis: communication of anterior to posterior circulation systems
            • Corticomeningeal (leptomeningeal) Anastomosis: overlap of ACA, MCA, and 
            PCA on superior/lateral cerebral hemispheres; referred to as the “watershed” 
            area


            .Anterior Intracranial Circulation
            • Stems from the internal carotid artery system 


            .Blood Supply to the Cerebral Hemispheres
            • Anterior cerebral artery (ACA)
            • Middle cerebral artery (MCA)
            • Posterior cerebral artery (PCA)


            .Posterior Intracranial Circulation - I
            • Stems from the vertebrobasilar 
            system
            • Vertebral arteries (right and left)
            • supplies lateral regions 
            medulla
            • Basilar artery
            • Supplies medial and lateral 
            pons


            .Posterior Intracranial Circulation - II


            .Blood Supply to the Brainstem and Cerebellum

                  Name this artery.
                        Posterior cerebral artery
                        Posterior communicating artery

                  This artery largely supplies which aspects of the brain?
                        Brainstem and cerebellum
                        Occipital lobe

                  If there is a lesion to this artery, which of the following deficits would you expect? (!!F)
                        Impaired strength and sensation in the contralateral foot
                        Impaired strength and sensation in the ipsilateral upper extremity
                        Visual field loss
                        Impaired strength and sensation in the contralateral upper extremity

                        Impaired strength and sensation in the contralateral upper extremity
                              (Γ)why? 
                                    The lesion described is likely to involve the middle cerebral artery (MCA) or one of its branches. The MCA supplies blood to areas of the brain that control motor and sensory functions of the upper limbs, face, and speech centers. A lesion to the MCA, specifically in the area of the primary motor cortex or sensory cortex (both located in the precentral and postcentral gyri of the lateral aspect of the cerebral hemisphere), can lead to impairments in strength and sensation in the contralateral upper extremity because of the contralateral motor and sensory pathways. These pathways decussate (cross) at the medulla, meaning damage to the MCA in the left hemisphere would affect the right upper extremity and vice versa.

                                    The other options are less likely for the following reasons:
                                    - Impaired strength and sensation in the contralateral foot: This would more likely result from a lesion to the anterior cerebral artery (ACA), which supplies the medial parts of the motor and sensory cortices controlling the lower limbs.
                                    - Impaired strength and sensation in the ipsilateral upper extremity: This would occur in cases of a lesion involving the upper motor neurons on the same side, or more likely from damage to structures outside of the motor cortex, such as the spinal cord, brainstem, or peripheral nerves, rather than a cortical lesion of the MCA.
                                    - Visual field loss: Visual disturbances typically result from damage to the occipital lobe, supplied by the posterior cerebral artery (PCA), not the MCA. Vision deficits can be seen with lesions in the occipital cortex or pathways of the visual system.

            ('2025-01-17 14_31_19.png')
                  Name this artery.
                        Basilar artery
                        Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
                        Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
                        Vertebral artery

                        Vertebral artery

                  What areas of the brain does this artery supply?
                        Superior cerebellum
                        Midbrain
                        Lateral medulla
                        Medial pons

                        Lateral medulla
                              (Γ)Rationale:
                                    The vertebral artery supplies the lateral medulla, which is part of the brainstem. The lateral medulla is critical for several functions, including sensory processing, balance, and autonomic control. The vertebral artery, along with its branches (such as the posterior inferior cerebellar artery), provides blood to the lateral part of the medulla and structures such as the inferior cerebellar peduncles and the nucleus ambiguus. A lesion in the vertebral artery or its branches can lead to symptoms of a Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome), which includes problems like vertigo, dysphagia, and loss of pain and temperature sensation.

                                    Incorrect Answers:
                                    - Superior cerebellum: The superior cerebellum is typically supplied by the superior cerebellar artery (SCA), which arises from the basilar artery, not the vertebral artery. The vertebral artery primarily supplies the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), which nourishes the inferior part of the cerebellum.
                                      
                                    - Midbrain: The midbrain is primarily supplied by branches from the posterior cerebral artery (PCA), which also arises from the basilar artery. While the vertebral artery contributes to the posterior circulation of the brain, it does not directly supply the midbrain.

                                    - Medial pons: The medial pons is typically supplied by branches of the basilar artery, particularly the paramedian branches, not the vertebral artery. The vertebral artery, through the basilar artery, does contribute to the pons' circulation, but it primarily supplies the lateral pons, not the medial portion.

            ('2025-01-17 14_32_33.png')
                  Name this artery.
                        Vertebral artery
                        Anterior spinal artery
                        Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
                        Basilar artery

                        Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)
                              (Γ)
                                    The Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) is a major artery in the posterior circulation of the brain. It is one of the key vessels that supplies the cerebellum and certain parts of the brainstem. Here’s an in-depth explanation of the PICA:

                                    Origin:
                                    - The PICA is a branch of the vertebral artery.
                                    - It typically arises from the vertebral artery at the level of the medulla, just before the vertebral arteries converge to form the basilar artery.
                                      
                                    Function:
                                    - Blood supply: PICA primarily provides blood to the posterior inferior cerebellum and parts of the medulla oblongata.
                                    - Cerebellum: It supplies the inferior portion of the cerebellum, including the flocculonodular lobe and parts of the vermis. These regions are important for maintaining balance and coordinating motor function.
                                    - Medulla oblongata: PICA also nourishes the lateral part of the medulla. This includes critical structures such as the nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal nucleus, inferior cerebellar peduncle, and spinocerebellar tract.
                                      
                                    Clinical Relevance:
                                    - Wallenberg Syndrome (Lateral Medullary Syndrome): A blockage or occlusion of PICA can lead to Wallenberg syndrome, characterized by a variety of symptoms due to damage to the lateral medulla. Symptoms may include:
                                      - Ipsilateral ataxia (loss of coordination), which affects the body’s ability to control voluntary movements.
                                      - Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation (due to damage to the spinothalamic tract).
                                      - Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) and dysarthria (difficulty speaking) due to involvement of the nucleus ambiguus.
                                      - Vertigo due to involvement of the vestibular nuclei.
                                      
                                    Pathways:
                                    - The PICA travels around the medulla and gives off several branches that supply both the cerebellum and the brainstem.
                                      - In the cerebellum, it supplies the posterior inferior portion, which plays a role in motor coordination and balance.
                                      - In the brainstem, PICA branches supply the lateral medulla, the inferior cerebellar peduncle, and some nuclei associated with cranial nerves IX, X, and XI.

                                    Anatomical Variability:
                                    - The origin of PICA can show some anatomical variations. In some cases, it may arise directly from the vertebral artery or from the basilar artery.
                                      
                                    Summary:
                                    The Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) is crucial for supplying blood to the inferior cerebellum and lateral medulla. Damage or occlusion of PICA can lead to severe neurological deficits, particularly those associated with coordination and balance. Its role in Wallenberg syndrome highlights the importance of PICA in maintaining critical functions related to motor control and sensory processing.

            .Cerebellum
            • 3 Major Functional Roles
            • Coordination of movement 
            • Maintenance of equilibrium (inputs from vestibular system)
            • Regulation of muscle tone
            • Major Structures
            • Cortex: Grey matter (periphery)
            • Medullary Center: White matter (nerve fibers to cortex, from cortex to deep nuclei, 
            from one cortical area to another
            • Deep Nuclei: 4 pairs: 1) Fastigial nucleus, 2) Globose nucleus, 3) Emboliform 
            nucleus (2 & 3 together referred to as Interposed nucleus), and 4) Dentate nucleus
            • Peduncles: afferent and efferent white matter pathways (nerve fibers) to and from 
            various brainstem regions


            .Cerebellar Lobes
            • Anterior lobe: smaller lobe located 
            superiorly
            • Posterior lobe: larger lobe 
            • Flocculonodular Lobe: consists of the 
            left and right flocculus and the 
            nodulus (midline) 
            • Primary fissure: separates smaller 
            anterior lobe from larger posterior 
            cerebellar lobe

            Anterior lobe

            Posterior lobe

      .('19 PT 2060_Brainstem Cross Sections.pdf')
            Brainstem Cross Sections

            .Objectives
            • Identify each level of the brainstem and 
            distinguish each level by physical 
            appearance and structure
            • Identify the location of various structures 
            within each level of the brainstem using 
            cross sections
            • Ascending/descending pathways
            • Cranial nerves and nuclei
            • Cerebellum, other nuclei
            • Recall the blood supply for each level of 
            the brainstem


            .Example

            Dorsal

            Ventral

            Lateral

            Medial

            Lateral


            .Blood Supply


            .Medulla (Section 6-12)


            .Upper/Rostral Medulla (Section 6-14)


            .Medulla
            • Gracile / cuneate nucleus and fasciculus
            • Lateral or Accessory Cuneate nucleus
            • Medial lemniscus
            • Medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)
            • Trigeminothalamic tract
            • Spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract
            • Spinothalamic tract
            • Pyramids/corticospinal tract
            • Hypoglossal nucleus
            • Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus
            • Solitary nucleus/tract
            • Nucleus ambiguous
            • Cochlear nuclei (dorsal/ventral)
            • Vestibular nuclei (medial, inferior)
            • Glossopharyngeal nerve


            .Pons (Section 6-19)


            .Pons
            • Medial longitudinal fasciculus
            • Medial lemniscus 
            • Trigeminothalmic tract
            • Spinothalamic tract
            • Corticospinal/corticobulbar fibers 
            • Spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract
            • Vestibular nuclei/nerve
            • Facial nuclei/nerve
            • Abducens nuclei/nerve
            • Reticular formation
            • Middle cerebellar peduncle
            • Pontine nuclei
            • 4th ventricle


            .Midbrain (Section 6-28)


            .Midbrain
            • Corticospinal/corticobulbar 
            fibers
            • Medial lemniscus
            • Spinothalamic tract
            • Trigeminothalamic tract
            • Medial longitudinal fasciculus
            • Oculomotor nucleus/nerve
            • Superior colliculus
            • Red nucleus
            • Substantia nigra
            • Cerebral aqueduct
            • Periaqueductal gray
            • Oculomotor nerve 
            parasympathetic nucleus 
            (Edinger-Westphal nucleus)

                  Inferior cerebellar peduncle
                  Medial lemniscus
                  Anterolateral system

                  Pyramid

                  If this structure was lesioned, what would be the resulting impairment?
                  Loss of limb movement/fractionated movement
                  Loss of sensory information (pain and temperature) from body
                  Loss of coordination of movements
                  Loss of sensory information (JPS, vibration, discriminative touch) from body

                  Loss of limb movement/fractionated movement

..4.0. Module Introduction

      .Welcome to Module 4!
            In this module, you will learn about the neural structures related to peripheral and central somatosensory system, different pathways of somatosensory system and how these system functions to help humans to sense and navigate the world around us eventually leading to execution of skilled movement. You will also learn the general clinical implications of lesion to the somatosensory system and how to identify the site of lesion based on symptom presentation.
                  Please contact faculty member Shilpa Gaikwad: sbgaikwad@pitt.edu if you have questions regarding this specific module and quiz.  

      .Learning Objectives
            Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to: 
                  Understand the functions of somatosensory system 
                  Describe the sensory receptors present in human body 
                  Understand the concept of the pathways to the brain 
                  Describe the Somatosensory pathways and different sensation carried by those pathways 
                  Describe the somatosensory cortex  
                  Explain the functions of somatosensory cortex 
                  Explain the clinical implications of the lesion to the somatosensory pathways and somatosensory cortex

      .('21 PT2060_Mod4_Peripheral Somatosensory System_Part 1.pdf')
            Peripheral Somatosensory System – Part I

            .Objectives
            • Understand the functions of somatosensory System
            • Describe the sensory receptors present in human body
            • Explain the cutaneous innervations
            • Explain how the different sensations are carried by different axons


            .Somatosensory System
            • Functions:
            • Investigate the world
            • Move accurately 
            • Avoid or minimize injuries


            .Sensory Receptors 1


            .Sensory Receptors 2
            • Mechanoreceptors
            o Touch, pressure, stretch, vibration
            • Chemoreceptors
            o Substance release by cells (injury)
            • Thermoreceptors
            o Heat or cooling
            • Sub type: Nociceptors
            o Sensitive to stimuli that damage or threaten to damage the tissues


            .Sensory Receptors 3
            • Tonic Receptors – Receptors that respond as long as stimulus is maintained.
            o Tonic stretch receptors in the muscle fire the entire time a muscle is stretched.

            • Phasic Receptors – Receptors that adapt to a constant stimulus and stop 
            responding.
            o Phasic stretch receptors in muscle respond only briefly to a quick stretch.
            o Phasic pressure receptors in skin respond briefly after putting on wrist watch


            .Sensations
            • Skin - Superficial or Cutaneous
            o Pain
            o Temperature
            o Touch
            • Superficial pressure
            • Vibration
            • Musculoskeletal system
            o Pain
            o Proprioception – Static joint sense and Kinesthetic sense
            • Muscle stretch
            • Tendon tension
            • Joint position
            • Deep vibration

            .CUTANEOUS AXONS AND RECEPTORS
                  Sure, here's the transcription of the image as an outline:

                  - CUTANEOUS AXONS AND RECEPTORS
                    - Axon Type
                      - Aβ
                        - Myelination: Myelinated
                        - Receptor End-Organs: Hair follicle ending
                          - Stimulus: Hair movement
                          - Tonic or Phasic: Phasic
                          - Receptive Field Diameter: Small
                        - Receptor End-Organs: Meissner’s corpuscle
                          - Stimulus: Dynamic movement across the skin, slippage during grip
                          - Tonic or Phasic: Phasic
                          - Receptive Field Diameter: Small
                        - Receptor End-Organs: Merkel cell
                          - Stimulus: Light pressure, curvature, edges
                          - Tonic or Phasic: Tonic
                          - Receptive Field Diameter: Small
                        - Receptor End-Organs: Pacinian corpuscle
                          - Stimulus: Vibration
                          - Tonic or Phasic: Phasic
                          - Receptive Field Diameter: Large
                        - Receptor End-Organs: Ruffini’s corpuscle
                          - Stimulus: Stretch of skin
                          - Tonic or Phasic: Tonic
                          - Receptive Field Diameter: Large
                      - Aδ

                        - Receptor End-Organs: Hair follicle

                          - Tonic or Phasic: Phasic

                          - Stimulus: Chemical stimuli
                          - Tonic or Phasic: Tonic
                          - Receptive Field Diameter: Medium

                  - a Small, 2–5 mm; medium, 5–10 mm; large, >10 mm.

            .Receptive Field
            Receptive Field
            • Area of skin innervated by a single afferent neuron.
            • Smaller distally an larger proximally
            • Distal regions- greater density of receptors than proximal 
            areas
            • Combination of smaller receptive fields and greater density 
            of receptors distally:
            ✓Allows to distinguish between two closely applied 
            stimuli on fingertip than when the same stimuli  are 
            applied on the back.
            Dermatome:
            • The area of skin innervated by axons from cell bodies in a 
            single dorsal root
            • Information from cutaneous receptors contribute to joint 
            position sense and movement: primarily kinesthetic.

            .DERMATOMES ('')

            .Key Take Aways
            • Understand the functions of somatosensory System
            • Describe the sensory receptors present in human body
            • Explain the cutaneous innervations
            • Explain how the different sensations are carried by different axons

            Peripheral Somatosensory System – Part 2

            .Objectives
            • Know the sensory receptors present in the musculoskeletal system
            • Explain the location, structure and function of muscle spindle
            • Explain the location, structure and function of Golgi tendon organ
            • Explain the location, structure and function of joint receptors 
            • Understand how the different sensations from the musculoskeletal system are 
            carried by different axons 


            .Sensory Receptors in Musculoskeletal System
            • Muscle Spindle
            • Golgi Tendon Organs
            • Joint Receptors


            .Muscle Spindle 1
            • Sensory organ in muscle
            • Consists of:
            o Muscle fibers
            o Sensory ending: Responds to stretch
            ▪ Change in muscle length
            ▪ Velocity of length change
            o Motor endings
            • Quick and tonic stretch of spindle – Ia afferents
            • Tonic stretch of the muscle – II afferents


            .Muscle Spindle 2
            • Intrafusal (inside the spindle) fibers & Extrafusal (outside the 
            spindle) fibers
            • Intrafusal fibers are contractile only at the ends; the central 
            region cannot contract.
            • Two types of intrafusal fibers include:
            o Nuclear bag fibers- clumps of nuclei.
            o Nuclear chain fibers - nuclei arranged in single file.


            .Muscle Spindle 3
            • Two different sensory endings include:
            o Primary/Annulospiral endings of type Ia neurons 
            wrap around the central region of each intrafusal fiber
            (has both, Phasic: quick and Tonic: sustained discharge)
            o Secondary/Flower-spray endings of type II afferents 
            end mainly on nuclear chain fibers adjacent to the 
            primary endings (Tonic only)
            • Gamma motor neurons: maintain the sensitivity of spindle 
            throughout the normal range of muscle lengths.


            .Golgi Tendon Organs (GTO)
            • Stretch receptor sensitive to slight changes in tension
            (< 1g) on a tendon
            • Respond to tension exerted both by active 
            contraction & passive stretch
            • Ib afferent enters capsule and branches into 
            endings that wrap around and between collagen 
            bundles. They carry information from GTO to spinal
            cord.


            .Joint Receptors
            • Respond to mechanical deformation of the capsule
            and ligaments
            • Ruffini’s endings (II)
            o In joint capsule, signal extremes of joint range,
            respond more to passive than active movement
            • Paciniform corpuscles (II)
            o Respond to movement, but not when joint 
            position is  constant
            • Ligament receptors (Ib)
            o Signal tension (similar to GTO)
            • Free nerve endings (Aδ, C)
            o Stimulated by inflammation

            .MUSCULAR AXONS AND RECEPTORS
            The tables in this presentation can be found in the Lundy-Ekman text

            .('')


            .Key Take Aways
            • Know the sensory receptors present in the musculoskeletal system
            • Explain the location, structure and function of Muscle spindle
            • Explain the location, structure and function of Golgi tendon organ
            • Explain the location, structure and function of Joint receptors 
            • Understand how the different sensations from the musculoskeletal system are 
            carried by different axons

            Pain

            .Objectives
            • Understand Chronic Pain
            • Understand Neuropathic Pain
            • Describe the mechanisms of Neuropathic Pain:
            o Central sensitization
            o Ectopic foci
            o Ephaptic transmission
            • Explain the Biopsychosocial Model of Chronic Pain


            .Chronic Pain ('')
                  Chronic pain (>3 months)
                  - Chronic primary pain
                    - Fibromyalgia
                    - Chronic non-specific low back pain
                    - Complex regional pain syndrome
                    - Migraines
                  - Chronic secondary pain
                    - Neuropathic pain
                      - Small fiber neuropathy
                      - Phantom pain
                    - Nociceptive chronic pain
                      - Arthritis pain
                      - Cancer pain
                      - Myofascial pain
                      - Pain due to traumatic injury

                  This outline reflects the hierarchical structure and interconnections between the different elements of chronic pain as depicted in the image.

            .CHRONIC PAIN CLASSIFICATION ('')
                  CHRONIC PRIMARY PAIN
                  - Definition/Explanation
                    - Pain occurring in the absence of clearly identifiable tissue injury. Pain is a disease, arising from dysfunction of the nociceptive system.
                  - Pathophysiology
                    - Central sensitization initiated by gain of function in central nociceptive pathways, resulting in increased pain perception in the absence of tissue damage.
                  - Examples
                    - Migraine, chronic nonspecific low back pain, fibromyalgia, complex regional pain syndrome

                  CHRONIC SECONDARY PAIN
                  - Definition/Explanation
                    - Pain initially arises from underlying disease or specific injury. Pain is a symptom.
                  - Pathophysiology
                    - Nociceptive: Pain arising from stimulation of nociceptors. Physiologic response to tissue damage or potential tissue damage. Usually well localized. Gain of function in central nociceptive pathways may also be present.
                    - Neuropathic: Pain arising from a lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory system. Gain of function in central nociceptive pathways may also be present.
                  - Examples
                    - Nociceptive: Tendonitis, osteoarthritis, cancer pain
                    - Neuropathic: Peripheral neuropathic pain: sciatica, carpal tunnel syndrome, denervation pain. Central neuropathic pain: spinal cord injury, poststroke, deafferentation, phantom limb pain

                  This outline reflects the hierarchical structure and interconnections between the different elements of chronic pain as depicted in the image.

            .Neuropathic Pain
            • The International Association for the Study of Pain defines neuropathic pain 
            as “pain arising as a direct consequence of a lesion or disease affecting the 
            somatosensory system.”


            .Symptoms of Neuropathic Pain (!!F)
            • Paresthesia: painless abnormal sensation in the absence of nociceptor 
            stimulation
            • Dysesthesia: unpleasant abnormal sensation, either evoked or spontaneous
            • Allodynia: pain evoked by a stimulus that normally would not cause pain
            • Secondary hyperalgesia: excessive sensitivity to stimuli that are normally 
            mildly painful in uninjured tissue


            .Mechanism of Neuropathic Pain
            Neuropathic pain is produced by three main mechanisms:
            • Central sensitization
            • Ectopic foci
            • Ephaptic transmission


            .Central Sensitization
            • Main neurophysiologic mechanism underlying chronic pain and 
            • Central nociceptive pathways exhibit increased activity in response to input from nociceptive 
            afferents, 
            • And become activated in response to input from afferents conveying innocuous sensory 
            information, and in some cases spontaneously generate signals without any input whatsoever.
            • This increased CNS activity is driven by the following changes:
            oIncreased excitatory transmitter/receptor activity in nociceptive neurons,
            oThis elicits long-term functional changes that lead to hyperexcitability, spontaneous activity, 
            and structural changes in connections
            oRewiring of connections within the CNS
            oFacilitation of pronociceptive signals and inhibition of antinociceptive signals


            .Central Sensitization ('')


            .Ectopic Foci 1
            • Ectopic means in an abnormal location
            • Ectopic foci describes locations outside of the receptor that generates action potentials, such as 
            in the nerve stump, in areas of myelin damage along the axon, or in the dorsal root ganglion 
            somas. 
            • When myelin is damaged, signals from the exposed axon alter the gene activity in the cell body, 
            stimulating excessive production of mechanosensitive, chemosensitive, and voltage-gated ion 
            channels.


            .Ectopic Foci 2
            • These channels are inserted into the axon membrane in the area of demyelination and allow the 
            demyelinated region to now generate action potentials, in addition to their normal role of 
            conducting action potentials. 
            • These foci can become so sensitive to mechanical stimulation that tapping on an injured nerve 
            can elicit pain or tingling (Tinel’s sign). 
            • Because ectopic foci can generate action potentials without peripheral stimulation, these foci 
            likely contribute to the sensation of spontaneous pain – pain that is temporally distinct from any 
            external stimulus.


            .Ectopic Foci 3 ('')


            .Ephaptic Transmission
            • Also called cross-talk
            • Ephaptic transmission occurs in demyelinated regions as a result of lack of 
            insulation between neurons. 
            • An action potential in one neuron may induce an action potential in another 
            neuron.
            • Ephaptic transmission is likely a mechanism for allodynia in neuropathic pain, 


            .Biopsychosocial Model of Chronic Pain ('')
                  Biopsychosocial Model of Chronic Pain

                  BIOLOGICAL FACTORS
                  - Sex
                  - Genetic factors
                  - Physical Conditioning
                  - Disease Processes
                  - Magnitude of Injury/Disease
                  - Medication Usage
                  - Sleep Patterns

                  PSYCHOLOGIC FACTORS
                  - Anxiety
                  - Beliefs
                  - Coping Skills
                  - Depression
                  - Emotional Stress
                  - Catastrophization
                  - Attitude

                  SOCIAL FACTORS
                  - Financial Burdens
                  - Healthcare Access
                  - Job satisfaction
                  - Support Systems
                  - Personal Relationships
                  - Societal Expectations

                  Pain experience

            .Key Take Aways
            • Understand Chronic Pain
            • Understand Neuropathic Pain
            • Describe the mechanisms of Neuropathic Pain:
            o Central sensitization
            o Ectopic foci
            o Ephaptic transmission
            • Explain the Biopsychosocial Model of Chronic Pain
