      .('24 PT2060_Mod4_Central Somatosensory System-Part 1.pdf')
            Central Somatosensory System – Part I

            .Objectives
            • Understand the concept of the pathways to the brain
            • Explain Somatosensory pathways
            oConscious relay pathways
            oDivergent pathways 
            oNonconscious relay pathways
            • Understand Light touch and conscious proprioception
            • Understand Temperature and pain sensation (fast and slow pain)
            • Clinical features of the lesion to the somatosensory pathways


            .Three-Neuron Somatosensory Pathway ('')


            .Pathways to the Brain
            • When describing pathways in the nervous system, only the neurons with long axons that 
            connect distant regions of the nervous system (projection neurons) are counted.
            • Tract, column, lemniscus or fascile: A bundle of axons with the same origin and a common 
            termination.
            • Somatosensory pathways are named by the origin and termination of the tract that contains the 
            second neuron in the series. 
            o Example: Second neuron in the spinothalamic pathway originates in the spinal cord and 
            terminates in the thalamus. 


            .Somatosensory Pathways
            Three types of pathways carry sensory information to the Brain
            1. Conscious relay pathways: 
            2. Divergent pathways: 
            3. Nonconscious relay pathways:


            .Conscious Relay Pathways
            • Brings information about location and type of stimulation to conscious awareness in 
            the cerebral cortex
            • Information is transmitted with high accuracy, thus providing accurate details 
            regarding the stimulus and its location
            • Conveys light touch, proprioception, nociceptive, and temperature information


            .Divergent Pathways
            • Transmits information to many locations in the brainstem and cerebrum
            • Sensory information is used at both conscious and nonconscious levels. 
            • Signals perceived as aching pain are transmitted via divergent pathways in the central 
            nervous system.


            .Nonconscious relay pathways
            • Brings nonconscious proprioceptive and other movement related information to 
            cerebellum.

            .Somatosensory Pathways ('')
                  Type
                      .Conscious relay ¦El cego i el llenyater
                        -Information Conveyed-
                          Light touch and conscious proprioception
                            -Anatomic Name-
                              Dorsal column / medial lemniscus
                                ¦El cego s'agarra a l'esquena (per darrere) d'algú per a guiar-se
                                -Termination-
                                  Primary somatosensory cortex Γ(fine touch and proprioception)
                          Fast nociception and temperature
                            -Anatomic Name-
                              Spinothalamic Γ(anterolateral tracts → pain and temperature sensations)
                                ¦El llenyater talla el tronc per el costat
                                -Termination-
                                  Primary somatosensory cortex
                      .Divergent
                        -Information Conveyed-
                          Slow nociception
                            -Anatomic Name-
                              Spinomesencephalic
                                -Termination-
                                  Periaqueductal gray of midbrain; superior colliculus
                              Spinoreticular
                                -Termination-
                                  Reticular formation
                              Spinolimbic
                                -Termination-
                                  Amygdala, ventral striatum of basal ganglia, insular cortex
                      .Nonconscious relay
                        -Information Conveyed-
                          Movement-related information
                            -Anatomic Name-
                              Spinocerebellar (see Chapter 15)
                                -Termination-
                                  Cerebellum

            .Conscious Relay Pathways to Cerebral Cortex
            • Four types of somatosensation reach 
            conscious awareness:
            o Light touch
            o Proprioception
            o Nociception 
            o Temperature
            • Pathways to consciousness travel upward in 
            the spinal cord via two routes:
            o Dorsal columns
            o Anterolateral tracts


            .Light Touch and Conscious Proprioception
            • Light touch is the localization of touch and vibration and the ability to discriminate 
            between two closely spaced points touching the skin.
            • Conscious proprioception is the awareness of the movements and relative position of body 
            parts.
            • Stereognosis is the ability to use touch and proprioceptive information to identify an object 
            without vision.
            • Pathways for light touch and conscious proprioception uses a three-neuron relay:
            • Primary neuron conveys information from the receptors to the medulla.
            • Secondary neuron conveys information from the medulla to the thalamus.
            • Tertiary neuron conveys information from the thalamus to the cerebral cortex.
            • Anatomic name: Dorsal Column/medial lemniscus pathway

            .('')


            .Temperature
            • Heat and cold are detected by specialized free nerve endings of small myelinated and 
            unmyelinated neurons
            • A-delta fibers carry impulses produced by cooling
                  ¦Una stalagmita de gel
            • C fibers carry information regarding heat
                  ¦Boca oberta | Olla de costat


            .Pain
            • Pain is composed of both sensation and the emotional response to the sensation
            • Nociceptive: receptors or neurons that receive or transmit information about stimuli 
            that damage or threaten to damage tissue
            • Fast pain (spinothalamic pain) is the initial and immediate sharp sensation that 
            indicates the location of the injury. Conveyed via conscious relay pathway
            • Slow pain (spinolimbic pain) is the dull, throbbing ache following fast pain that is 
            not well localized. Conveyed via divergent pathway


            .Fast, Localized Pain: Lateral Nociceptive System
            • Fast pain uses a three-neuron system:
            • Primary neurons bring information into the dorsal horn of 
            the spinal cord.
            • Axons of secondary neurons cross the midline and 
            project from the  spinal cord to the thalamus.
            • Tertiary neurons project from the thalamus to the 
            cerebral cortex.


            .Slow Nociception: Medial Nociceptive System 1
            • Medial nociceptive system: divergent ascending network of neurons in anterolateral 
            column
            • Uses several pathways with variable numbers of projection neurons, not a three-
            neuron pathway like fast pain.
            • Activity of the medial pain system elicits affective, motivational, withdrawal, 
            arousal, and autonomic responses.


            .Slow Nociception: Medial Nociceptive System 2
            • Information is not somatotopically organized, so slow pain cannot be precisely 
            localized.
            • First neuron: a small, unmyelinated C fiber. Receptors are free nerve endings, sensitive
                  ¦En este cas, la olla bull la mielina i la fa desapareixer
            to noxious heat, chemical, or  mechanical stimulation
            • Axons of ascending projection neurons reach the midbrain, reticular formation, and 
            limbic areas via three tracts in the anterolateral spinal cord.
            • Spinomesencephalic
            • Spinoreticular: Modulates arousal, attention, and sleep-waking cycles.
                  ¦Una malla de dormir (amaca = dormir mal o alçar-se del susto cuan es balançetja) feta de cordetes reticulaes; acuadrets
            • Spinolimbic: arousal, withdrawal, autonomic, and affective responses to pain.
                  ¦Caracter retirat, automàticament trist i molt concient 


            .Fast Vs Slow Pain
            • When fast pain information reaches the somatosensory cortex, the individual 
            is consciously aware of sharp pain in a specific location.
            • If tissue damage has occurred, fast pain is followed by a slow, aching pain.
            • Onset of slow pain is later than fast pain because the impulses travel on smaller, 
            unmyelinated axons.


            .Anatomy and Functions of the Nociceptive Pathways ('') (!!E).Lv1

            .('') (!!E).Lv1


            .Key Take Aways
            • Understand the concept of the pathways to the brain
            • Explain Somatosensory pathways
            oConscious relay pathways
            oDivergent pathways 
            oNonconscious relay pathways
            • Understand Light touch and conscious proprioception
            • Understand Temperature and pain sensation (fast and slow pain)
            • Clinical features of the lesion to the somatosensory pathways

      .('25 PT2060_Mod4_Central Somatosensory System - Part 2.pdf')
            Central Somatosensory System – Part 2

            .Objectives
            • Describe the somatosensory cortex 
            • Explain the functions of somatosensory cortex


            .Primary Somatosensory Area 1
            • The primary somatosensory cortex is located in the 
            postcentral gyrus
            • Postcentral gyrus is, the gyrus posterior to the central 
            sulcus
            • The primary somatosensory cortex receives 
            somatotopically organized information and discriminates 
            the size, texture, and shape of objects


            .Primary Somatosensory Area 2
            • The primary somatosensory cortex receives information from tactile and 
            proprioceptive receptors via a three-neuron pathway: peripheral afferent/dorsal 
            column neuron, medial lemniscus neuron, and thalamocortical neuron
            • Neurons in the primary somatosensory cortex identify the location of stimuli and 
            discriminate among various shapes, sizes, and textures of objects
            • Crude awareness of somatosensation occurs in the ventral posterolateral and ventral 
            posteromedial nuclei of the thalamus,
            • The cortical termination of nociceptive and temperature pathways is more widespread 
            than the discriminative tactile and proprioceptive information and thus is not limited to 
            the primary somatosensory cortex.

            .('')
                  Somatosensory (3-1-2)
                  Lesion: loss of tactile localization
                  and conscious proprioception
                  Somatosensory (3-1-2)
                  Cortical Area
                  Primary somatosensory
                  Function
                  Discriminates shape,
                  texture, or size of objects
                  Lesions cause
                  Loss of tactile localization
                  and conscious proprioception

            .Perception
            • Perception is the interpretation of sensation into meaningful forms. 
            • Perception is an active process, requiring interaction among the brain, the body, and 
            the environment. 
            • For example, eye movements are essential for visual perception, and manipulating 
            objects improves the ability to recognize objects via tactile input. 
            • Perception involves memory of past experiences, motivation, expectations, selection of 
            sensory information, and active search for pertinent sensory information. 
            • Many areas of the cerebrum are involved in perception, including the secondary 
            sensory areas and the cortical association areas.


            .Secondary Somatosensory Area 1
            • The secondary somatosensory area, analyzes information from the primary 
            somatosensory cortex and the thalamus to provide stereognosis and memory of the tactile 
            and spatial environment. 
            • The secondary somatosensory area is located posterior to the primary somatosensory 
            cortex.


            .Secondary Somatosensory Area 2
            • Secondary sensory areas contribute to the analysis of one type of sensory information. 
            • For example, if one picks up a pen, the primary somatosensory cortex registers that the object is 
            small, smooth, and cylindrical.
            • The secondary somatosensory area recognizes the object as a pen, although a different area of 
            the cortex is required to name the object
            • Secondary somatosensory areas integrate tactile and proprioceptive information obtained from 
            manipulating an object
            • Neurons in the secondary somatosensory area provide stereognosis by comparing 
            somatosensation from the current object with memories of other objects

            .('')


            .Key Take Aways
            • Describe the somatosensory cortex 
            • Explain the functions of somatosensory cortex

            Ascending Tracts: DCML, Spinothalamic and Trigeminothalamic Tract

            .Template Cortex ('')

            Midbrain

            Pons

            Medulla

            Spinal Cord

            C
            T
            L Dorsal Horn
            Ventral Horn


            .3-Neuron Chain Tracts

            • Dorsal Column Medial Lemniscus (DCML)
            • Spinothalamic
            • Trigeminothalamic Tract

            Important Points:
            What division do sensory fibers take to reach the spinal cord (Medial vs. Lateral)?
            Where does each synapse occur?
            Where does the tract cross?
            If a lesion occurred at a certain level, what would be the deficit and what part of the body would be affected?
            What sensory information does the tract carry and how would we test that the tract is intact?


            .Dorsal Column Medial Lemniscus (DCML) 
            • Carries discriminative touch, vibration, and joint position 
            sense information
            • 1st order neuron
            • Cell body in dorsal root ganglion
            • Enters spinal cord as medial division fiber
            • Synapses on ipsilateral gracile or cuneate nuclei
            • 2nd order neuron
            • Cell body in gracile or cuneate nuclei
            • Immediately crosses
            • Ascends to synapse in VPL of thalamus
            • 3rd order neuron
            • Cell body in VPL of thalamus
            • Ascends through posterior limb of internal capsule
            • Terminates in primary somatosensory cortex


            .Lesions to the DCML ('')


            .Spinothalamic (SpTH) Tract
            • Carries pain and temperature information
            • 1st order neuron
            • Cell body in dorsal root ganglion
            • Enters spinal cord through lateral division fibers 
            into Lissaurs tract
            • Synapses in dorsal horn
            • 2nd order neuron
            • Cell body in dorsal horn gray matter
            • Immediately crosses the spinal cord to the 
            contralateral anterolateral system
            • Ascends to synapse in the VPL of the thalamus
            • 3rd order neuron
            • Cell body in VPL of thalamus
            • Ascends through posterior limb of internal 
            capsule
            • Terminates in primary somatosensory cortex

            .Lesions to the SpTH Tract ('')

            .Trigeminothalamic Tract ('') (!!F)

      .('27 PT2060_Mod4_ Ascending Tracts - Spinocerebellar.pdf')
            Spinocerebellar Tracts

            .2 Neuron Chain Ascending Sensory Tracts

            • Dorsal Spinocerebellar Tract
            • Cuneocerebellar Tract
            • Ventral Spinocerebellar Tract

            Important Points:
            What division do sensory fibers take to reach the spinal cord (Medial vs. Lateral)?
            Where does each synapse occur?
            Where does the tract cross?
            What sensory information does the tract carry?
            Compare and contrast these with the DCML and SpTH tracts.


            .Spinocerebellar Tracts ('')


            .Dorsal Spinocerebellar Tract ('')
            • Receptors in the muscle spindles in trunk/LEs
            • Carries nonconscious proprioceptive information from 
            trunk/LEs
            • 1st order neuron 
            • Cell body in dorsal root ganglion
            • Enters via medial division of dorsal roots
            • Synapses in Clarke’s nucleus of intermediate grey
            • 2nd order neuron
            • Cell body in Clarke’s nucleus
            • Stays in ipsilateral white matter of spinal cord 
            traveling through inferior cerebellar peduncle
            • Terminates in the cerebellum


            .Cuneocerebellar Tract
            • Receptors in muscle spindles of UEs
            • Carries non-conscious proprioceptive information from UEs
            • 1st order neuron
            • Cell body in dorsal root ganglion
            • Enters via medial division of dorsal roots
            • Ascends in white matter lateral aspect of cuneate 
            fasciculus 
            • Synapses in the accessory cuneate nucleus in medulla
            • 2nd order neuron
            • Cell body in accessory cuneate nucleus
            • Stays ipsilateral traveling through the inferior cerebellar 
            peduncle
            • Terminates in the cerebellum

            .Ventral spinocerebellar Tract
            • Receptors in golgi tendon organs
            • Carries nonconscious proprioceptive information 
            about limb movement
            • 1st order neuron
            • Cell body in dorsal root ganglion
            • Enters via medial division dorsal roots
            • Synapses on lateral spinal border neurons of 
            the intermediate gray
            • 2nd order neuron
            • Cell body in intermediate gray
            • Crosses in spinal cord and at the level of the 
            superior cerebellar peduncle
            • Majority of fibers will terminate on ipsilateral 
            cerebellum (due to 2 crossings) and some will 
            terminate on contralateral cerebellum

..5.0. Module Introduction

      .Welcome to Module 5!
            -In this module you will attend Immersion 2A where you use brain specimens to review the neuroanatomy of the brain and supportive structures, including the dural venous sinuses and reflections,  the external and internal morphology of the cerebral hemispheres, cerebral blood supply, brainstem, and cerebellum. This will provide you with the foundational knowledge to recognize structures and areas of the brain that may be involved in common diagnoses physical therapists treat in the clinic.
                  -Please contact faculty member Pam Dunlap: dunlappm@pitt.edu if you have questions regarding this specific module and labs. 

      .Learning Objectives
            Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to: 
                  Explain the principles of general nervous system organization and function.  
                  Identify the external morphology of the brain including the cerebral hemispheres, the supportive systems of the meninges, the ventricles and cerebrospinal fluid. 
                  Relate the clinical manifestations of neural dysfunction or injury and probable sites of lesions.  
                  Identify the external and internal morphology of the medial cortex, the brainstem, cranial nerves and cerebellum.  
                  Identify the structure and function of the anterior and posterior circulatory systems.

      .('https://www.safety.pitt.edu/ehs/laboratory-safety')
      .('PT_2060_Lab_5_safety_in_the_human_anatomy_lab_templated.pdf')
            PT2060 SAFETY IN THE HUMAN ANATOMY LABORATORY LAB 5 1 

            PT2060 
 
            SAFETY IN THE HUMAN ANATOMY LABORATORY 

            The experience of working with brain specimens is a unique privilege. The people 
            who donate their brains for study do so out of the highest motivation: the desire to 
            benefit society and other individuals by aiding in the training of health 
            professionals. Because of their generosity, students at the University of Pittsburgh 
            have an opportunity to experience firsthand the human brain. It is, therefore, the 
            responsibility of every student who uses the human anatomy lab to always 
            demonstrate appropriate respect for the human beings who make this experience 
            possible. 

            This includes:  
            1. Returning the brain specimens to the appropriate bin and ensuring the brain 
            is adequately covered in solution. 
            2. Keeping all parts of the brains on the tables. 
            3. Being careful where items are placed, both to ensure the integrity of the 
            brain structures and for the respect and safety of your peers (e.g., don’t place 
            soiled items on the stool seats or sharp instruments where they pose a 
            hazard). 
            4. Placing tools used in the dishwasher. 
            5. Wiping up around the sink after use. 
            6. Demonstrating a respectful attitude to others. 

            The brains are stored in a diluted cleaning solution. It is important for everyone 
            who uses the Human Anatomy lab to take appropriate safety precautions. The 
            lab has an excellent negative air-flow system in which air is continuously pulled 
            through the room. For the airflow system to work correctly, the lab doors must 
            be closed. Please do not prop open the doors at any time. Also, do not hold 
            doors open while waiting for your classmate to come down the hall or to finish 
            cleaning up at the end of the class period. 

            Students must wear gloves whenever handling human specimens or lab 
            equipment. Please do your best to conserve the resources and only use one pair 
            per class. Goggles, safety glasses or face shields must also be worn at all times 
            when being in the SHRS Human Anatomy lab. While there is limited liquid 
            chemical splash risk, the brain specimens are submerged in liquid, which does 

            PT2060 SAFETY IN THE HUMAN ANATOMY LABORATORY LAB 5 2 

            pose a risk for splashing when removing and returning the brains to the 
            appropriate bin. Should an injury happen, eyewash stations and first-aid kits are 
            available in the lab. Your instructor will show you where these are located. 
            Students have the option to change into clothing to be worn only during lab time 
            and may wear protective over clothing (e.g., lab coat) while working in the lab if 
            they wish; the quantity of disposable lab coats in the lab is limited. Closed-toe 
            shoes and socks are required whenever in the lab. Crocs are not acceptable 
            shoe wear due to the numerous ventilation holes which would allow spilled 
            contents to come into direct contact with your feet.  

            The use of sharp instruments including scalpels and scissors are not allowed 
            unless the procedure is supervised by the instructor. For the purpose of the 
            class, probes and tweezers are the recommended tools when pointing and 
            moving structures around. Please do not use a pencil. 

            Students who are pregnant or who become pregnant during the semester must 
            inform their obstetrical health care provider that they are working with human 
            cadavers and must take any additional precautions (e.g., wearing a respirator) as 
            required by their obstetrical practitioner. A written note allowing the student to 
            participate in the lab along with any additional precautions clearly indicated 
            must be received from the obstetrical practitioner prior to a student being 
            allowed to return to the cadaver lab. 

            Access to the Human Anatomy lab is restricted to currently enrolled students, 
            faculty, and staff. No one who is not enrolled in the programs is allowed in the 
            lab at any time except in the presence of a faculty member. While students 
            enrolled in anatomy have access to the lab outside of regularly scheduled class 
            time for studying, please note that no student is allowed in the lab alone. There 
            must always be two or more students currently enrolled in one of the courses 
            listed above unless accompanied by a faculty member or tutor and you must 
            have your ID card with you. This is for your safety. 

            Please note that food and beverages (or their containers), lip balm, gum, and all 
            other substances that may come in contact with your lips or mouth are not 
            allowed in the lab at any time! 

            If there are any other safety concerns about the Human Anatomy lab, please 
            bring them to the neuroscience professor and to the PT program directors. We 

            PT2060 SAFETY IN THE HUMAN ANATOMY LABORATORY LAB 5 2 

            will do our best to address such concerns so that all students can benefit from 
            this unique opportunity to study the human brain.

..Module 6: Peripheral & Central Motor Systems
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////


//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
..6.0. Module Introduction
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

      In this module, you will review spinal cord organization and reflexes before learning about the major descending pathways that relay motor commands from the central nervous system (CNS) to the peripheral nervous system (PNS), enabling movement and motor control.  

      Important Information
      Please contact faculty member Jasmine Edwards: jsedwards@pitt.edu if you have questions regarding this specific module.

      OR 

      Please contact faculty members Shilpa Gaikwad: sbgaikwad@pitt.edu or Pam Dunlap: dunlappm@pitt.edu if you have questions regarding the Midterm Exam. 

      .Learning Objectives
            Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to:  
                  Describe lower motor neurons (LMN) and signs of LMN lesions. 
                  Identify and describe spinal cord reflexes. 
                  Describe the descending motor pathways. 
                  Describe the motor cortex and its components. 
                  Identify upper motor neuron lesions (UMN) and differentiate them from LMN lesions.

//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
..6.1. Background Readings and Materials
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

      .('28 Mod6_Peripheral Motor System - Lower Motor Neurons.pdf')
            Neuroscience

            Peripheral Motor System: Skeletal Muscles & Lower Motor Neurons

            University of Pittsburgh Department of Physical Therapy

            Jasmine Edwards, PT, DPT, NCS


            .To Be Covered
            • Review skeletal muscle contraction.
            • Define and describe lower motor neurons.
            • Review myotomes.
            • Describe motor units.


            .Skeletal Muscle


            .Lower Motor Neurons

            • Only neurons that send signals to skeletal muscle fibers
            • Cell bodies are located in ventral horn and axons exit via ventral root

            Lundy-Ekman, L. 2023. Neuroscience (6th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .Alpha & Gamma Neurons
                  Axon Size and Myelination
                        .Large myelinated
                              Axon Type
                                    Aα
                              Innervates
                                    alpha Extrafusal muscle fibers           
                        .Medium myelinated
                              Axon Type
                                    Aγ
                              Innervates
                                    gamma Intrafusal muscle fibers 

            .Golgi Tendon Organ

            • Responds to muscle tension
            • Adjusts muscle contraction during movement

            Lundy-Ekman, L. 2023. Neuroscience (6th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .Motor Units

            • An alpha motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates
            • Slow twitch (Type I)
            • Smaller motor neuron, slower conduction → slow twitch muscle fibers 
            • More resistant to fatigue (e.g. postural muscles)
            • Ex: soleus
            • Fast twitch (Type II)
            • Larger motor neuron, faster conduction → fast twitch muscle fibers 
            • High levels of force for shorter time periods
            • Ex: gastrocnemius
            • ↑ fine control of a muscle
            • ↓ size or innervation ratio of the motor unit 


            .Lower Motor Neurons

            • Motor pools: all the motor neurons that innervate a single muscle

            Haines, D. E., & Mihailoff, G. A. 2018. Fundamental Neuroscience for Basic and Lundy-Ekman, L. 2023. Neuroscience (6th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).
            Clinical Applications (5th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .Myotomes

            • Group of muscles innervated by a single spinal nerve

            From: https://asia-spinalinjury.org/international-standards-neurological-classification-sci-isncsci-worksheet/


            .Key Take Aways
            • Peripheral nervous system is comprised of lower motor neurons (alpha & 
            gamma) and the muscles they innervate
            • Alpha and gamma neurons work together to maintain stretch sensitivity of the 
            muscle over various lengths
            • Motor units are an alpha motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates and 
            its size is dependent on the task to be performed
            • Motor pools are arranged topographically in the anterior horn of the spinal cord

            Peripheral Motor System: Spinal Cord Motor Function

            University of Pittsburgh Department of Physical Therapy

            Jasmine Edwards, PT, DPT, NCS


            .To Be Covered

            .Spinal Reflexes 1

            • Can operate without brain input 
            • Brain modulates neural activity in spinal 
            cord to influence stretch reflex
            • Muscle stretch reflex
            • Muscle contraction that occurs with a 
            quick stretch

            2. Quick stretch of 
            muscle sensed by 
            muscle spindle

            3. 1A fibers project to 
            motor neurons in spinal 
            cord that innervate quad 

            4. Motor neuron sends 
            signal to contract muscle

            1. Quad tendon 
            tapped with hammer

            Haines, D. E., & Mihailoff, G. A. (2018). Fundamental Neuroscience for Basic and Clinical 
            Applications (5th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .Spinal Reflexes 2

            • Reciprocal inhibition: inhibits 
            antagonist muscle

            2. Quick stretch of 
            muscle sensed by 
            muscle spindle

            3. 1A fibers project to 
            motor neurons in spinal 
            cord that innervate 
            hamstring 

            4. Motor neuron is 
            inhibited – hamstring 
            remains passive.

            1. Quad tendon 
            tapped with hammer

            Haines, D. E., & Mihailoff, G. A. (2018). Fundamental Neuroscience for Basic and Clinical 
            Applications (5th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .Spinal Reflexes 3

            • Autogenic inhibition: tendon 
            receptor responds to high tension

            2. Tension in tendon 
            sensed by golgi 
            tendon organ

            3. 1b fibers project to 
            motor neurons in spinal 
            cord that innervate quad

            4. Motor neuron is 
            inhibited – quads stops 
            contracting.

            1. Quad tendon 
            tapped with hammer

            Haines, D. E., & Mihailoff, G. A. (2018). Fundamental Neuroscience for Basic and Clinical 
            Applications (5th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .Spinal Reflexes 4

            • Withdrawal & crossed extension reflex

            Lundy-Ekman, L. 2023. Neuroscience (6th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .Lower Motor Neuron Lesions

            • Signs include:
            • Decrease or loss of reflexes - hyporeflexia
            • Paresis or paralysis
            • Muscle atrophy
            • Hypotonia, flaccidity


            .Key Take Aways
            • Spinal reflexes can occur without brain input
            • Deep tendon reflex is a monosynaptic reflex that occurs due to a quick stretch 
            of the muscle while reciprocal inhibition prevents the antagonist muscle from 
            contracting
            • Autogenic inhibition responds to high tension in the muscle
            • Flexor withdrawal reflex occurs due to a noxious stimulus being applied to a 
            limb and the flexor muscles being activated to pull limb away 
            • Lower motor neuron lesions signs are hyporeflexia, paresis or paralysis, muscle 
            atrophy, and hypotonia or flaccidity

                              .Vestibulospinal Tracts
                                    Medial VST (Blue)
                                          1. Origin: medial vestibular nuclei
                                          2. Descends bilaterally to upper spinal cord as part of medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)
                                          3. Terminates: medial alpha motor neurons & 
                                          interneurons in cervical spine
                                          4. Function: control of neck musculature; head-
                                          on-trunk stabilization
                                    Lateral VST (Red)
                                          1.Origin: lateral vestibular nucleus
                                          2.Descends ipsilateral to all cord 
                                          3.Terminates: medial alpha motor neurons & 
                                          interneurons at all levels of spinal cord
                                          4.Function: excites motor neurons to trunk and 
                                          ipsilateral proximal limb extensors (antigravity 
                                          muscles) for control of posture and balance
                              .Reticulospinal Tract
                                    1. Origin: reticular formation in pons and 
                                    medulla
                                    2. Descends ipsilateral 
                                    3. Terminates: medial interneurons to influence 
                                    motor neurons to axial muscles and limb 
                                    extensors throughout entire body
                                    4. Function: responsible for anticipatory 
                                    postural adjustments during movements
                              .Lateral Motor Pathways
                                    .Rubrospinal Tract
                                          1. Origin: red nucleus in midbrain
                                          2. Decussates in midbrain and 
                                          descends contralaterally from origin
                                          3. Terminates: lateral motor neurons and 
                                          interneurons in the ventral horn of 
                                          spinal cord (mostly cervical spine)
                                          4. Function: movement of contralateral 
                                          upper extremity
                                    .Corticospinal
                                          1. Origin: motor cortex 
                                          2. Travels through corona radiata and internal 
                                          capsule down through brainstem
                                          3. Includes:
                                          oLateral tract: 80-90% decussate in caudal 
                                          medulla, travel contralaterally 
                                          oAnterior tract: 10-20% remain uncrossed, 
                                          travel ipsilaterally
                                          4. Terminates: Interneurons and alpha motor 
                                          neurons in ventral horn of spinal core
                                          5. Function: voluntary movement of limbs; 
                                          enables fractionation of movement
                                    .Corticobulbar
                                          1. Origin: motor cortex for the face
                                          2. Travels through the internal capsule
                                          3. Descends into the pons and medulla
                                          4. Terminates: cranial nerve nuclei
                                          5. Function: voluntary movement of the 
                                          face, head, and neck
                              .Key Take Aways
                                    • There are medial and lateral motor pathways that are responsible for movement.
                                          • Medial:
                                                • Vestibulospinal
                                                • Reticulospinal
                                          • Lateral:
                                                • Rubrospinal
                                                • Corticospinal
                                                • Corticobulbar

                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              Module 6  
                              Motor System - Descending Pathways  
                              Transcript  

                              Introduction 
                              Jasmine Edwards: In this interactive, we will discuss the central motor system, focusing on the descending 
                              pathways.  

                              .Motor Pathways 
                              In this figure of the cross section of the spinal cord, we can see the ascending sensory pathways in blue on the 
                              right and the descending motor pathways in red on the left. We will be focusing on the motor pathways. 
                              Descending upper motor neuron pathways in red arise from the cerebral cortex and brain stem. 
                              These descending motor pathways can be divided into lateral motor systems and medial motor systems based on 
                              their location in the spinal cord.   

                              .Medial Motor Pathways 
                              We will now begin discussing the descending pathways starting with the medial motor pathways.  

                              .Vestibulospinal Tracts 
                              There are two vestibulospinal tracts, the medial in blue and the lateral in red. The medial vestibulospinal tract 
                              begins in the medial vestibular nuclei, descends bilaterally, and is associated with the spinal accessory nerve for 
                              neck control rotation, and lifting of the head and shoulder blade orientation for postural control. The lateral 
                              vestibulospinal tract begins in the lateral vestibular nucleus in the brainstem and descends to all levels of the 
                              spinal cord. 

                              This tract is important for the maintenance of upright posture and balance. It is always active when upright to 
                              maintain the center of gravity over the base of support, thus allowing it to respond to the slightest destabilization. 
                              Please select each component on the diagram to learn more details about the vestibulospinal tracts. 

                              .Reticulospinal Tract 
                              The reticulospinal tract arises from the reticular formation in the brainstem and descends ipsilaterally to activate 
                              postural muscles and limb extensors while modulating muscle tone. This tract provides anticipatory postural 
                              adjustments to prepare the body for upcoming movements that would otherwise be destabilizing. 

                              Please select each component on the diagram to learn more details about the reticulospinal tract on the 
                              flashcards. On each flashcard, click on "Turn" to reveal the answer. Use the arrows to navigate between 
                              flashcards. 

                              .Lateral Motor Pathways  
                              We will now move on to discuss the lateral motor pathways. 

                              .Rubrospinal Tract 
                              The rubrospinal tract shown in blue, originates in the mid brain from the red nucleus and immediately crosses, 
                              terminating mostly in the cervical spine, thus being mostly responsible for upper extremity limb movement. It is 
                              involved in stimulation of flexor muscles and hand and finger movement along with the lateral cortical spinal tract. 
                              It is often not lesioned in isolation, so there will often be other motor deficits present. It travels in close proximity to 
                              the lateral corticospinal tract and works closely together with it for upper extremity movement. 
                              Please select each component on the diagram to learn more details about the rubrospinal tract.  
     
                              .Corticospinal 
                              The lateral corticospinal tract is the most important pathway controlling voluntary movement. It performs selective 
                              motor control of limb movements or fractionated movement, which is the ability to activate individual muscles 
                              independently of other muscles. 

                              This tract arises in the motor planning areas and in the primary motor cortex. On the figure, you can see the tract 
                              arising from different areas of the cortex associated with different parts of the body. It then travels from the 
                              primary motor cortex through the internal capsule, the anterior ponds, to cross in the lower medula at the 
                              pyramids of the medulla and terminates in the lateral spinal cord. Approximately 90% of lateral corticospinal axons 
                              cross to the contralateral side, and 10% travel ipsilaterally in the anterior corticospinal tract. 

                              Please select each component on the diagram to learn more details about the corticospinal tract. 

                              .Corticobulbar 
                              The corticobulbar tracts provide voluntary control of muscles in the head and many muscles in the neck. These 
                              tracts arise in the motor areas of the cerebral cortex for the face, travels medially to the cortical spinal tract, and 
                              then projects to cranial nerve nuclei in the brain stem for all cranial nerves with a motor component, which is 
                              cranial nerves 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, and 12. 

                              Corticobulbar tracts facilitate lower motor neurons, innervating the muscles of the face, tongue, varyx and larynx, 
                              as well as the trapezius and sternal lydid mastoid muscles, Also, information from the frontal eye fields project to 
                              cranial nerves 3, 4, and 6 for control of eye movement. You can see that the tract terminates in the various cranial 
                              nerve nuclei, including the trigemital nerve nuclei, for control of muscles of mastication, facial nerve nuclei for 
                              control of facial musculature, cranial nerve 12 nuclei for control of the tongue, and cranial nerve 11 nuclei for 
                              control of the trapezius external clydoid mastoid muscles. 

                              Please select each component on the diagram to learn more details about the corticobulbar tract on the 
                              flashcards. On each flashcard, click on "Turn" to reveal the answer. Use the arrows to navigate between 
                              flashcards. 

                              .Key Takeaways 
                              The key takeaways from this interactive, are there remedial and lateral motor pathways that are responsible for 
                              movement? 
                              The medial pathways are the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts, and the lateral pathways are the 
                              rubrospinal, corticospinal, and corticobulbar tracts.

                  Neuroscience

                  Central Motor System: Motor Cortex

                  University of Pittsburgh Department of Physical Therapy

                  Jasmine Edwards, PT, DPT, NCS


                  .To Be Covered

                  • Describe the motor cortex and its role in the control of movement.


                  .Motor Cortex Components

                  • Primary motor cortex
                  • Supplementary motor cortex
                  • Premotor cortex
                  • Posterior parietal cortex
                  • Cingulate motor cortex

                  https://www.brainhq.com/brain-connection/the-anatomy-of-movement/


                  .Primary Motor Cortex (M1)

                  • Located in precentral gyrus
                  • Source of most neurons in the corticospinal and 
                  corticobulbar tracts
                  • Voluntary movements especially of the fingers 
                  and hands
                  • Somatotopically organized

                  Haines, D. E., & Mihailoff, G. A. (2018). Fundamental Neuroscience for Basic and Clinical 
                  Applications (5th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US). 


                  .Supplementary Motor Cortex (SMA)

                  • Map of body musculature (less 
                  organized)
                  • Involved in:
                  • Sequence of movements and 
                  orientation of body and limb in 
                  space
                  • Organization or planning 
                  sequence of muscle activation

                  https://www.brainhq.com/brain-connection/the-anatomy-of-movement/

                  .N/A
                  A: Random movement (no 
                  planning) = increased 
                  activity in hand area of 
                  motor cortex

                  B: Planned and executed 
                  movement in a specific 
                  sequence: increased 
                  activity in M1 & SMA

                  C: Mentally planned, never 
                  executed: SMA only

                  Haines, D. E., & Mihailoff, G. A. (2018). Fundamental Neuroscience for Basic and Clinical 
                  Applications (5th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US). 


                  .Premotor Cortex

                  • Primarily responsible for movement planning
                  • Organizes postural adjustments that are required 
                  to make a movement
                  • Ventral premotor cortex (PMv): 
                  • Transform visual information about the properties 
                  of objects (shape) into commands for movement 
                  (e.g grasp) 
                  • Dorsal premotor cortex (PMd):
                  • Transform information about location of objects 
                  in extrapersonal space into direction for reaching
                  • Lesion may result in motor apraxia 

                  Kandel, E. R., Schwartz, J. H., Jessell, T. M., Siegelbaum, S. A., & Hudspeth, A. 
                  J. (2012). Principles of Neural Science (5th ed.). McGraw-Hill Professional. 


                  .Posterior Parietal Cortex

                  • An association area that integrates 
                  sensory and motor information for 
                  motor planning and sensory guidance 
                  of movements
                  • Demonstrated selective activations 
                  for the physical properties of the 
                  object (shape, size, orientation…)
                  • Activated during observation of 
                  movements

                  https://www.brainhq.com/brain-connection/the-anatomy-of-movement/


                  .Cingulate Motor Cortex

                  • Close to limbic cortex
                  • Motivational and emotional roles in motor planning and execution (reward-based 
                  movements)
                  • Pain info projected here, helping to drive pain-related motor behaviors


                  .Key Take Aways
                  • The primary motor cortex is responsible for voluntary movements.
                  • The supplementary motor cortex is responsible for organizing or planning the 
                  sequence of movements. 
                  • The premotor cortex is responsible for movement planning and organizing 
                  postural adjustments for movement.
                  • The motor portion of the posterior parietal cortex creates a map of space for 
                  movement.
                  • The cingulate motor cortex is involved in movements that have a motivational 
                  and emotional role.

            .('33 PT2060_Mod6_Central Motor System - UMN Lesions.pdf')
                  Neuroscience

                  Central Motor System: UMN Lesions

                  University of Pittsburgh Department of Physical Therapy

                  Jasmine Edwards, PT, DPT, NCS


                  .To Be Covered

                  • Describe signs and symptoms of an upper motor neuron lesion.
                  • Differentiate an upper motor neuron lesion from a lower motor neuron lesion.


                  .UMN Lesion

                  • Damage to the motor neurons in the cerebrum, brainstem, or spinal cord
                  • Signs:
                  • Paresis or paralysis
                  • Increased muscle tone
                  • Hyperreflexia
                  • Abnormal reflexes: Babinski, Hoffman
                  • Disuse muscle atrophy


                  .UMN Lesion Signs 1

                  • Spasticity
                  • “disordered sensory-motor control, resulting from 
                  an upper motor neuron lesion” (Burridge, 2005)
                  • Velocity-dependent hypertonia
                  • Results from neuromuscular overactivity


                  .UMN Lesion Signs 2

                  • Rigidity
                  • Decerebrate rigidity: corticospinal and 
                  rubrospinal influence are removed
                  • Reticulospinal and vestibulospinal tracts 
                  predominate on spinal extensor motor neurons
                  • Decorticate rigidity: cortical input to red 
                  nucleus removed


                  .UMN Lesion Signs 3

                  • Abnormal muscle synergies
                  • Activation of muscle groups that are unable to 
                  achieve the desired result


                  .UMN vs LMN Lesion
                        Upper Motor Neuron Lesion
                              Hyperreflexia
                              Contralateral paresis or paralysis (ipsilateral if below level of decussation)
                              Disuse muscle atrophy
                              Hypertonia, spasticity
                        Lower Motor Neuron Lesion
                              Hyporeflexia
                              Ipsilateral paresis or paralysis (peripheral nerve pattern)
                              Neurogenic muscle atrophy
                              Hypotonia, flaccidity

                  .Key Take Aways
                  • Upper motor neuron lesions are due to damage to the motor neurons in the 
                  cerebrum, brainstem, or spinal cord and have different signs than a lower motor 
                  neuron lesion.

//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
..7.0. Module Introduction
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

      This module will examine the cerebellum and basal ganglia, two fundamental brain structures involved in movement, cognition, and emotional regulation. The cerebellum is critical for ensuring smooth and coordinated motor functions, whereas the basal ganglia are essential in initiating and maintaining movement. Throughout this module, we will analyze their respective roles in motor control and motor learning. 

      Important Information
            Please contact faculty member Jasmine Edwards: jsedwards@pitt.edu if you have questions regarding this specific module and quiz. 
                  Learning Objectives
                        Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to: 

                        Describe the structure and function of the cerebellar cortex, including cell types.  
                        Identify and explain the main functional divisions of the cerebellum. 
                        Describe the cerebellum’s role in motor control and motor learning. 
                        Identify and explain the components of the basal ganglia and their functions. 
                        Describe the primary circuits of the basal ganglia and its role in motor control and motor learning.

..7.1. Background Readings and Materials

      .Required Readings:
            -Lundy-Ekman Neuroscience: Fundamentals for Rehabilitation 6th edition (2023):   
                  Chapter 15, pages 258-261, 264-266
                  Chapter 16, pages 270-278, 283-284
            -Haines Neuroanatomy Atlas in Clinical Context 10th edition: 
                  Chapter 2, pages 33-34 
                  Chapter 6, pages 127-129 
            -Middleton, F. A., & Strick, P. L. (1998). Cerebellar output: motor and cognitive channels Links to an external site.. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 2(9), 348–354. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1364-6613(98)01220-0
                  ('Cerebellar output - motor')
                        In the past 15 years there have been some dramatic
                        changes in our concepts about the cortical areas that are the
                        target of cerebellar output. It has long been known that
                        multiple cortical areas project to the cerebellum via the cor-
                        tico-ponto-cerebellar pathway1–6. However, as late as 1983,
                        cerebellar output via the thalamus was thought to influence
                        only the primary motor cortex (M1) (Refs 1–3,7). Subse-
                        quently, several studies have shown that the thalamic targets of
                        cerebellar output project more widely to the cerebral cortex
                        than previously recognized. In anatomical experiments, Schell
                        and Strick8 showed that part of the thalamic region which
                        receives cerebellar input innervates a lateral portion of area
                        six, now designated the ventral premotor area (PMv) (see
                        also Orioli and Strick9). Wiesendanger and Wiesendanger10
                        found that another cerebellar recipient zone of the thalamus
                        projects to a cortical region now known as the pre-supple-
                        mentary motor area (pre-SMA). In electrophysiological and
                        anatomical experiments, Sasaki and his colleagues11–13 pro-
                        vided evidence that the cerebellum projected to a region of
                        the frontal lobe that includes the supplementary eye field
                        (SEF) and a portion of posterior parietal cortex. Notably,
                        most of these cortical areas are known to be involved in
                        motor control. An even more radical departure in our con-
                        cepts about cerebellar output was the proposal by Leiner and
                        colleagues14–17 that a portion of the lateral output nucleus of the
                        cerebellum, the dentate, projects via the thalamus to cortical
                        areas concerned with language and cognitive function.
                        In the last five years, we have mapped some of the cor-
                        tical targets of cerebellar output using a novel neuroanatomical

                        tracing technique, retrograde transneuronal transport of
                        neurotropic viruses. Our results confirm that cerebellar output
                        is not limited to M1. Rather, the cerebello-thalamocortical
                        system appears to extend to multiple cortical areas including
                        regions of premotor and prefrontal cortex. Furthermore,
                        virus tracing has shown that distinct regions within the deep
                        cerebellar nuclei form the origin of projections to different
                        cortical areas. We have termed these regions ‘output channels’.
                        In this article, we will briefly review some of our recent find-
                        ings on the anatomical and physiological properties of these
                        output channels.

                        Defining the cortical targets of cerebellar output with
                        virus tracing
                        We found that one strain of herpes simplex virus type 1
                        (HSV1), the McIntyre-B strain, is transported transneur-
                        onally in the retrograde direction in the primate central 
                        nervous system18,19. For example, three days after injections
                        of McIntyre-B into the arm area of M1 (see Fig. 1), densely
                        labeled neurons were found in subdivisions of the ventro-
                        lateral thalamus that are known to innervate M1, such 
                        as ventralis posterior lateralis pars oralis (VPLo) and ven-
                        tralis lateralis pars oralis (VLo). After five days, virus was
                        transported transneuronally in the retrograde direction
                        from first-order neurons in the ventrolateral thalamus to
                        second-order neurons in the deep cerebellar nuclei (dentate
                        and interpositus) and the internal segment of the globus
                        pallidus (GPi). Thus, retrograde transneuronal transport 
                        of the McIntyre-B strain is able to identify the origin of

                        348

                        Cerebellar output: motor
                        and cognitive channels
                        Frank A. Middleton and Peter L. Strick

                        The input to the cerebellum has long been known to originate from widespread regions
                        of the cerebral cortex including the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes. The output of
                        the cerebellum, however, was thought to project mainly to the primary motor cortex.
                        Recent anatomical observations have challenged this view. It is now apparent that
                        cerebellar output goes to multiple cortical areas, including not only the primary motor
                        cortex, but also areas of premotor and prefrontal cortex. In fact, there is growing
                        evidence that each of the areas of cerebral cortex that project to the cerebellum is also
                        the target of cerebellar output. The cerebellar output to individual cortical areas
                        originates from distinct clusters of neurons in the deep nuclei which we have termed
                        ‘output channels’. The individual output channels to the cortical areas we have
                        examined display little or no overlap. Physiological recordings in awake trained
                        primates indicate that neurons in different output channels appear to be involved in
                        distinct aspects of behavior, and in both motor and cognitive functions. These
                        observations indicate that the cerebellar influence on the cerebral cortex is more
                        extensive than previously recognized.

                        T r e n d s i n C o g n i t i v e S c i e n c e s – V o l . 2 , N o . 9 , S e p t e m b e r 1 9 9 8


                        cerebellar and basal ganglia output to specific cortical 
                        areas.
                        To date we have used retrograde transneuronal trans-
                        port of HSV1 to examine subcortical projections via the
                        thalamus to approximately 15 different cortical areas 
                        (Fig. 1). These have included regions of prefrontal cortex
                        involved in cognitive functions such as planning and work-
                        ing memory, regions of inferotemporal cortex involved 
                        in higher order visual processing, as well as cortical areas 
                        concerned with the control of eye, face and limb move-
                        ments18–25. The results of these studies and an analysis of the
                        results of previous studies with conventional tracers have led
                        us to propose three general principles of cerebro–cerebellar
                        interactions:
                        (1) Cerebral cortical areas that project to the cerebellum
                        are the target of cerebellar output. We have observed promi-
                        nent transneuronal labeling of neurons in the deep cerebel-
                        lar nuclei after virus injections into at least six different
                        functional areas of the cerebral cortex. These include: the
                        face, arm and leg representations of M1; the arm represen-
                        tation of the ventral premotor area (PMv); the saccadic 
                        region of the frontal eye field (FEF); the lateral intraparietal
                        area (LIP); and three non-motor areas of prefrontal cortex,
                        the lateral and medial portions of area 9 (9l, 9m) and the
                        dorsal portion of area 46 (46d) (see Refs 18–25 and Fig. 1).
                        Experiments with conventional tracers have shown that each
                        of these cortical regions projects to the pons, and that these
                        projections are topographically organized4–6,26. Moreover,
                        each of these cortical areas is known to be targeted by cer-
                        ebellar recipient regions of the thalamus8,10,13,21,22,24,25,27.
                        Thus, our present results suggest an important principle of
                        reciprocal interconnections, namely the cortical areas that
                        project to the cerebellum via the pons are themselves the
                        target of cerebellar output via the thalamus.
                        The general applicability of this principle needs to be
                        examined in detail. For example, regions of the primary 
                        somatosensory cortex (S1) may provide one exception: S1 
                        is known to provide an input to the ponto-cerebellar sys-
                        tem4,5, but there is as yet no evidence that it is the target of
                        cerebellar output. However, there is a region of the thala-
                        mus where spinothalamic and cerebellar input overlap7. If
                        this region of the thalamus projects to somatosensory cor-
                        tex, then parts of S1 may be reciprocally connected with the
                        cerebellum as well.
                        In addition to the areas already mentioned, anatomical
                        studies have shown that the cerebellum receives projections
                        from a remarkably diverse set of cortical areas, including
                        some prestriate areas in the occipito-temporal region that
                        are involved in visual processing, portions of the cingulate
                        gyrus that are thought to be involved in regulating attention
                        and emotion, and regions of the parahippocampal
                        gyrus4–6,26,28–30. Schmahmann31 has suggested that each of
                        these areas receives input from thalamic regions that are the
                        target of the cerebellar efferents. If this suggestion is correct,
                        and reciprocal cerebro–cerebellar interconnections exist 
                        for these areas, then the cerebellar influence over the cer-
                        ebral cortex will be much more widespread than previously
                        imagined.
                        (2) Cerebral cortical areas that do not project to the 
                        cerebellum are themselves not the target of cerebellar output.

                        Injections of HSV1 into another set of cortical areas labeled
                        very few neurons in the deep cerebellar nuclei, often as few
                        as one or two cells in total. The same virus injections, how-
                        ever, did label many neurons in the output nuclei of the basal
                        ganglia32. Cortical areas without substantial cerebellar input
                        include the ventral portion of area 46 (46v), the lateral 
                        portion of area 12 (12l), and area TE in inferotemporal 
                        cortex32. These cortical areas are known from other studies
                        to have very limited projections to pontine nuclei that in-
                        nervate the cerebellum4–6,26,30. Preliminary results from virus
                        injections into several other cortical areas that do not pro-
                        ject heavily to the pons (area TEO in inferotemporal cortex,
                        and orbital areas 12 and 13) support the general principle
                        that the cerebellum directs its output to those cortical areas
                        that project to it.
                        (3) The cerebellar output channels to different cortical
                        areas are distinct. Virus injections into different cortical
                        areas labeled topographically distinct populations of neur-
                        ons in the deep cerebellar nuclei. For example, dentate 
                        neurons labeled after virus injections into M1 were con-
                        fined to approximately the dorsal third of the nucleus.
                        Moreover, projections from this region of the dentate were
                        somatotopically organized. Neurons labeled from leg M1
                        were located rostrally, those from face M1 caudally, and
                        those from arm M1 at intermediate levels 25. In contrast, the
                        populations of dentate neurons that projected to premotor

                        tral, medial and caudal regions of the nucleus (Fig. 2)20–25,32.
                        Based on these and other observations we have proposed
                        that each population of neurons in the deep cerebellar nu-
                        clei that projects to a specific cortical area is organized into
                        a distinct output channel20,24. To date, we have observed
                        limited overlap in the output channels to different cortical
                        areas.

                        Physiological and behavioral correlations
                        The anatomical findings described above raised an impor-
                        tant question: what is the nature of the information con-
                        veyed to the cerebral cortex by cerebellar projections to dif-
                        ferent cortical areas? For example, it is generally agreed that
                        the dentate neurons that project to M1 send signals related
                        to the control of movement parameters. What type of sig-
                        nals does the dentate send to premotor and prefrontal areas
                        of cortex? To begin to address this issue we examined the 
                        activity of dentate neurons in monkeys and humans during
                        the performance of motor and cognitive tasks.

                        Neuron recording in awake trained primates
                        We recorded the activity of single neurons in the dentate
                        nucleus of awake monkeys trained to perform sequential
                        pointing movements under two different task conditions
                        (Fig. 3)33. In both conditions, the monkey faced a panel
                        with five touch pads numbered 1 to 5 from left to right. A
                        small red light emitting diode (LED) was located over each
                        touch pad. The monkey began a trial by placing his right
                        hand on a hold key for a variable ‘Hold’ period. In the ‘re-
                        membered sequence task’ (REM task24,33), LEDs over three
                        touch pads were illuminated in a pseudo-random sequence
                        as an instruction to the monkey. At the end of a variable
                        ‘Instruction’ period, an auditory ‘Go’ signal told the mon-
                        key to release the hold key and press the three touch pads in
                        the same order that they were illuminated. Thus, the se-
                        quence of movements that the monkey performed during
                        each trial of the REM task was initially stored in ‘working
                        memory’ and then internally guided.
                        In the ‘tracking task’ (TRACK task), an LED over a 
                        single touch pad was illuminated after the ‘Hold’ period,
                        and an auditory ‘Go’ signal was turned on at the same time.

                        Following this signal, the monkey was required to release
                        the hold key and press the indicated touch pad. As soon as
                        the monkey contacted the first touch pad, an LED over a
                        second touch pad was illuminated. The monkey was re-
                        quired to move quickly to this second touch pad. When the
                        monkey contacted the second touch pad, an LED over a
                        third touch pad was illuminated and the monkey was re-
                        quired to move to this touch pad. Thus, the sequence of
                        movements that the monkey performed during each trial of
                        the TRACK task was externally cued.
                        We recorded 172 neurons that were task-related during
                        the reaction time (RT) period in the dentate nucleus of two
                        trained monkeys33. Most task-related neurons were located
                        in the middle third of the dentate, rostro-caudally.
                        Approximately 60% of the task-related neurons (102/172)
                        were classified as ‘task-independent’. These neurons dis-
                        played movement-related activity during the RT period of
                        both the REM and TRACK tasks. Most task-independent
                        neurons were located dorsally in the dentate. This region is
                        likely to be within the output channel that projects to M1
                        (see Figs 2 and 4). Based on their firing patterns, it is likely
                        that the neurons in this output channel are involved in con-
                        trolling aspects of sequential pointing movements, indepen-
                        dent of whether the movements were internally guided or
                        externally cued.
                        On the other hand, approximately 40% of the task-
                        related neurons in the dentate (70/172) were considered
                        ‘task-dependent’ because their activity patterns differed
                        substantially during the TRACK and REM tasks33. More
                        than 75% of the task-dependent neurons (54/70) were
                        termed ‘TRACK’ neurons because they either displayed ac-
                        tivity changes during the RT period only for the TRACK
                        task, or their changes in activity were more pronounced
                        (.650%) for the TRACK task than for the REM task.
                        Many of the TRACK neurons were located ventral and lat-
                        eral to dentate neurons which were task-related, but ‘task-
                        independent’. This localization suggests that TRACK neur-
                        ons are within the output channel that innervates the PMv
                        (Figs 2 and 4). Thus, we can infer from the function of the
                        PMv that the neurons in this output channel appear to be
                        preferentially involved in the generation and control of 
                        sequential movements that are visually guided33.

                        In addition to the TRACK neurons, approximately 16%
                        (27/172) of the task-related neurons in the dentate were ‘in-
                        struction-related’ (I-related)24; that is, they displayed changes
                        in activity during the instructed delay period (Fig. 5). Some

                        activity seen in parts of prefrontal cortex during instructed-

                        tivity in prefrontal cortex used a sequential movement task
                        very similar to the one we used for analysis of activity in the
                        dentate37. Thus, the portion of the dentate nucleus that is
                        connected with the prefrontal cortex appears to be involved
                        in some of the same cognitive functions as that cortical area.
