      .('PT_2060_Control_of_posture_and_gait_templated.docx')
            CONTROL OF POSTURE AND GAIT USING A DUAL-TASK PARADIGM 

            Agenda:
                  5 min
                        -Break up into groups and read through the lab instructions below. Decide who will be the participant, experimenter, and the assistant 
                  5 min
                        Instructor demonstration of all conditions
                  15 min
                        Groups complete and record results for all conditions
                  10 min
                        Class results are compiled, and groups work through the discussion questions
                  5 min
                        Group discussion

            Purpose:
                  -To investigate cortical control of different actions (sitting, walking, obstacle course) using a dual-task paradigm. 

            Objectives: 
                  -Course Objective: Explain general concepts of a global organization and basic functions of the normal, intact nervous system; and theoretical explanations of the nervous system including less well-understood neural mechanisms.

            Unit Objectives: 
                  -Describe brainstem structures and connections and explain their role in motor control. 
                  -Describe the structure and connections of the cerebellum and explain its role in motor control. 
                  -Describe motor-related areas of the cerebral cortex and explain their role in motor control. 

            Specific Session objectives:
                  -To explain the differences in motor control for sitting, walking and a skilled sequential task. 
                  -To explain the use of the dual-task paradigm in probing cortical involvement. 

            Equipment:
                  obstacle course

            Task:
                  -To answer math questions as accurately as possible while sitting, walking and negotiating an obstacle course. 

            General Procedures and Guidelines:
                  -You and your partners will function as a team. One of you will be the experimenter (asking math questions), one will be the participant (the individual performing the movement and answering the math questions), and one the recorder/assistant (keeping track of time, assisting the experimenter). Your roles will stay the same for all three conditions, i.e., the same participant completes all three conditions.  

                  Additionally:
                        1.The participant for this activity should be wearing supportive shoes with no history of ankle injury/instability.

                        2.The experimenter will read the math problems in a loud and clear voice at a consistent pace and will mark correct answers. If the participant does not respond in 3 seconds, count that as an error and keep going to the next math question. If your participant completes all 20 questions, repeat the incorrect ones. If there were no incorrect answers, just start back at the beginning and mark again. 

                        3.The recorder will time each condition for 2 minutes and report when the time expires.

                        4.During the experiment, the participant is to move at a consistent pace and NOT stop to answer math questions. After all the conditions are completed, you are to count the number of correct responses in each condition and report to the class.

            I.Completing the Conditions: Instructions to/for the participant
                  1.Condition 1:
                        -Sitting: Have the participant sit unsupported on the edge of the chair or mat. Instructions: “I would like for you to sit quietly. I will ask you math questions and want you to tell me out loud the answer to each question. Let’s practice. Here’s the question: 10 + 4 – 8. I will give you several seconds to respond before I move to the next question. Your goal is to be 100% accurate in responding to the math questions. We will be doing this for several minutes. Just respond the best you can. Any questions?” 
                        -The experimenter should read the math problems and keep track of correct responses, the recorder keeps track of two minutes and calls TIME. 

                  2.Condition 2:
                        -Walking: Have the participant stand at one of the taped lines. 
                        -Instructions: “I would like for you to walk at your comfortable pace back and forth between the taped lines. Walk naturally, just like you would in your own home. After you walk back and forth two times, I will start asking you math questions just like I did before. Your goal is to be 100% accurate in responding to the math questions. Again, I will give you several seconds to respond before I move to the next question. Try not to stop walking at any time. Any questions?” 
                        -The experimenter should read the questions and keep track of correct responses, the recorder keeps track of two minutes and calls TIME. The recorder should take note of if/how the coordination of walking changes from no-math to math conditions and oversee participant safety. 

                  3. Condition 3:
                        -Obstacle course. Demonstrate going through the obstacle for your participant. Instructions: “I would like for you to go through the obstacle course as accurately as possible. After you go through the obstacle course two times, I will start asking you math questions just like I did before. Your goal is to be 100% accurate in responding to the math questions. Again, I will give you several seconds to respond before I move to the next question. Try not to stop moving at any time. Any Questions?” 
                        -The experimenter should read the questions and keep track of correct responses, the recorder keeps track of two minutes and calls TIME. The recorder should take note of if/how the coordination of completing the obstacle course changes from no-math to math conditions and oversee participant safety.

            II.Analysis
                  1. Each group will report their scores for each condition and a class average of the number of correct responses will be computed for each condition (sitting, walking, and obstacle)

            III.Discussion Questions - Answer the questions below with your group. 
                  1.What are your hypotheses? Which condition did you think would have the highest number of correct answers? Why? What is different about the motor control in each of the conditions?

                  2.In research, having participants do two things at once is called dual-task research. How would this type of design, or doing a dual task with a patient, inform you about the motor control of the task?  

                  3.Why was it important to stress that the participant needed to be 100% accurate with the cognitive task?

                  4.If someone practiced the obstacle course for 10 minutes over the course of two weeks, would the results be any different? Why? What will the individual have learned?

..10.0. Module Introduction

      .This module will explore the autonomic nervous system and its role in maintaining homeostasis, the limbic system's regulation of emotions and drives, and the processes of memory, including the cortical structures involved. 

      Important Information
      Please contact faculty member Jasmine Edwards: jsedwards@pitt.edu if you have questions regarding this specific module and quiz. 

      Learning Objectives
      Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to: 

      Describe the autonomic system and its role in homeostasis 
      Explain the functions of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system. 
      Define and describe the different types of memory. 
      Identify components and functions of the limbic system. 
      Understand higher order cerebral functioning including cognition and executive functioning.

..10.1. Background Readings and Materials
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

      .Required Readings:
            -Lundy-Ekman Neuroscience: Fundamentals for Rehabilitation 6th edition (2023):   
                  Chapter 9, pages 132-134, 137-142
                  Chapter 27, pages 475, 484
                  Chapter 28, pages 495-498
                  Chapter 29, pages 507-509
            -Buccino, G., Binkofski, F., Fink, G. R., Fadiga, L., Fogassi, L., Gallese, V., Seitz, R. J., Zilles, K., Rizzolatti, G., & Freund, H.-J. (2001). Action observation activates premotor and parietal areas in a somatotopic manner: an fMRI studyLinks to an external site.. The European Journal of Neuroscience, 13(2), 400–404. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1460-9568.2001.01385.x
                  ('Action observation activates premotor.pdf')
                        SHORT COMMUNICATION
                        Action observation activates premotor and parietal areas
                        in a somatotopic manner: an fMRI study

                        G. Buccino, F. Binkofski,1 G. R. Fink,1,2 L. Fadiga, L. Fogassi, V. Gallese, R. J. Seitz,1 K. Zilles,2 G. Rizzolatti and
                        H.-J. Freund1
                        Istituto di Fisiologia Umana, UniversitaÁ di Parma, Via Volturno 39, I-43100 Parma, Italy
                        1Department of Neurology, Heinrich Heine University of Duesseldorf, 5 Moorenstrasse, D-40225, Duesseldorf, Germany
                        2Institute of Medicine, Research Center Juelich GmbH, Germany

                        Keywords: action observation, humans, mirror system, parietal lobe, premotor cortex

                        Abstract
                        Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was used to localize brain areas that were active during the observation of
                        actions made by another individual. Object- and non-object-related actions made with different effectors (mouth, hand and foot)
                        were presented. Observation of both object- and non-object-related actions determined a somatotopically organized activation of
                        premotor cortex. The somatotopic pattern was similar to that of the classical motor cortex homunculus. During the observation of
                        object-related actions, an activation, also somatotopically organized, was additionally found in the posterior parietal lobe. Thus,
                        when individuals observe an action, an internal replica of that action is automatically generated in their premotor cortex. In the
                        case of object-related actions, a further object-related analysis is performed in the parietal lobe, as if the subjects were indeed
                        using those objects. These results bring the previous concept of an action observation/execution matching system (mirror
                        system) into a broader perspective: this system is not restricted to the ventral premotor cortex, but involves several
                        somatotopically organized motor circuits.
                        Introduction
                        In the monkey premotor cortex (area F5) there are neurons that
                        discharge both when the monkey performs speci®c hand actions (e.g.
                        grasping an object) and when it observes another individual perform-
                        ing the same or a similar action (Gallese et al., 1996; Rizzolatti et al.,
                        1996a). The hypothesis was forwarded that these neurons, called
                        `mirror neurons', subserve the capacity of individuals to recognise
                        actions made by others.
                        There is growing evidence that a `mirror' system, similar to that
                        described in the monkey, also exists in humans. Electrophysiological
                        studies (Hari et al., 1998; Cochin et al., 1999) showed that when a
                        human subject observes hand actions there is a desynchronization of
                        the motor cortex similar, although weaker, to that occurring during
                        active movements. In agreement with these ®ndings, transcranial
                        magnetic stimulation (TMS) experiments showed that motor-evoked
                        potentials recorded from hand muscles increase during the observation
                        of hand movements (Fadiga et al., 1995; Strafella & Paus 2000).
                        Because the motor cortex of primates does not receive a signi®cant
                        visual input, its activation, during observation of actions made by
                        others, ought to be mediated by the premotor areas that are connected
                        with it. This conclusion has been supported by brain imaging studies
                        showing that during observation of hand/arm actions there is an
                        activation of the ventral premotor cortex centred to the Broca's region
                        (Grafton et al., 1996; Rizzolatti et al., 1996b; Decety et al., 1997;
                        Grezes et al., 1998; Iacoboni et al., 1999). Considering, however, that
                        Broca's area is the cortical motor speech centre, the possibility cannot

                        be excluded that Broca's area activation, during action observation,
                        were due to an internal verbalization of the observed actions rather
                        than to a `mirror' mechanism.
                        The main aim of the present study was to assess whether the
                        observation of actions made with different effectors would activate
                        speci®c parts of the premotor cortex in accord with the somatotopic
                        motor organization of the region. This activation speci®city, if proved,
                        would show on one side, that the mirror system is not limited to hand
                        action and on the other, would allow one to rule out the hypothesis that
                        the activation of Broca's area, reported during hand action observa-
                        tion, was due to verbalization. If the verbalization hypothesis were
                        true, Broca's area should be the major activation focus during action
                        observation, regardless of the effector used.
                        The second aim was to determine to what extent the presence of an
                        object in¯uences the analysis of an observed action. When an
                        individual acts on an object, a speci®c, pragmatic analysis of the
                        object is carried out in the parietal lobe. This analysis is distinct from
                        the semantic processing performed in the temporal lobe (Jeannerod,
                        1994; Milner & Goodale, 1995). Would the observation of object-
                        related actions evoke this pragmatic analysis? An activation of
                        pragmatic representations would be evidence, that during action
                        observation, individuals internally `re-act' the observed action in terms
                        of both action and the object acted upon.

                        Materials and methods
                        Subjects
                        Twelve healthy, right-handed subjects, aged 25±38 years-old took part
                        in the experiment. All subjects (except two) were naive as to the
                        purpose of the experiment. They all gave their written consent to the

                        Correspondence: Dr G. Rizzolatti, as above.
                        E-mail: ®sioum@symbolic.pr.it
                        Received 27 July 2000, revised 16 October 2000, accepted 2 November 2000

                        European Journal of Neuroscience, Vol. 13, pp. 400±404, 2001 ã Federation of European Neuroscience Societies


                        experimental procedure. The study was approved by the Ethical
                        Committee of the Heinrich Heine University, Duesseldorf.
                        MRI scanner and scanning sequences
                        Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) measurements were
                        performed on a 1.5 Tesla Siemens Vision scanning system using
                        standard echo-planar imaging (EPI) and a standard radio frequency
                        head coil for signal transmission and reception. Thirty consecutive
                        slices orientated parallel to the anterior±posterior commissure plane
                        and covering the whole brain were acquired. The following EPI
                        sequences were used: repetition time, 5 s; signal-gathering time
                        (echo-time), 66 ms; a, 90°; voxel size, 33334 mm.
                        Experimental protocol
                        While being scanned, subjects were asked to carefully observe
                        different videotaped object- and non-object-related actions, per-
                        formed by another individual with different effectors (mouth, arm/
                        hand and foot). These videotaped actions were presented on a screen,
                        situated outside the scanner. Subjects could see them through a mirror
                        (10315 cm) which was positioned in the scanner in front of them.
                        Videotaped actions were presented in sequences 25 s long. During
                        each sequence the same action was presented 3±4 times. Each
                        sequence was presented twice during the experimental session. The
                        observed actions were: biting an apple and chewing (mouth actions);
                        reaching and grasping a ball or a little cup with the hand and
                        mimicking these actions without the object (hand actions) or kicking
                        a ball or pushing a brake and mimicking these actions without the
                        object (foot actions). Observation of both object- and non-object-
                        related mouth, hand and foot actions (active condition) was
                        contrasted with the observation of a static face, a static hand and a
                        static foot, respectively, as a control condition. Static stimuli were
                        presented for 25 s continuously. At the end of the experimental
                        session, subjects had to report the actions they were presented with.
                        All subjects reported them correctly.
                        Image analysis
                        Image analysis was performed on a SPARC II workstation (Sun
                        Microsystems) using MATLAB (Mathworks Inc., Natick, MA, USA)
                        and statistical parametric mapping package SPM97d (Friston et al.,
                        1995, 1997). Firstly, functional images of each conditions were
                        realigned to the tenth image to correct for head movements between
                        scans. Then the images were coregistered and transformed into a
                        standard stereotactic space, using the intercommissural line as the
                        reference plane for transformation (Friston et al., 1997). Active and
                        control conditions were modelled using a delayed box-car reference
                        vector, accounting for the delayed cerebral blood ¯ow change after
                        stimulus presentation. Signi®cantly activated pixels were searched for
                        by using the general linear model approach for time series proposed by
                        Friston et al. (1995). Group activation maps were calculated by
                        pooling the data for each condition across all subjects. Pixels were
                        identi®ed as signi®cantly activated if they passed the highest threshold
                        of Z-score (3.09) and belonged to a cluster of at least 10 activated
                        pixels (P < 0.05, corrected for multiple comparisons). The activated
                        pixels surviving this procedure were superimposed on high-resolution
                        magnetic resonance (MR) scans of a standard brain (Montreal
                        Neurological Institute, MNI). Clusters of activated foci were assigned
                        to the regions of interest according to their centres of mass activity
                        with the aid of Talairach coordinates (1988) and prominent sulcal
                        landmarks. Furthermore, as far as Broca's region is concerned,
                        Talairach coordinates were also compared with the coordinates of
                        cytoarchitectonically de®ned probability maps (Amunts et al., 1999)

                        Results
                        The results of the experiment are shown in Figs 1±3. Frontal and
                        parietal activations related to action observation are presented in
                        colour. Other activations (mostly occipital) are shown in grey. These
                        latter activations (probably due to stronger activation of visual areas
                        with moving stimuli) will not be discussed here.
                        Activations during mouth action observation are shown in Fig. 1.
                        During the observation of non-object-related mouth actions (chewing,
                        a), activation foci were present in areas 6 and 44 on both sides and in
                        area 45 in the right hemisphere. Right hemisphere activation was
                        larger and stronger than left hemisphere activation. During the
                        observation of object-related mouth actions (biting an apple, b), the
                        pattern of premotor activation was similar, although weaker, to that
                        found during non-object-related actions. In addition, two activation
                        foci were present in the parietal lobe. These foci were larger in the left
                        than in the right hemisphere. The rostral focus was located in area 40
                        (area PF of von Economo, 1929), the caudal focus in area 39 (area PG).
                        Figure 2 shows activation foci relative to observation of arm/hand
                        actions. During the observation of non-object-related hand actions
                        (mimicking reaching to grasp, a) there was a bilateral activation of
                        area 6 that was located dorsal to that found during mouth movement
                        observation. During the observation of object-related arm/hand
                        actions (reaching-to-grasp movements, b) there was a bilateral
                        activation of premotor cortex plus an activation site in area 44.
                        Most interestingly, as in the case of the observation of mouth
                        movements, two activation foci were present in the parietal lobe. The
                        rostral one was located inside the intraparietal sulcus, in an area
                        caudal and dorsal to that found in the mouth movement observation
                        condition. This area probably corresponds to the anterior intraparietal
                        area of the monkey. The caudal focus was in area 39 (area PG). This
                        last focus considerably overlapped that found during mouth move-
                        ment observation.
                        Figure 3 shows activation foci elicited by observation of foot
                        actions. During the observation of non-object-related foot actions
                        (mimicking ball kicking or brake pushing, d), there was an activation
                        of a dorsal sector of area 6. There also was an activation of the frontal
                        lobe (rostrally located). Because we have no explanation for this
                        activation (found only in this condition), we will not comment on it
                        further. During the observation of object-related foot actions (kicking
                        a ball or pushing a brake, b), there was, as in the previous condition,
                        an activation of a dorsal sector of area 6. In addition, there was an
                        activation of the posterior part of the parietal lobe. The parietal
                        activation was in part located in Brodmann's area 7 [(PE)], in part it
                        overlapped the activation seen during mouth and hand actions
                        (Brodmann's area 39/PG).
                        Figure 4 gives a global picture of the activations found during
                        observation of mouth, hand and foot actions. It is evident that both the
                        premotor cortex and the parietal lobe activation foci are somatoto-
                        pically organized. The premotor somatotopy follows a pattern similar
                        to that of the classical motor homunculus (Pen®eld & Rasmussen,
                        1952). In the parietal lobe, the mouth is represented rostrally while
                        the foot is located caudally.
                        Table 1 shows the Talairach coordinates and Z scores of the
                        activated foci during the observation of object- and non-object-
                        related mouth, hand, and foot actions.

                        Discussion
                        The results of the present experiment show that when an individual
                        observes actions (made by another individual) performed with
                        different effectors, different sectors of the premotor cortex are

                        activated. During mouth actions, there is a bilateral activation of
                        ventral area 6 and area 44 plus an activation of the right area 45.
                        During hand actions, a more dorsal part of ventral area 6 plus a dorsal
                        sector of area 44 are recruited in both hemispheres. Finally, the
                        observation of foot actions elicits an activation of a dorsal sector of
                        area 6, bilaterally. There is, therefore, a clear topographic shift in the
                        premotor cortex activation from ventral to dorsal when the effector
                        used in the observed action moves from mouth to arm/hand and to
                        foot, respectively. This shift is congruent with the classical motor
                        organization of the region (see Pen®eld & Rasmussen, 1952).
                        These results are important for two reasons. First, the effector
                        related somatotopic activation pattern in the premotor cortex during

                        the mere observation of actions proves that, in humans, the mirror
                        system is not restricted to hand actions, but includes a rich repertoire
                        of body actions. It therefore constitutes the neural substrate for a
                        matching mechanism mapping the observed actions on the observer's
                        motor representations. Second, these results de®nitively rule out the
                        interpretation that cortical activation during action observation is due
                        to verbalization.
                        A further important result of the present experiment is the
                        demonstration of a marked difference between the activation during
                        the observation of object-related and non-object-related actions. Any
                        time an object is the target of an action, the parietal lobe is strongly
                        activated. This object-related activation is also somatotopically

See the Terms and Conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License


                        organized and depends on the effector used. During the observation
                        of mouth actions, there is an activation of the rostral part of the
                        inferior parietal lobule (area 40). During the observation of hand
                        actions, a more posterior sector of area 40, inside the intraparietal
                        sulcus, becomes active. This sector closely corresponds to that shown
                        to be active during object manipulation (Binkofski et al., 1999). It has
                        been suggested that this sector is the human homologue of monkey
                        anterior intraparietal area. The observation of foot actions activates
                        predominantly the posterior part of the superior parietal lobule.
                        Finally, in all conditions there is activation of area 39 (area PG).
                        Although the motor organization of the parietal lobe is not fully
                        established, an organization similar to that here described for action
                        observation in humans can be recognized for active movements in
                        nonhuman primates. In the monkey, mouth movements are repre-
                        sented in the rostral part of PF (Leinonen & Nyman, 1979; Fogassi
                        et al., 1998), distal hand movements in the anterior intraparietal area
                        (Sakata et al., 1995) and arm reaching movements, posteriorly on the
                        medial bank of the intraparietal sulcus (Colby & Duhamel, 1991;
                        Snyder et al., 1997). Furthermore, clinical and brain imaging studies
                        strongly suggest that a segregated pattern of effector representations
                        in the parietal lobe is also present in humans (De Renzi, 1982;
                        Jeannerod, 1986; Pause et al., 1989; Seitz et al., 1991).
                        It is generally accepted that a fundamental role of the parietal lobe
                        is to describe objects for action (Jeannerod, 1994; Jeannerod et al.,
                        1995; Milner & Goodale, 1995). This `pragmatic', action-orientated
                        object description has been contrasted with the `semantic' description
                        coded in the infero-temporal lobe (Milner & Goodale, 1995;
                        Jeannerod et al., 1995). The results of the present experiment
                        indicate that a `pragmatic' analysis is also carried out when an
                        individual observes an object-directed action made by another
                        individual. If action understanding were based on higher cognitive
                        functions, this parietal analysis would be unnecessary.
                        Taken together, the results of the present experiment strongly
                        support the view that during action observation there is a recruitment
                        of the same neural structures which would be normally involved in
                        the actual execution of the observed action. When individuals observe
                        an action, they code that action in terms of the related voluntary
                        movements. The `seen' actions are mapped onto the corresponding
                        motor representations of the frontal lobe and, in the case of object-
                        related actions, the `seen' objects on the effector-related, pragmatic
                        representations, in the parietal lobe.

                        Abstract
                              Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was used to localize brain areas that were active during the observation of actions made by another individual. Object- and non-object-related actions made with different effectors (mouth, hand and foot) were presented. Observation of both object- and non-object-related actions determined a somatotopically organized activation of premotor cortex. The somatotopic pattern was similar to that of the classical motor cortex homunculus. During the observation of object-related actions, an activation, also somatotopically organized, was additionally found in the posterior parietal lobe. Thus, when individuals observe an action, an internal replica of that action is automatically generated in their premotor cortex. In the case of object-related actions, a further object-related analysis is performed in the parietal lobe, as if the subjects were indeed using those objects. These results bring the previous concept of an action observation/execution matching system (mirror system) into a broader perspective: this system is not restricted to the ventral premotor cortex, but involves several somatotopically organized motor circuits.

                        Discussion

                        Brain State-Dependent Motor Skill Improvement
                        While practice on the motor skill task improved perfor-
                        mance within the training session for all groups equally,
                        subjects went on to demonstrate remarkably different
                        time courses of subsequent motor skill improvement,
                        specifically dependent on sleep. Subjects trained at 10
                        a.m. in the morning demonstrated no significant im-
                        provement when retested after 12 hr of wake, but
                        showed a significant 18.9% improvement at 10 a.m. the
                        following morning. Similarly, subjects trained at 10 p.m.
                        in the evening demonstrated a significant 20.5% im-
                        provement overnight, just 12 hr post-training, but
                        showed no significant additional improvement after a
                        further 12 hr of wake. Thus, significant improvement
                        was only seen across a night of sleep and not over a
                        similar period of waking, regardless of whether the time
                        awake or time asleep came first.
                        The possibility that circadian factors prevented ex-
                        pression of learning after 12 hr of wake is unlikely. First,
                        motor learning across the 12 training trials was similar
                        for subjects trained at 10 a.m. or 10 p.m., as was the
                        case for subjective ratings of alertness across all testing
                        points. Furthermore, repeated testing across the day
                        (group A, Figure 1) showed only a slow linear improve-
                        ment in performance, similar to that predicted by task
                        repetition, and showed no circadian fluctuations. Like-
                        wise, the possibility that the sleep-dependent improve-
                        ment resulted from hand rest during sleep is unlikely
                        since 11 hr of total hand rest during the day resulted in
                        no significant improvement beyond practice effects and
                        actually led to an increase in errors. Thus, we consider
                        sleep itself to be the most reasonable source of the
                        delayed improvement in motor skill performance.

                        Figure 4. Experimental Protocol
                        62 subjects were allocated into five experimental groups (A–E) and either trained at 10 a.m. or 10 p.m. on day 1. They were then retested
                        across the following 12–24 hr period with different retest schedules.
                        Group A: Trained at 10 a.m. and retested at 2 p.m., 6 p.m., and 10 p.m.
                        Group B: Trained at 10 a.m. and retested after 12 hr of wake and again after an additional 12 hr following a night of sleep.
                        Group C: Identical to group B, except that subjects wore mittens on both hands from 10:15 a.m. until 9 p.m. as a control for potential motor
                        interference from dexterous finger movements.
                        Group D: Trained at 10 p.m. and retested 12 hr later immediately following a night of sleep and again following an additional 12 hr of wake.
                        Group E: Trained at 10 p.m., and following a full night of recorded sleep, retested at 10 a.m. the next morning.

            Neuroscience

            Autonomic Nervous System

            University of Pittsburgh Department of Physical Therapy

            Jasmine Edwards, PT, DPT, NCS


            .To Be Covered
            • Describe the autonomic nervous system.
            • Discuss the functions of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous 
            systems.


            .Autonomic Nervous System Overview

            • Autonomic nervous system
            • Ensures tissues of body have 
            appropriate nutrients, oxygen, 
            and proper regulation of 
            osmolarity and temperature
            • Control and coordination of 
            homeostatic mechanisms 
            (maintain stable internal 
            environment) 
            • Occurs without conscious control

                  (Γ)### Transcription

                        AFFERENT PATHWAYS
                        - Visceral and vascular receptors
                        - Spinal cord
                        - Reticular formation
                        - Hypothalamus
                        - Emotion system

                        CENTRAL PROCESSING

                        EFFERENT PATHWAYS
                        - Sympathetic
                        - Parasympathetic
                        - Hormonal

                        ### Reflection and Interconnections

                        1. Afferent Pathways: This section represents the incoming signals, known as sensory pathways. These signals originate from different receptors and travel through various structures to reach central processing areas.
                           - Visceral and vascular receptors: Detect changes in internal organs and blood vessels.
                           - Spinal cord: Transmits sensory information to higher brain centers.
                           - Reticular formation: Plays a role in alertness and integrating sensory information.
                           - Hypothalamus: Regulates autonomic functions and integrates information related to homeostasis.
                           - Emotion system: Involves the limbic system, which processes emotions and related physiological responses.

                        2. Central Processing: This is where the brain processes and interprets sensory information. It involves integrating signals and making decisions about appropriate responses.

                        3. Efferent Pathways: These are the outgoing signals, known as motor pathways, that carry responses from the brain to the body.
                           - Sympathetic: Controls the body's "fight or flight" response, increasing alertness and energy.
                           - Parasympathetic: Controls the "rest and digest" response, promoting relaxation and energy conservation.
                           - Hormonal: Involves the release of hormones from glands to regulate various body functions.

                        ### Interconnections

                        - Sensory to Central Processing: The afferent pathways carry sensory information from receptors to central processing areas. For example, signals from visceral and vascular receptors travel through the spinal cord and reticular formation to reach the hypothalamus and emotion system.
                        - Central Processing to Response: After processing the sensory information, the brain sends appropriate responses through efferent pathways. These responses can be autonomic (sympathetic or parasympathetic) or hormonal.
                        - Feedback Loops: There are feedback mechanisms where the responses can influence the sensory input. For example, the hormonal response can affect visceral receptors, creating a loop of regulation and adjustment.

            Lundy-Ekman, L. 2023. Neuroscience (6th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .General Features of Autonomic NS

            • 2 neuron system
            • Preganglionic: thinly myelinated, 
            projects to autonomic ganglion
            • Postganglionic: unmyelinated, 
            projects to visceral effectors

            Haines, D. E., & Mihailoff, G. A. (2018). Fundamental Neuroscience for Basic 
            and Clinical Applications (5th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .Central Processing

            • Do not directly control visceral function but 
            influence activity
            • Pons – regulates respiration
            • Medulla – regulates heart rate, respiration, 
            vasoconstriction/dilation
            • Hypothalamus – maintains homeostasis 
            (equilibrium) in the body
            • Thalamus – projects to emotion/motivation 
            system

            Lundy-Ekman, L. 2023. Neuroscience (6th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .Sympathetic Nervous System

            Lundy-Ekman, L. 2023. Neuroscience (6th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).

            • Increases:
            • heart rate, blood pressure, blood flow to 
            skeletal muscles, blood glucose levels, 
            sweating, pupil diameter
            • Decreases: 
            • gut motility, digestive gland secretion, and 
            blood flow to abdominal viscera and skin
            • Condition of extreme excitement and 
            exertion brings mass sympathetic activities 
            with widespread effects


            .Parasympathetic Nervous System

            Lundy-Ekman, L. 2023. Neuroscience (6th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).

            • Cell body location:
            • Brainstem:
            • Cranial nerves 3, 7, 9, 10
            • Sacral spinal cord
            • Promotion of restorative processes (rest and 
            digest)


            .Urinary Bladder and Micturition

            • Emptying of bladder: contraction of smooth 
            muscle of bladder (detrusor m) and 
            relaxation of external urinary sphincter
            • Contraction of detrusor m - parasympathetic NS 
            (from sacral cord)
            • External sphincter - voluntary and 
            parasympathetic control from S3 and S4 
            segments
            • Sympathetic NS (from lumbar cord) - 
            inhibitory on detrusor mm and 
            parasympathetic neurons
            • Lesion of either lumbar or sacral spinal cord 
            segments can affect bladder function

            Haines, D. E., & Mihailoff, G. A. (2018). Fundamental Neuroscience for Basic 
            and Clinical Applications (5th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .Bladder Dysfunction

            • Spastic/reflex type: lesion above conus medullaris and sacral segment of S2-4
            • Cannot sense fullness, sphincter remains closed
            • Causes frequency and urge incontinence
            • Reflex arc is intact
            • Flaccid (nonreflex) type: lesion at S2-S4 or conus medallaris
            • Loss of parasympathetic outflow and no reflex action
            • Bladder muscles don’t contract when bladder is full
            • Sphincter may stay open at all times
            • Overflow incontinence occurs


            .Autonomic Dysreflexia

            • May occur after a spinal cord injury with damage above T6 level
            • Dysregulation of ANS leads to uncoordinated sympathetic response
            • Caused by noxious stimuli below level of lesion
            • Signs:
            • Hypertension
            • Severe headache
            • Bradycardia, facial flushing
            • Urinary retention
            • Profuse sweating
            • Reduced blood flow to peripheral tissue


            .Neurotransmitters & Receptors

            Lundy-Ekman, L. 2023. Neuroscience (6th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .Horner’s Syndrome

            • A lesion to the sympathetic nervous 
            system
            • Symptoms
            • Drooping of the ipsilateral upper eyelid (ptosis)
            • Constriction of the ipsilateral pupil (miosis)
            • Absence of sweating on the ipsilateral face and 
            neck (anhidrosis)

            Lundy-Ekman, L. 2023. Neuroscience (6th ed.). Elsevier Health Sciences (US).


            .Key Take Aways
            • The autonomic system maintains homeostasis and is a 2 neuron system.
            • Central processing occurs in the brainstem, hypothalamus, and thalamus.
            • The sympathetic nervous system turns on during times of extreme excitement 
            and exertion.
            • The parasympathetic nervous system promotes restorative processes.
            • The bladder is controlled voluntarily and also through the autonomic system.

                        ### Reflection and Interconnections

                        1. Prefrontal Cortex
                           - The prefrontal cortex is involved in complex cognitive functions, decision-making, and personality expression.
                           
                        2. Association Cortex
                           - The association cortex integrates information from different sensory modalities and contributes to complex mental processes.

                        3. Cingulate Gyrus
                           - The cingulate gyrus is part of the limbic system and plays a role in emotional regulation and cognitive processing.

                        4. Anterior Thalamic Nuclei
                           - The anterior thalamic nuclei relay information between the limbic system and the cerebral cortex, contributing to emotional and memory processing.

                        5. Mamillo-Thalamic Tract
                           - The mamillo-thalamic tract connects the mammillary bodies to the anterior thalamic nuclei, forming part of the Papez circuit involved in memory processing.

                        6. Mamillary Body
                           - The mammillary bodies are part of the limbic system and are involved in recollective memory.

                        7. Hypothalamus
                           - The hypothalamus regulates autonomic functions, endocrine activity, and emotional responses.

                        8. Fornix
                           - The fornix is a major output tract of the hippocampus, connecting it to the hypothalamus and other parts of the limbic system.

                        9. Hippocampal Formation
                           - The hippocampal formation is critical for the consolidation of information from short-term to long-term memory and spatial navigation.

                        10. Amygdala
                            - The amygdala is involved in processing emotions, particularly fear and pleasure.

                        ### Interconnections

                        - Prefrontal Cortex to Association Cortex: The prefrontal cortex communicates with the association cortex to integrate higher cognitive functions and sensory information.
                        - Association Cortex to Cingulate Gyrus: Information processed in the association cortex is relayed to the cingulate gyrus for emotional and cognitive integration.
                        - Cingulate Gyrus to Anterior Thalamic Nuclei: The cingulate gyrus sends signals to the anterior thalamic nuclei as part of the emotional and memory processing pathways.
                        - Anterior Thalamic Nuclei to Mamillo-Thalamic Tract: The anterior thalamic nuclei are connected to the mammillary bodies via the mamillo-thalamic tract, playing a role in memory processing.
                        - Mamillary Body to Hypothalamus: The mammillary bodies relay information to the hypothalamus, influencing autonomic functions and emotional responses.
                        - Hypothalamus to Fornix: The hypothalamus is connected to the hippocampus via the fornix, integrating memory and autonomic functions.
                        - Fornix to Hippocampal Formation: The fornix serves as a pathway for the hippocampus to send and receive information related to memory and spatial navigation.
                        - Hippocampal Formation to Amygdala: The hippocampal formation interacts with the amygdala to process and store emotionally charged memories.


            .Cingulate Cortex

            • Responsible for motivation, emotion, and affective properties of pain
            • Receives and projects information from cortex and other areas to and 
            from limbic system

            Kandel, E. R., Schwartz, J. H., Jessell, T. M., Siegelbaum, S. A., & Hudspeth, A. J. 
            (2012). Principles of Neural Science (5th ed.). McGraw-Hill Professional.


            .Hippocampal Formation

            • Composed of dentate gyrus, hippocampus, subiculum
            • Receives cortical input from:
            • superior and middle frontal gyri (prefrontal cortex)
            • superior temporal gyri (primary auditory cortex) 
            • cingulate gyri (neocortical-type, limbic gyrus)
            • occipital cortex (visual input)
            • occipitotemporal gyri (visual-memory-association ctx) 
            • Projects reciprocally to many cortical regions, hypothalamic nuclei (e.g. mammillary 
            bodies), and amygdala
            • Diffuse connections to many brainstem regions including reticular formation nuclei


            .Amygdala

            • Group of nuclei in anteromedial temporal lobe
            • Function: emotions and drives
            • Attaches emotional significance to stimuli
            • Emotions regulated include fear, anxiety, aggression, 
            pleasure
            • Provides psychological and physiological responses 
            to stimuli
            • Lesion leads to diminished capacity for fear
            • Link to basal ganglia
            • Nucleus accumbens receives input from amygdaloid 
            complex
            • Role in behaviors related to addiction and chronic 
            pain

            Kandel, E. R., Schwartz, J. H., Jessell, T. M., Siegelbaum, S. A., & 
            Hudspeth, A. J. (2012). Principles of Neural Science (5th ed.). 
            McGraw-Hill Professional.


            .Hypothalamus

            • Group of nuclei and connections essential for regulation 
            of visceral motor, appetitive, emotional, and vasomotor 
            activities
            • Cardiovascular and temperature regulation
            • Respiration
            • Digestion
            • Reproduction
            • Nuclei related to ANS control are heavily connected to 
            the brainstem
            • Nuclei related to endocrine control are connected 
            through the pituitary gland
            • Hypothalamus synthesizes hormones of the posterior 
            pituitary gland and hormonal releasing factors that 
            influence endocrine activity of the anterior pituitary lobe 


            .Activation of Stress Response ('')


            .Limbic Thalamic Nuclei

            • Functions: impressions of sensations
            • Dysfunctions = hyper or hypo sensitivity to pain 
            • Severe pain due to hypersensitivity of thalamic nuclei is called 
            Thalamic Pain Syndrome
            • Can be treated with pain meds, opiod analgesics, or an electrode stimulus 
            device placed directly into specific nuclei of the thalamus to inhibit firing


            .Key Take Aways
            • The limbic system is composed of several different structures with different 
            functions.
            • The functions of the limbic system are memory, emotions, and homeostatic 
            function.

      .('48 PT2060_Mod10Memory.pdf')
            Neuroscience

            Memory

            University of Pittsburgh Department of Physical Therapy

            Jasmine Edwards, PT, DPT, NCS


            .To Be Covered

            • Define and describe memory and the different types of memory.
            • Identify the anatomical locations where memories are processed and stored.
            • Discuss memory impairments.
            • Discuss cognition and executive functioning.


            .Executive Function
            • Intentional activity that requires initiation and organizational structure
            • Orbital prefrontal cortex, medial prefrontal cortex/network, dorsolateral 
            prefrontal network

            Hanna-Pladdy


            .Memory

            • Processes that permit learning, storage, retrieval of declarative and procedural 
            information
            • Types:
            • Long term:
            ▪ Declarative: semantic, episodic, autobiographical
            ▪ Nondeclarative: procedural, sensorimotor, emotional
            • Working memory


            .Declarative Memory

            • Collection of memory systems that acquires, retains, and retrieves information 
            that is consciously recalled
            • Two types:
            • Episodic memory: memory for personally experienced events
            • Includes information on the time and place in which the events occurred
            • Specific spatial/temporal contexts and the internal states (emotions) of the person 
            associated with the memory
            • Medial temporal lobe, diencephalon, frontal lobe
            • Semantic memory: memory for facts including conceptual knowledge
            • Retrieval of information allows for efficient language production, comprehension, 
            reasoning, higher order cognitive processes
            • Medial temporal lobe, diencephalon

            LaVoie, 2007


            .Nondeclarative Memory

            • Set of systems that cannot be accessed through consciousness
            • Expressed through task performance
            • Two types:
            • Procedural memory: supports cognitive, motor, and perceptual skill learning
            • Known through task performance – with repetition the performance of skills can be 
            automatic
            • Basal ganglia, cerebellum, motor cortex, occipital visual cortex
            • Perceptual representation system: identification of perceptual features and 
            previously encountered objects
            • Occipital visual cortex, association cortices of frontal and temporoparietal regions

            LaVoie, 2007


            .Working Memory

            • Temporarily stores, manages, and processes information required for learning, 
            task completion, comprehension, and reasoning
            • Ability to hold information in memory while also carrying out processes on that 
            information
            • Dorsolateral prefrontal region, L temporoparietal region, L premotor cortex, R 
            inferior parietal cortex, R premotor cortex, R inferior frontal cortex, R frontal 
            cortex

            LaVoie, 2007


            Kandel, E. R., Schwartz, J. H., Jessell, T. M., Siegelbaum, S. A., & Hudspeth, A. J. (2012). Principles of Neural Science (5th ed.). McGraw-Hill Professional.

            .('')


            .Hippocampal Formation Function

            • Case of H.M.
            • Facilitates consolidation of long-term 
            memories from immediate and short-term 
            info 
            • If hippocampus is lesioned…
            • “short term” memory is not stored into “long 
            term” memory, i.e. anterograde amnesia
            • Person is not able to “remember” what they were 
            doing, reading (Memento, Dory from Finding 
            Nemo)
            • Does not store memories but rather 
            processes them for storage

            LeDoux, 2006

            https://www.brainfacts.org/in-the-lab/tools-and-techniques/2018/the-curious-case-
            of-patient-hm-082818


            .Hippocampus Clinical Implications

            • Bilateral injury to hippocampus 
            • Loss of or impaired ability to remember recent (new) events
            • Difficulty in acquiring new information and skills (learning)
            • Memory that depends on visual, tactile, or auditory discrimination is 
            noticeably affected
            • Long-term memories stored in remote cortical memory areas are unaffected


            .Forms of memory loss ('')


            .Key Take Aways

            • There are three types of memory: 
            • Working: short-term
            • Long-term:
            • Declarative: consciously recalled
            • Non-declarative: unconsciously recalled
            • The hippocampal formation plays a key role in memory

      Items to share:
            1.I have learned that the ANS keeps the body running on autopilot—like a backstage crew managing heart rate, breathing, and digestion without you even noticing. It’s split into two parts: the "fight or flight" sympathetic system and the "rest and digest" parasympathetic system. Together, they balance your body’s needs depending on the situation, whether you’re chilling or stressed.

            2.Also, I have learned that The limbic system is like the brain’s emotional control center—it helps process feelings, memories, and drives. Structures like the amygdala light up when you’re scared or excited, while the hippocampus acts as the memory librarian, storing and retrieving info. It also ties emotions to experiences, which explains why some memories feel so vivid.

      Item that is unclear - "muddiest point"
            1.One thing that’s still unclear is how exactly the hypothalamus communicates with all these systems at once—it seems like it’s juggling a million tasks. While I get its role in regulating hormones, emotions, and autonomic functions, the sheer complexity of its connections feels overwhelming. Breaking down those pathways step by step would help clarify things.

      .Summary/Key points:
            -Neuron communication/use of transmitter requires energy (oxygen/glucose) which requires blood flow. Neuroimaging techniques measure rates of cerebral blood flow (PET) or can measure changes in blood oxygenation due to changes in cerebral blood flow (fMRI).
            -FMRI is widely used for brain activity mapping due to its high spatial resolution and temporal resolution in the order of seconds.
            -Integration of multiple imaging methods (multimodal neuroimaging) can result in a more comprehensive view of brain processes.
            -Linking brain activity to behavior means BOTH need to be measured!

      Explain the principles of general nervous system organization and function.

            Objectives for Lesson 1B Part 1
               • Describe the development of the nervous system and basis for movement control; neuron morphology, types of neurons, axonal transport. (Unit 1, Outcome 2).
               • Specific objectives for Part 1 of Lesson 1B:

            Active recall!
               • Write down the difference between gastrulation and neurulation
               • Write down the names of the three vesicles of the early brain.
               • Which vesicles of the three-vesicle brain changes/differentiates? What do they become?

            Summary/Key points:
               • Processes of cell differentiation follow processes of determination. Differentiation is when the neuron gains unique characteristics needed for its future role in the NS.
               • Gastrulation is a major developmental event where the three germ layers are formed. Neurulation is the process of differentiating neural elements 
               (neural plate, neural tube, neural crest). Neurulation follows gastrulation.
               • The end of the neural tube expands to form three vesicles, then further grows/differentiates into five vesicles which then become the primary regions of the mature brain. Each vesicle associates with part of the ventricular system.

      ----------------------------------------------------- .MCh
            1. What is the primary focus when seeking to understand the development of nervous system circuitry?
               A) Understanding synaptic transmission
               B) Exploring neural stem cell function
               C) Examining the emergence of behavior

               C) Examining the emergence of behavior
               Understanding the development of nervous system circuitry primarily focuses on examining how behaviors emerge, as behaviors are ultimately driven by neural circuits.

            2. Which aspect of behavior do neural circuits primarily underlie?
               A) Sensory perception
               B) Motor control
               C) Cognitive processes

               B) Motor control
               Neural circuits primarily underlie motor behaviors such as locomotion, which are essential for movement and coordination.

            3. What is a characteristic feature of neural circuits across animal nervous systems?
               A) Constant adaptation
               B) High variability
               C) Conservation

               C) Conservation
               Neural circuits for motor behaviors, visual and auditory processing, and other essential functions are often highly conserved across animal nervous systems, indicating their fundamental importance.

            4. What is key to how circuits are assembled during nervous system development?
               A) Genetic mutations
               B) External stimuli
               C) Internal signaling processes

               C) Internal signaling processes
               Internal signaling processes play a crucial role in guiding the assembly of neural circuits during nervous system development, influencing cell differentiation, migration, and connectivity.

            5. What term describes the process by which diverse behaviors emerge across species and evolution?
               A) Neural plasticity
               B) Synaptic pruning
               C) Patterning

               C) Patterning
               Patterning in development leads to the diversity and adaptability of behaviors across species and evolution, shaping the organization and function of neural circuits.

            6. Which behavior is primarily regulated by circuits for motor behaviors?
               A) Memory formation
               B) Movement and locomotion
               C) Language processing

               B) Movement and locomotion
               Circuits for motor behaviors primarily regulate movement and locomotion, coordinating muscle activity and enabling physical actions.

            7. What is the significance of understanding synaptic transmission in the context of nervous system development?
               A) Synaptic transmission shapes neural connectivity
               B) Synaptic transmission controls gene expression
               C) Synaptic transmission determines cell migration

               A) Synaptic transmission shapes neural connectivity
               Understanding synaptic transmission is crucial as it shapes neural connectivity, influencing the formation and refinement of neural circuits during development.

            8. What role does neural stem cell function play in nervous system development?
               A) Neural stem cells regulate synaptic plasticity
               B) Neural stem cells guide axon guidance
               C) Neural stem cells generate neurons and glia

               C) Neural stem cells generate neurons and glia
               Neural stem cells play a key role in nervous system development by generating neurons and glial cells, which are essential for building neural circuits.

            9. How does constant adaptation contribute to nervous system function?
               A) It ensures genetic stability
               B) It promotes circuit rigidity
               C) It allows for flexibility in responding to environmental changes

               C) It allows for flexibility in responding to environmental changes
               Constant adaptation allows the nervous system to remain flexible and responsive to environmental changes, enabling organisms to adjust their behavior accordingly.

            10. Which process involves the elimination of excess synapses to refine neural circuits?
               A) Synaptic transmission
               B) Axon guidance
               C) Synaptic pruning

               C) Synaptic pruning
               Synaptic pruning is the process by which excess synapses are eliminated, refining neural circuits and optimizing synaptic connectivity during nervous system development.

            1. What is the primary function of behavior according to Lesson A of this module?
               A) Sensory processing
               B) Communication between neurons
               C) Muscle coordination

               B) Communication between neurons
               Behavior is primarily a function of the communication and connections between neurons, which form neural circuitry. This communication allows for the generation of complex behaviors.

            2. What is the term used to describe the process by which neurons mature and acquire specific functions?
               A) Synaptic transmission
               B) Neural determination
               C) Differentiation

               C) Differentiation
               Differentiation refers to the process by which neurons undergo maturation and acquire specific anatomical and functional characteristics. It involves the diversification of neuronal stem cells into various types of neurons.

            3. How many types of neurons can differentiate from neuronal stem cells, according to Jacobson (1974)?
               A) Hundreds
               B) Thousands
               C) Dozens

               B) Thousands
               According to Jacobson (1974), neuronal stem cells can differentiate into thousands of anatomically and functionally different types of neurons during development, highlighting the complexity of neural differentiation.

            4. What process precedes neural differentiation and programs cells for their future development?
               A) Synaptic pruning
               B) Neural determination
               C) Axon guidance

               B) Neural determination
               Neural determination is the process that precedes neural differentiation, programming cells for their future course of development. It sets the stage for the differentiation of neurons into specific types with distinct functions.

            5. Which aspect of neuron development involves the formation of connections between neurons?
               A) Synaptic transmission
               B) Axon guidance
               C) Neurogenesis

               B) Axon guidance
               Axon guidance is the process by which developing neurons extend their axons to specific target areas and form connections with other neurons. This process is crucial for the establishment of neural circuits and functional connectivity in the nervous system.

            6. What is the primary determinant of a neuron's future course of development?
               A) Synaptic plasticity
               B) Neural activity
               C) Neural determination

               C) Neural determination
               Neural determination is the primary process that programs cells for their future course of development, influencing the type and function of neurons that they will differentiate into.

            7. During neural differentiation, what happens to neuronal stem cells?
               A) They become less specialized
               B) They acquire specific characteristics
               C) They stop dividing

               B) They acquire specific characteristics
               During neural differentiation, neuronal stem cells acquire specific anatomical and functional characteristics as they mature into distinct types of neurons.

            8. What role does synaptic transmission play in the process of neural differentiation?
               A) It determines the fate of neuronal stem cells
               B) It regulates gene expression in developing neurons
               C) It facilitates communication between mature neurons

               C) It facilitates communication between mature neurons
               Synaptic transmission is the process by which mature neurons communicate with each other, transmitting signals across synapses. While important for neural function, synaptic transmission does not directly influence neural differentiation.

            9. What is the significance of synaptic plasticity in nervous system development?
               A) It shapes the formation of neural circuits
               B) It determines the fate of neural stem cells
               C) It regulates neurotransmitter release

               A) It shapes the formation of neural circuits
               Synaptic plasticity refers to the ability of synapses to strengthen or weaken over time in response to activity. This process is crucial for shaping the formation of neural circuits during nervous system development.

            10. How does neurogenesis contribute to nervous system development?
               A) It promotes axon guidance
               B) It generates new neurons
               C) It regulates synaptic transmission

               B) It generates new neurons
               Neurogenesis is the process by which new neurons are generated from neural stem cells. This process contributes to the growth and development of the nervous system, increasing neuronal diversity and enabling the formation of complex neural circuits.

            1. What is a primary outcome of the process of determination during nervous system development?
               A) Formation of neural circuits
               B) Production of primary processes
               C) Acquisition of unique characteristics

               B) Production of primary processes
               Determination in nervous system development involves the formation of neurons, their correct positioning, and the production of primary processes such as the cell body (soma) and axon.

            2. What is a characteristic feature of neurons during the process of differentiation?
               A) Decrease in size
               B) Increase in size
               C) No change in size

               B) Increase in size
               During differentiation, neurons typically increase in size as they mature and acquire unique characteristics for their future roles in neural circuits.

            3. What is one of the specific characteristics that neurons gain during differentiation?
               A) Production of secondary processes
               B) Decrease in dendritic connections
               C) Production of terminal dendrites

               C) Production of terminal dendrites
               Terminal dendrites are produced by neurons during differentiation, which are essential for making specific connections and forming neural circuits.

            4. What marks the beginning of the emergence of behavior during nervous system development?
               A) Production of terminal dendrites
               B) Formation of neural circuits
               C) Acquisition of unique characteristics

               B) Formation of neural circuits
               The formation of neural circuits marks the beginning of the emergence of behavior during nervous system development, as neural circuits are essential for generating and coordinating behaviors.

            5. Which process precedes the acquisition of unique characteristics by neurons during differentiation?
               A) Determination
               B) Synaptogenesis
               C) Neurogenesis

               A) Determination
               Determination precedes differentiation and involves the formation of neurons, their correct positioning, and the production of primary processes before neurons acquire unique characteristics for their future roles.

            6. What is the primary role of neurons during the process of determination?
               A) Synaptic transmission
               B) Production of secondary processes
               C) Formation of primary processes

               C) Formation of primary processes
               During determination, neurons are primarily involved in the formation of primary processes such as the cell body (soma) and axon, which are essential for their structural development.

            7. What is one of the key functions of terminal dendrites produced during neuron differentiation?
               A) Synthesizing neurotransmitters
               B) Transmitting electrical signals
               C) Making specific connections

               C) Making specific connections
               Terminal dendrites play a crucial role in making specific connections between neurons, which is essential for the formation of neural circuits and the transmission of information in the nervous system.

            8. Which process involves the diversification of neuronal stem cells into thousands of anatomically and functionally different types of neurons?
               A) Neurogenesis
               B) Synaptogenesis
               C) Differentiation

               C) Differentiation
               Differentiation is the process by which neuronal stem cells diversify into various types of neurons with distinct anatomical and functional characteristics, contributing to the complexity of the nervous system.

            9. What happens to neurons as they assume correct positions during the process of determination?
               A) They migrate to specific locations
               B) They decrease in number
               C) They differentiate into glial cells

               A) They migrate to specific locations
               During determination, neurons migrate to specific positions within the developing nervous system, ensuring proper organization and connectivity for the formation of neural circuits.

            10. What is the ultimate outcome of neural circuit formation during nervous system development?
               A) Synaptic plasticity
               B) Emergence of behavior
               C) Regulation of gene expression

               B) Emergence of behavior
               The formation of neural circuits is essential for the emergence of behavior during nervous system development, as neural circuits underlie the generation and coordination of various behaviors in organisms.
