.Effect of cerebellar dysfunction on balance
   Recall that in previous lessons, ‘ we talked about the cerebellum, ‘ particularly the spinocerebellum being important for postural responses. ‘ Let's take a look at Figure B,  the lower figure first. ‘ In this experiment, subjects stood on a normal size platform that was moved backward. ‘ This causes the person to sway fon/vard and ‘ they need a corrective backwards sway response. ‘ On the left, you can see the EMG traces from a healthy control subject. ‘ — The onset of the platform movement evokes a small burst of activity in the gastrocs, ‘ and this is the normal ankle strategy. ‘ On the right, you see the response of a person with damage ‘ to the spinocerebellum and it looks a lot different. ‘ The muscle responses are very overly large with abnormal bursts of ‘ activity alternating between the gastrocs and its antagonist, the tibialis anterior. ‘This is an inefficient and very likely ineffective partial response. ‘ Going to the top figures, ‘ here, again, ‘ subjects stood on a platform that was moved horizontally, ‘ but the velocity was increased on each trial. ‘ Maintaining balance required scaling their responses to the velocity of the platform. ‘ In the left-hand figure, ‘ you can see the results for a control participant in black, ‘ and the results for a person with ‘ spinocerebellar damage in yellow or kind of an orange color. ‘ The adjustments in a subject with a spinocerebellar disorder ‘ have a slope that's similar to that of the control subject, ‘ though, in each trial, ‘ the muscle responses are much larger, ‘ that's why the line is all the way up here; ‘ the muscle responses are much larger and they are much more variable, c you can see the standard deviations here. ‘The person with spinocerebellar damage, I they were able to scale the force, ‘ but they used much greater force than necessary and ‘ their responses were much more variable or less consistent across trials. ‘ The right-hand top figure shows you results when ‘ the translations were repeated or predictable, ‘ and that's the solid line, ‘ or when they were random and unpredictable, ‘ that's the dashed line. ‘ When translation amplitude is random, ‘ responses are generally large as if the subject expects a large translation. ‘ When trials with the same amplitude are repeated, ‘ which is this black solid line here, ‘ a control subject learns to predict the amplitude ‘ of the disturbance and adjust his or her response. ‘ In contrast, when trials with the same platform speed are ‘ repeated, a spinocerebellar patient, ‘that's the solid yellow line,  shows no improvement in performance, ‘ they can't use their experience in one trial to adjust responses in subsequent trials. ‘ All the responses from the person with ‘ spinocerebellar damage are just larger than the control participants. ‘ Together, these findings illustrate that cerebellar damage results ‘ — in compromised reactive postural responses.

.Anticipatory postural control
   • Activating postural muscles in advance of a skilled movement
   • Feedforward
   • Arm raising experiments
   oActivated in advance of the prime mover - preparatory

   Let's move on to discuss anticipatory postural control or feedfonNard control. ‘ This is when postural synergies are activated in advance ‘ of a skilled movement in preparation for that movement. ‘ Much of this work was originally done on arm-raising experiments. ‘ If you voluntarily raise your arm, ‘ say to reach something on a shelf, ‘ you first activate postural muscles on the dorsal surface of the body, ‘ gastrocs, hamstrings, paraspinals. ‘ Why? The voluntary movement of the arm is itself destabilizing, ‘ it causes a center of gravity to shift fonNard. ‘ To counteract those de-stabilizing forces created by voluntary movement, ‘ anticipatory adjustments are initiated prior to the voluntary movement.

.APAs precede voluntary movement, are scaled to upcoming movements, and are only used when needed
   APAs or anticipatory postural adjustments proceed voluntary movement, ‘ they're scaled to the upcoming movements, ‘ and they're only used when needed. ‘ Let's look at this in more detail. ‘ Let's start with A, the left-hand figure. ‘ In this experiment, ‘ subjects were asked to pull on a handle attached to the wall by a wire. ‘ This is the setup over here. ‘ They are asked to pull on this handle that's attached to the wall. ‘ Subjects stood on a force plate and at a signal pulled ‘ rapidly on the handle to reach a specified peak force, I varying between five percent and 95 percent of their maximum pulling force, ‘ abbreviated MPF, maximum pulling force. ‘ The dashed line that you see right here, ‘ time 0, was the onset of the voluntary pool. ‘ If you think about this setup, ‘ if you are pulling on a fixed handle, ‘ that would cause you to lean or rotate fonNard towards the handle. ‘ The APAs generated to counteract that and keep the body vertical. ‘ You can see that each voluntary pull of the handle down ‘ here was preceded by ‘ leg muscle activation that produced a rotational force or torque about the anklejoints. ‘ Remember, the actual voluntary pull on the handle by the person who was at time 0, ‘ and you can see this ankle torque is generated before they start pulling on the handle. ‘ If they're asked to produce a larger pulling force, ‘ they produce a larger ankle torque before they even start to pull. ‘ This demonstrates that the APA was scaled, ‘ that as the voluntary pulling force increased,  the muscle response and the ankle increased to offset that. ‘ Looking at B, subjects were, ‘ again, asked to pull on a handle fixed to a wall. ‘ EMG traces are aligned at time 0, ‘ that's this line here and this gray arrow here. ‘ — Time zero is the onset of activity in the arm muscle or biceps brachii, ‘ which is right here in this top one, ‘ and right here in this bottom one. ‘ During unsupported stance, ‘ so in this top figure, ‘ the leg muscle, ‘ the hamstrings and gas strokes are activated prior to the biceps,  to prevent the body from rotating fonrvard during the arm pull. ‘ The red arrow shows the onset of leg gas stroke activation. ‘ The gray arrow, that of the arm, biceps brachii. ‘ In the lower part of the figure, ‘ when the subject was supported by a rigid bar at the shoulder, - the anticipatory leg muscle activity was not necessary. I The body could not rotate forward, I so they didn't need to activate and they didn't. - This demonstrates that postural adjustments accompany : voluntary movement only when needed, I so they are task specific.

.External support and balance
   Haptic cues from fingertip contact with a stable surface attenuate body sway in subjects even when the 
   contact forces are too small to provide physical support of the body.
   We investigated how haptic cues derived from contact of a cane with a stationary surface at low force levels aids 
   postural control in sighted and congenitally blind individuals. Five sighted (eyes closed) and five congenitally blind 
   subjects maintained a tandem Romberg stance in five conditions: (1) no cane; (2,3) touch contact «2 N of applied 
   force) while holding the cane in a vertical or slanted orientation; and (4, 5) force contact (as much force as 
   desired) in the vertical and slanted orientations. Touch contact of a cane at force levels below those 
   necessary to provide significant physical stabilization was as effective as force contact in reducing 
   postural sway in all subjects, compared to the no-cane condition.

   We've talked about how anticipatory postural adjustments are task specific, While this slide is not specific to APAs, : I wanted to include it in our talk about balance, I and how changing the task can significantly alter the balance requirements. - This was a study conducted in individuals with : congenital blindness and those with normal vision. I They had participants stand with their feet, - one foot in front of the other without any assistance, - just touching a cane, : and then being allowed to use force contact with the cane. - The important point here is highlighted in yellow. - They found thatjust touching the cane, : at force levels below those necessary to provide any stabilization, : cause the same reduction in postural sway as actually using the cane. - This means that when evaluating balance in our patients, I we need to understand that if they are touching us or surface, I even if they're not using a lot of force that is enough to alter their balance performance. i It might make us think their balance is better than what it really is.

.Balance: distributed control
   Signals from specific areas in all 
   lobes of the cortex converge and 
   are integrated to determine 
   appropriate motor output

   Balance is the clinically observable outcome of I the integration of all the information coming from these sources, - visual, vestibular, somatosensory. - It's an example of distributed control. : While the cerebellum is heavily involved, I it is not the sole generator or controller of balance. - Areas of frontal, parietal, - temporal and occipital cortex, : as well as basal ganglia. - Cerebellum that we discussed, PPN, - the peduncle pontine nucleus provide inputs to I the reticulospinal and vestibulospinal pathways that descend to spinal motor neurons. : Afferent inputs from the visual, - vestibular and somatosensory systems are integrated in the brain stem and cortex, : to update the body schema and then form future postural commands.

.Active Recall!
   • Write down everything you can remember about the ankle strategy.
   • How is it different from the hip strategy?

Summary/Key points
   • Ankle, hip and stepping strategies are reactive postural adjustments to external perturbations.
   • Reactive strategies are specific both to action and to context.
   • Anticipatory postural adjustments are also specific to action and context.

      c) Regulating muscle tone

         What is the vestibulocerebellum and what is its function?
            ('BRAIN FROM TOP TO BOTTOM')
            ('Ventromedial descending pathways')
            ('vestibulocerebellum')
            ('vestibulocerebellum 2')
            ('vestibulocerebellum 3')
            ('vestibulocerebellum 4')
            
            The vestibulocerebellum, also known as the flocculonodular lobe, is one of the functional subdivisions of the cerebellum. It primarily receives input from the vestibular system, which is responsible for sensing balance, spatial orientation, and head movement.

            Functionally, the vestibulocerebellum plays a crucial role in coordinating balance and eye movements, as well as maintaining postural stability. It helps integrate sensory information from the vestibular organs with motor commands to ensure smooth and coordinated movements, particularly those related to maintaining equilibrium and stabilizing gaze during head movements.

            Specifically, the vestibulocerebellum contributes to:

            1. Balance Control: It receives vestibular input related to body position and movement, allowing it to adjust muscle activity and posture to maintain balance, particularly during activities such as standing, walking, and changes in body position.

            2. Eye Movement Coordination: The vestibulocerebellum influences eye movements, including gaze stabilization and the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR), which enables the eyes to remain fixed on a target while the head is in motion. This function is crucial for maintaining visual acuity and stability during head movements.

            3. Spatial Orientation: By integrating vestibular information with proprioceptive and visual cues, the vestibulocerebellum helps orient the body in space and coordinate movements in relation to the environment.

            Overall, the vestibulocerebellum plays a vital role in motor coordination and spatial awareness, contributing to the smooth execution of movements and the maintenance of postural stability, especially in dynamic and challenging environments.

.Balance: Definitions
   1. According to Fell et al. (2018), what is balance?
      a) The ability to recover from episodes of instability
      b) The ability to anticipate and avoid instability and falling
      c) The ability to maintain physical equilibrium in an upright posture

      c) The ability to maintain physical equilibrium in an upright posture
      Fell et al. define balance as the ability to maintain physical equilibrium in an upright posture, emphasizing the stability aspect of balance.
         ΓHowever, a) & b) are also balance

   2. What is postural control, as defined by Horak (1987)?
      a) The ability to anticipate and move in ways to avoid instability
      b) The process of controlling the body's equilibrium for a given purpose
      c) The ability to maintain equilibrium in a gravitational environment

      c) The ability to maintain equilibrium in a gravitational environment
      Postural control, according to Horak, refers to the ability to maintain equilibrium in a gravitational environment, highlighting the role of gravity in maintaining stability.

   3. How does Fell (2018) differentiate balance from postural control?
      a) Balance involves reactive recovery, while postural control involves proactive anticipation
      b) Balance is a clinical outcome, while postural control refers to the underlying physiological processes
      c) Balance is required for specific functional tasks, while postural control is a general ability
      
      b) Balance is a clinical outcome, while postural control refers to the underlying physiological processes
      Fell distinguishes balance as the clinically observable outcome of postural control, emphasizing that postural control represents the underlying physiological processes that contribute to maintaining equilibrium.

   4. What is the essential component of all upright tasks, according to Fell (2018)?
      a) Reactive recovery from instability
      b) Proactive anticipation and avoidance of instability
      c) Both reactive recovery and proactive anticipation
      
      c) Both reactive recovery and proactive anticipation
      Fell highlights that balance involves both the ability to recover from instability reactively and the ability to anticipate and avoid instability proactively, making it an essential component of all upright tasks.

   5. How does Fell (2018) characterize balance in relation to functional tasks?
      a) Balance is a specific functional task
      b) Balance is not a functional task but is essential for all functional tasks
      c) Balance is unrelated to functional tasks
      
      b) Balance is not a functional task but is essential for all functional tasks
      Fell emphasizes that balance, while not a specific functional task itself, is a required component in all specific functional tasks, indicating its importance in various activities.
         -(Γ)So, we do not "work on balance" but in the specific functional activities that require the "balance component." So, if you say -Let's work on balance- you shouls ask -For what functional task? or, balance for what? (See question 7 too)

   6. Which part of the body integrates information from various sources to maintain equilibrium?
      a) Cerebellum
      b) Cerebral cortex
      c) Basal ganglia
      
      a) Cerebellum
      The cerebellum integrates information from sources such as the vestibular apparatus, somatosensation, and descending pathways to contribute to maintaining equilibrium.

   7. According to Horak (1994), what is the process of balance?
      a) The ability to recover from episodes of instability
      b) The ability to maintain equilibrium for a given purpose
      c) The ability to anticipate and avoid instability and falling
      
      b) The ability to maintain equilibrium for a given purpose
      Horak defines balance as the process whereby the body's equilibrium is controlled for a given purpose, emphasizing the purposeful nature of maintaining stability.

.Two types of postural control
   1. Which type of postural control involves initiating corrective responses in response to perturbations?
      a) Reactive postural control
      b) Proactive postural control
      c) Anticipatory postural control
      
      a) Reactive postural control
      Reactive postural control is characterized by initiating corrective responses in response to external perturbations or unexpected disturbances to maintain or recover balance.

   2. When does anticipatory postural control occur?
      a) Before or during voluntary movement
      b) After experiencing perturbations
      c) During static standing
      
      a) Before or during voluntary movement
      Anticipatory postural control occurs before or during voluntary movement, where the system is pretuned to counteract internally generated destabilizing forces and prepare for upcoming movement.

   3. Which type of postural control uses feedback systems to initiate corrective responses?
      a) Anticipatory postural control
      b) Reactive postural control
      c) Proactive postural control
      
      b) Reactive postural control
      Feedback systems are utilized in reactive postural control to provide sensory inputs and initiate corrective responses in response to perturbations.

   4. What is the essential component of all upright tasks, according to the provided information?
      a) Recovery from episodes of instability
      b) Anticipation and avoidance of instability
      c) Both recovery from instability and anticipation of instability
      
      c) Both recovery from instability and anticipation of instability
      The essential component of all upright tasks involves both the ability to recover from episodes of instability reactively and the ability to anticipate and move in ways to avoid instability proactively.

   5. How is anticipatory postural control different from reactive postural control?
      a) Anticipatory control occurs before voluntary movement, while reactive control occurs after perturbations.
      b) Anticipatory control uses feedback systems, while reactive control uses feedforward systems.
      c) Anticipatory control involves externally generated disturbances, while reactive control involves internally generated destabilizing forces.
      
      a) Anticipatory control occurs before voluntary movement, while reactive control occurs after perturbations.
      Anticipatory postural control occurs before or during voluntary movement, while reactive postural control occurs in response to perturbations after they occur.

   6. What type of information does anticipatory postural control utilize to prepare for upcoming movement?
      a) Feedback information
      b) Feedforward information
      c) Visual information
      
      b) Feedforward information
      Anticipatory postural control uses feedforward information to pretune the system for upcoming movement and counteract internally generated destabilizing forces.

   7. In which scenario would anticipatory postural adjustments likely occur?
      a) Standing still with eyes closed
      b) Walking on a flat surface
      c) Preparing to catch a ball
      
      c) Preparing to catch a ball & a) Standing still with eyes closed
      Anticipatory postural adjustments are likely to occur when preparing to catch a ball, as the body pre-adjusts to stabilize the trunk and prevent forward leaning during the catching motion.
         What type would be a)?
            Scenario a) "Standing still with eyes closed" would likely involve anticipatory postural adjustments as well. When standing still with eyes closed, the sensory input from vision is removed, which can challenge the body's balance control mechanisms. In response to this challenge, the nervous system may anticipate the need for postural adjustments to maintain stability and prevent falls. Anticipatory postural adjustments in this scenario might involve subtle shifts in muscle activation and joint stiffness to counteract potential perturbations in balance.

.Reactive control: ankle strategy

   1. Which term describes a corrective action triggered quickly and unconsciously in response to a perturbation?
      a) Voluntary strategy
      b) Reactive strategy
      c) Anticipatory strategy
      b) Reactive strategy
      Reactive strategies are corrective actions that are quickly and typically unconsciously triggered in response to an unexpected perturbation.

   2. In the ankle strategy, which muscle group responds first to a perturbation?
      a) Quadriceps
      b) Tibialis anterior
      c) Gastrocnemius
      c) Gastrocnemius
      In the ankle strategy, the muscles at the ankle, specifically the gastrocnemius, respond first to a perturbation, initiating the distal-to-proximal recruitment pattern.

   3. When would a reactive ankle strategy typically be utilized?
      a) During voluntary movements
      b) When the perturbation is large
      c) When the surface is firm and the perturbation is small
      c) When the surface is firm and the perturbation is small
      A reactive ankle strategy is typically utilized when the perturbation is small and the surface is firm, allowing for quick and precise corrective responses.

   4. How soon after a perturbation does muscle activity occur in the ankle strategy?
      a) 20-30 milliseconds
      b) 80-100 milliseconds
      c) 200-300 milliseconds
      b) 80-100 milliseconds
      Muscle activity in the ankle strategy occurs very quickly, typically within 80-100 milliseconds after the perturbation, enabling rapid corrective responses.

   5. Which muscle group follows the gastrocnemius in the ankle strategy?
      a) Hamstrings
      b) Quadriceps
      c) Tibialis anterior
      a) Hamstrings
      Following the activation of the gastrocnemius, the hamstrings are recruited in the ankle strategy to further assist in correcting the sway.

   6. What is the characteristic recruitment pattern of muscles in the ankle strategy?
      a) Proximal-to-distal
      b) Bilateral
      c) Distal-to-proximal
      c) Distal-to-proximal
      The ankle strategy is characterized by the distal-to-proximal recruitment pattern, where muscles at the ankle respond first, followed by muscles more proximally located.

   7. In which direction does the body sway if the platform is unexpectedly moved forward during the ankle strategy?
      a) Backward
      b) Forward
      c) Sideways
      b) Forward
      If the platform is unexpectedly moved forward during the ankle strategy, the body sways backward to realign the center of mass, necessitating a forward corrective sway.

   8. What is the primary purpose of the ankle strategy?
      a) To maintain balance during voluntary movements
      b) To counteract large perturbations
      c) To quickly realign the center of mass after small perturbations
      c) To quickly realign the center of mass after small perturbations
      The primary purpose of the ankle strategy is to quickly realign the center of mass after small perturbations, maintaining stability on a firm surface.

.Reactive control: hip strategy
   1. What is the primary difference between the hip strategy and the ankle strategy?
      a) Timing of muscle activation
      b) Direction of body sway
      c) Recruitment pattern of muscles
      c) Recruitment pattern of muscles
      The primary difference between the hip strategy and the ankle strategy lies in the recruitment pattern of muscles, with the hip strategy characterized by proximal-to-distal muscle activation.

   2. During the hip strategy, which muscle group responds first to a perturbation?
      a) Tibialis anterior
      b) Abdominals
      c) Gastrocnemius
      b) Abdominals
      In the hip strategy, the abdominals are among the first muscle groups to respond to a perturbation, initiating the proximal-to-distal recruitment pattern.

   3. When would a reactive hip strategy typically be utilized?
      a) When the perturbation is small
      b) When the support surface is firm
      c) When the perturbation is larger or faster
      c) When the perturbation is larger or faster
      A reactive hip strategy is typically utilized when the perturbation is larger or faster, or when the support surface is compliant or smaller.

   4. What is the characteristic recruitment pattern of muscles in the hip strategy?
      a) Distal-to-proximal
      b) Proximal-to-distal
      c) Bilateral
      b) Proximal-to-distal
      The hip strategy is characterized by the proximal-to-distal recruitment pattern, where muscles closer to the body's center respond first, followed by more distal muscles.

   5. Which muscle group follows the abdominals in the hip strategy?
      a) Quadriceps
      b) Tibialis anterior
      c) Gastrocnemius
      a) Quadriceps
      Following the activation of the abdominals, the quadriceps are recruited in the hip strategy to further assist in correcting the sway.

   6. What is the primary purpose of the hip strategy?
      a) To maintain balance during voluntary movements
      b) To counteract small perturbations
      c) To quickly realign the center of mass after larger or faster perturbations
      c) To quickly realign the center of mass after larger or faster perturbations
      The primary purpose of the hip strategy is to quickly realign the center of mass after larger or faster perturbations, providing stability in challenging conditions.

   7. How soon after a perturbation does muscle activity occur in the hip strategy?
      a) 20-30 milliseconds
      b) 80-100 milliseconds
      c) 90-100 milliseconds
      c) 90-100 milliseconds
      Muscle activity in the hip strategy occurs very quickly, typically within 90-100 milliseconds after the perturbation, facilitating rapid corrective responses.

   8. Which muscle group follows the paraspinals in the hip strategy?
      a) Hamstrings
      b) Tibialis anterior
      c) Gastrocnemius
      a) Hamstrings
      Following the activation of the paraspinals, the hamstrings are recruited in the hip strategy to further assist in correcting the sway.

.Reactive control: stepping strategies
   1. When is a stepping strategy typically recruited?
      a) In response to slow, small perturbations
      b) In response to fast, large perturbations
      c) In response to voluntary movements
      b) In response to fast, large perturbations
      Stepping strategies are typically recruited in response to fast, large perturbations that cannot be adequately addressed by ankle or hip strategies.

   2. What is the primary purpose of a stepping strategy in reactive control?
      a) To maintain balance during voluntary movements
      b) To provide a rapid change in base of support
      c) To counteract slow, small perturbations
      b) To provide a rapid change in base of support
      The primary purpose of a stepping strategy is to provide a rapid change in the base of support, capturing the center of mass within a larger area to maintain balance.

   3. When is an ankle or hip strategy not sufficient in reactive control?
      a) During voluntary movements
      b) When the perturbation is slow and small
      c) When the perturbation is fast and large
      c) When the perturbation is fast and large
      An ankle or hip strategy may not be sufficient in reactive control when the perturbation is fast and large, necessitating the recruitment of a stepping strategy.

   4. What is the characteristic movement involved in a stepping strategy?
      a) Movement of the limbs to make a new contact with the support surface
      b) Rapid twisting of the torso
      c) Sudden jerking of the head
      a) Movement of the limbs to make a new contact with the support surface
      A stepping strategy involves movement of the limbs to make a new contact with the support surface, typically taking a rapid step in the direction of the displacing force.

   5. In which scenario would a stepping strategy be most likely employed?
      a) When the perturbation is small or slow
      b) When the perturbation is large and slow
      c) When the perturbation is large and fast
      c) When the perturbation is large and fast
      A stepping strategy is most likely employed when the perturbation is both large and fast, requiring a quick and decisive change in base of support.

   6. What occurs when the center of gravity moves outside the base of support?
      a) The person leans in the opposite direction
      b) The person shifts their weight to one side
      c) The person takes a step or reaches to maintain balance
      c) The person takes a step or reaches to maintain balance
      When the center of gravity moves outside the base of support, the person typically takes a step or reaches to maintain balance and prevent a fall.

   7. What distinguishes a stepping strategy from ankle and hip strategies?
      a) It involves movement of the limbs to change the base of support
      b) It relies solely on feedback mechanisms
      c) It is only utilized as a last resort
      a) It involves movement of the limbs to change the base of support
      A stepping strategy is distinguished from ankle and hip strategies by its characteristic movement, involving the limbs to make a new contact with the support surface.

   8. When does a stepping strategy become necessary in reactive control?
      a) When the perturbation is minimal
      b) When the perturbation is moderate
      c) When the perturbation exceeds the limits of ankle and hip strategies
      c) When the perturbation exceeds the limits of ankle and hip strategies
      A stepping strategy becomes necessary in reactive control when the perturbation exceeds the limits of ankle and hip strategies, such as during fast and large perturbations.

.Do we use ankle/hip strategies as discrete synergies
   1. What do the EMG results from the study by Runge et al. suggest about ankle and hip strategies?
      a) They are always used as discrete synergies
      b) They are more blended and exist on a continuum
      c) They are only utilized in response to slow perturbations
      b) They are more blended and exist on a continuum
      The EMG results indicate that ankle and hip strategies are more blended and exist on a continuum rather than being discrete synergies, suggesting that they are not used exclusively but rather in combination depending on the circumstances.

   2. At lower translation velocities in the study, which muscles show activity first in response to the platform translation?
      a) Rectus abdominis and quadriceps
      b) Gastrocnemius and hamstrings
      c) Sternocleidomastoid and paraspinals
      b) Gastrocnemius and hamstrings
      At lower translation velocities, muscle activity on the posterior aspect of the body appears first, including the gastrocnemius and hamstrings, indicating the initiation of an ankle strategy.

   3. At higher translation velocities in the study, which additional muscles show activity in response to the platform translation?
      a) Rectus abdominis and quadriceps
      b) Gastrocnemius and hamstrings
      c) Sternocleidomastoid and paraspinals
      a) Rectus abdominis and quadriceps
      At higher translation velocities, muscles on the anterior aspect of the body, including the rectus abdominis and quadriceps, show additional activity, suggesting a more comprehensive postural correction involving both ankle and hip strategies.

   4. What is the significance of the observed continuum of postural corrections in the study?
      a) It confirms the discrete nature of ankle and hip strategies
      b) It suggests that ankle and hip strategies are only used separately
      c) It indicates that ankle and hip strategies are more complex and can be blended
      c) It indicates that ankle and hip strategies are more complex and can be blended
      The observed continuum of postural corrections suggests that ankle and hip strategies are more complex than previously thought and can be blended rather than being used exclusively.

   5. What conclusion can be drawn from the EMG results regarding ankle and hip strategies?
      a) Ankle and hip strategies are always utilized separately
      b) Ankle and hip strategies adapt based on the speed of perturbations
      c) Ankle and hip strategies are fixed and do not vary
      b) Ankle and hip strategies adapt based on the speed of perturbations
      The EMG results show that ankle and hip strategies adapt based on the speed of perturbations, indicating a dynamic and adaptable response rather than fixed strategies.

   6. What does the study by Runge et al. suggest about the application of ankle and hip strategies in real-world conditions?
      a) They are only effective in a controlled laboratory setting
      b) They are utilized in a more blended manner and vary based on circumstances
      c) They are rarely used in response to perturbations
      b) They are utilized in a more blended manner and vary based on circumstances
      The study suggests that ankle and hip strategies are utilized in a more blended manner and vary based on circumstances rather than being discrete and fixed responses, indicating their applicability in real-world conditions.

.Effect of cerebellar dysfunction on balance
   1. In the experiment described, what is the primary function of the cerebellum in maintaining balance?
      a) Initiating voluntary movements
      b) Scaling postural responses to the velocity of perturbations
      c) Modulating sensory input from the environment
      b) Scaling postural responses to the velocity of perturbations
      The cerebellum is responsible for scaling postural responses to the velocity of perturbations, ensuring appropriate adjustments to maintain balance.

   2. What is the observed difference in muscle responses between healthy control subjects and those with spinocerebellar damage during backward platform movement?
      a) Similar muscle responses but with larger amplitude in spinocerebellar damage
      b) Overly large and alternating bursts of activity in spinocerebellar damage
      c) Absence of muscle responses in spinocerebellar damage
      b) Overly large and alternating bursts of activity in spinocerebellar damage
      Individuals with spinocerebellar damage exhibit overly large and alternating bursts of activity in antagonist muscles, indicating inefficient and likely ineffective partial responses.

   3. What is the consequence of damage to the spinocerebellum on the ability to scale postural responses?
      a) Inability to initiate any postural responses
      b) Ability to scale force but with greater variability
      c) Ability to scale force but with much greater force than necessary
      c) Ability to scale force but with much greater force than necessary
      Individuals with spinocerebellar damage can scale the force of postural responses but do so with much greater force than necessary, leading to inefficient responses.

   4. How do individuals with spinocerebellar damage respond to repeated translations of the platform compared to healthy control subjects?
      a) They show improved performance and adjust responses accordingly
      b) They demonstrate consistent responses regardless of repetition
      c) They exhibit no improvement in performance and cannot adjust responses based on experience
      c) They exhibit no improvement in performance and cannot adjust responses based on experience
      Individuals with spinocerebellar damage show no improvement in performance and cannot use their experience in one trial to adjust responses in subsequent trials, indicating an inability to adapt based on past experiences.

   5. What does the experiment reveal about the role of the cerebellum in reactive postural responses?
      a) The cerebellum is not involved in reactive postural responses
      b) Cerebellar damage results in enhanced reactive postural responses
      c) Cerebellar damage compromises reactive postural responses
      c) Cerebellar damage compromises reactive postural responses
      The experiment demonstrates that cerebellar damage compromises reactive postural responses, leading to inefficient and ineffective adjustments to perturbations.

   6. What is the significance of the variability in muscle responses observed in individuals with spinocerebellar damage?
      a) It indicates superior adaptability to changing conditions
      b) It suggests a lack of coordination and control over postural adjustments
      c) It reflects enhanced proprioceptive feedback mechanisms
      b) It suggests a lack of coordination and control over postural adjustments
      The variability in muscle responses suggests a lack of coordination and control over postural adjustments in individuals with spinocerebellar damage, contributing to compromised balance control.

.Anticipatory postural control
   1. What is anticipatory postural control?
      a) Activating postural muscles during skilled movement
      b) Activating postural muscles in advance of a skilled movement
      c) Activating postural muscles after a skilled movement
      b) Activating postural muscles in advance of a skilled movement
      Anticipatory postural control involves activating postural muscles before a skilled movement to prepare the body for maintaining balance during the movement.

   2. Which term best describes the process of activating postural muscles before a voluntary movement?
      a) Reactive postural control
      b) Anticipatory postural control
      c) Proactive postural control
      b) Anticipatory postural control
      Anticipatory postural control refers to the activation of postural muscles in anticipation of a voluntary movement to maintain balance.

   3. What is the purpose of activating postural muscles before a voluntary movement?
      a) To destabilize the body
      b) To counteract destabilizing forces created by the movement
      c) To prevent movement altogether
      b) To counteract destabilizing forces created by the movement
      Anticipatory activation of postural muscles helps counteract destabilizing forces created by voluntary movements, ensuring balance is maintained.

   4. In arm-raising experiments, which muscles are typically activated in advance of the prime mover?
      a) Muscles on the ventral surface of the body
      b) Muscles on the lateral surface of the body
      c) Muscles on the dorsal surface of the body
      c) Muscles on the dorsal surface of the body
      In arm-raising experiments, postural muscles on the dorsal surface of the body, such as gastrocnemius, hamstrings, and paraspinals, are activated in advance to counteract the forward shift of the center of gravity caused by the arm movement.

   5. What is the main goal of anticipatory adjustments in postural control?
      a) To create instability
      b) To maintain stability during movement
      c) To delay movement initiation
      b) To maintain stability during movement
      Anticipatory adjustments in postural control aim to maintain stability during voluntary movements by preparing the body to counteract destabilizing forces.

.APAs precede voluntary movement, are scaled to upcoming movements, and are only used when needed
   1. What are anticipatory postural adjustments (APAs) primarily designed to do?
      a) Create instability during voluntary movement
      b) Counteract destabilizing forces before voluntary movement
      c) Delay the onset of voluntary movement
      b) Counteract destabilizing forces before voluntary movement
      APAs are designed to counteract destabilizing forces that occur before voluntary movements, ensuring stability is maintained during the movement.

   2. How are APAs scaled in relation to upcoming movements?
      a) They remain constant regardless of the movement intensity
      b) They increase in magnitude with greater movement intensity
      c) They decrease in magnitude with greater movement intensity
      b) They increase in magnitude with greater movement intensity
      APAs are scaled to the intensity of upcoming movements, meaning they increase in magnitude as the intensity of the movement increases.

   3. When are anticipatory postural adjustments (APAs) typically utilized?
      a) Only during voluntary movements
      b) Only during involuntary movements
      c) Both during voluntary movements and when standing still
      a) Only during voluntary movements
      APAs are primarily utilized during voluntary movements to prepare the body and counteract destabilizing forces before the movement occurs.

   4. In the experiment involving pulling on a handle attached to a wall, what muscle group shows activation prior to pulling?
      a) Arm muscles
      b) Leg muscles
      c) Abdominal muscles
      b) Leg muscles
      In the experiment, leg muscles, specifically the hamstrings and gastrocnemius, show activation prior to pulling to prevent the body from rotating forward during the arm pull.

   5. How do supported and unsupported stances affect anticipatory leg muscle activity during arm pulling?
      a) Supported stance increases leg muscle activity
      b) Unsupported stance increases leg muscle activity
      c) Supported stance decreases leg muscle activity
      c) Supported stance decreases leg muscle activity
      In supported stance, where the subject is supported by a rigid bar at the shoulder, anticipatory leg muscle activity is not necessary as the body cannot rotate forward, resulting in decreased leg muscle activation.

.APAs
   1. What is the role of the tibialis anterior (TA) muscle during reaching in sitting?
      a) It helps maintain balance sideways
      b) It assists in initiating forward body movement
      c) It supports backward body movement
      b) It assists in initiating forward body movement
      The TA muscle is activated prior to and during reaching movements in sitting, assisting in the initiation of forward body movement.

   2. Why is soleus activation important during reaching in sitting?
      a) To accelerate forward movement
      b) To prevent backward movement
      c) To brake forward movement and maintain balance
      c) To brake forward movement and maintain balance
      The soleus muscle is activated during reaching in sitting to brake forward movement, preventing the individual from losing balance forward.

   3. When do anticipatory postural adjustments (APAs) occur during reaching in sitting?
      a) Only after the reaching movement is completed
      b) Prior to and during the reaching movement
      c) Only during the backward movement after reaching
      b) Prior to and during the reaching movement
      APAs occur prior to and during the reaching movement, indicating the activation of postural muscles to prepare for and support the movement.

   4. What type of muscle activation is observed in the leg muscles during reaching in sitting?
      a) Activation of leg muscles is absent during sitting activities
      b) Activation of leg muscles occurs only after the reaching movement
      c) Activation of leg muscles occurs prior to and during the reaching movement
      c) Activation of leg muscles occurs prior to and during the reaching movement
      Leg muscles, including the tibialis anterior, are activated prior to and during reaching movements in sitting, indicating their involvement in the initiation and support of the movement.

   5. How does leg muscle activation contribute to reaching in sitting?
      a) Leg muscles contribute to trunk stability only
      b) Leg muscles assist in initiating and braking forward movement
      c) Leg muscles contribute to arm movement exclusively
      b) Leg muscles assist in initiating and braking forward movement
      Leg muscles, particularly the tibialis anterior and soleus, assist in initiating forward movement during reaching in sitting and brake forward movement to maintain balance. They play a crucial role in the coordination and stability of the reaching movement.

.Gait initiation: feedforward, anticipatory
   1. What is the purpose of the anticipatory medio-lateral trunk acceleration observed during gait initiation?
      a) To shift the body weight towards the stepping leg
      b) To shift the body weight away from the stepping leg
      c) To maintain equilibrium during quiet stance
      a) To shift the body weight towards the stepping leg
      The anticipatory medio-lateral trunk acceleration shifts the body weight towards the stance side, preparing the leg that will be stepping forward.

   2. What happens to the anticipatory medio-lateral trunk acceleration in individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD) during gait initiation?
      a) It becomes larger and more effective
      b) It remains the same as in control subjects
      c) It becomes smaller and often ineffectual
      c) It becomes smaller and often ineffectual
      In individuals with PD, the anticipatory medio-lateral trunk acceleration is significantly reduced and often ineffective, making it difficult for them to initiate walking.

   3. Why is the anticipatory medio-lateral trunk acceleration important for gait initiation?
      a) It helps maintain balance during quiet stance
      b) It prepares the leg for stepping forward by shifting body weight
      c) It prevents lateral sway during walking
      b) It prepares the leg for stepping forward by shifting body weight
      The anticipatory medio-lateral trunk acceleration prepares the leg for stepping forward by shifting the body weight towards the stance side, aiding in the initiation of walking.

   4. What would happen if there is a lack of anticipatory medio-lateral trunk acceleration during gait initiation?
      a) The stepping leg would be excessively loaded
      b) It would be easier to lift and advance the stepping leg
      c) It would not significantly affect gait initiation
      a) The stepping leg would be excessively loaded
      Without the anticipatory medio-lateral trunk acceleration, the stepping leg would not be adequately prepared, leading to excessive loading of the leg and making it difficult to lift and advance during gait initiation.

   5. How does Parkinson's disease affect anticipatory postural adjustments during gait initiation?
      a) It enhances anticipatory postural adjustments
      b) It has no effect on anticipatory postural adjustments
      c) It diminishes anticipatory postural adjustments, particularly the medio-lateral trunk acceleration
      c) It diminishes anticipatory postural adjustments, particularly the medio-lateral trunk acceleration
      Parkinson's disease diminishes anticipatory postural adjustments, including the medio-lateral trunk acceleration, which can lead to difficulties in initiating walking.

.External support and balance
   1. What effect did haptic cues from touching a cane have on postural sway in the study?
      a) They increased postural sway compared to not using a cane.
      b) They decreased postural sway even at force levels insufficient for physical stabilization.
      c) They had no effect on postural sway.
      b) They decreased postural sway even at force levels insufficient for physical stabilization.
      The study found that merely touching the cane, even at force levels below those needed for physical stabilization, effectively reduced postural sway in both sighted and congenitally blind individuals.

   2. How did the reduction in postural sway compare between touch contact and force contact with the cane?
      a) Touch contact had a greater reduction in postural sway.
      b) Force contact had a greater reduction in postural sway.
      c) Both touch and force contact had similar effects on postural sway.
      c) Both touch and force contact had similar effects on postural sway.
      The study observed that both touch contact and force contact with the cane resulted in a similar reduction in postural sway compared to not using a cane.

   3. What was the main finding regarding postural sway in participants who touched the cane without applying significant force?
      a) Their postural sway increased compared to not using a cane.
      b) Their postural sway decreased compared to not using a cane.
      c) Their postural sway remained unchanged compared to not using a cane.
      b) Their postural sway decreased compared to not using a cane.
      Merely touching the cane, even without applying significant force, resulted in a decrease in postural sway compared to not using a cane.

   4. How did the study participants maintain balance while touching the cane with force levels below those needed for physical stabilization?
      a) By exerting excessive force on the cane.
      b) By relying on proprioceptive and haptic cues from touching the cane.
      c) By minimizing contact with the cane.
      b) By relying on proprioceptive and haptic cues from touching the cane.
      Participants maintained balance by relying on proprioceptive (sensory feedback from muscles and joints) and haptic (sensory feedback from touch) cues from touching the cane, even at force levels insufficient for physical stabilization.

   5. What implication does the study have for assessing balance in patients?
      a) Patients should be encouraged to minimize contact with supportive surfaces.
      b) Patients' balance performance may be overestimated if they are touching a surface, even with minimal force.
      c) Patients' balance performance may be accurately assessed regardless of surface contact.
      b) Patients' balance performance may be overestimated if they are touching a surface, even with minimal force.
      The study suggests that patients' balance performance may be overestimated if they are touching a surface, even with minimal force, as this can effectively reduce postural sway, potentially masking underlying balance deficits.

.Balance: distributed control
   1. Which of the following is an example of distributed control in balance regulation?
      a) Sole involvement of the cerebellum
      b) Integration of signals from various brain areas for motor output
      c) Exclusively relying on the visual system for balance
      b) Integration of signals from various brain areas for motor output
      Distributed control in balance involves the integration of signals from multiple brain areas, including the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital cortex, as well as the basal ganglia and cerebellum, to determine appropriate motor output.

   2. What role does the cerebellum play in balance regulation?
      a) It solely controls balance without input from other brain regions.
      b) It integrates signals from various brain areas for balance control.
      c) It provides feedback only to the visual system during balance tasks.
      b) It integrates signals from various brain areas for balance control.
      The cerebellum integrates signals from various brain areas, including the cortex and basal ganglia, to contribute to balance regulation.

   3. What are the inputs to the reticulospinal and vestibulospinal pathways?
      a) Signals exclusively from the somatosensory system
      b) Afferent inputs from the visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems
      c) Signals originating solely from the cerebellum
      b) Afferent inputs from the visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems
      The reticulospinal and vestibulospinal pathways receive inputs from the visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems, which are integrated in the brainstem and cortex for balance control.

   4. What contributes to updating the body schema for future postural commands?
      a) Signals from the cerebellum only
      b) Integration of afferent inputs from sensory systems in the brainstem
      c) Sole involvement of the parietal cortex
      b) Integration of afferent inputs from sensory systems in the brainstem
      Afferent inputs from sensory systems, including the visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems, are integrated in the brainstem and cortex to update the body schema for future postural commands.

   5. What is an essential characteristic of distributed control in balance?
      a) Sole reliance on the cerebellum for balance regulation
      b) Integration of signals from various brain areas for motor output
      c) Exclusively using the vestibular system for balance adjustments
      b) Integration of signals from various brain areas for motor output
      Distributed control in balance involves the integration of signals from multiple brain areas to determine appropriate motor output, rather than relying solely on one brain region.

   6. What role do the basal ganglia play in balance regulation?
      a) Solely providing feedback to the cerebellum
      b) Integrating sensory inputs for postural adjustments
      c) Exclusively controlling balance through the somatosensory system
      b) Integrating sensory inputs for postural adjustments
      The basal ganglia contribute to balance regulation by integrating sensory inputs, along with other brain areas, to generate appropriate postural adjustments.

   7. How does the brainstem contribute to balance regulation?
      a) By processing visual information exclusively
      b) By integrating afferent inputs from sensory systems and cortex
      c) By relying solely on the cerebellum for postural commands
      b) By integrating afferent inputs from sensory systems and cortex
      The brainstem integrates afferent inputs from sensory systems and cortex to generate postural commands and contribute to balance regulation.

   8. What type of inputs do the vestibulospinal pathways receive?
      a) Signals only from the cerebellum
      b) Inputs exclusively from the visual system
      c) Afferent inputs from the vestibular system
      c) Afferent inputs from the vestibular system
      The vestibulospinal pathways receive afferent inputs from the vestibular system, which contribute to balance regulation and postural adjustments.

   9. What is the significance of balance being an outcome of distributed control?
      a) It indicates sole reliance on the cerebellum for balance adjustments.
      b) It underscores the importance of integrating signals from various brain areas.
      c) It suggests that balance is solely controlled by the somatosensory system.
      b) It underscores the importance of integrating signals from various brain areas.
      Balance being an outcome of distributed control highlights the importance of integrating signals from various brain areas, including the cortex, basal ganglia, and cerebellum, for effective balance regulation.

   10. How does distributed control contribute to balance regulation?
      a) By relying solely on the cerebellum for postural adjustments
      b) By integrating signals from different brain regions to determine appropriate motor output
      c) By excluding inputs from sensory systems during postural tasks
      b) By integrating signals from different brain regions to determine appropriate motor output
      Distributed control in balance regulation involves integrating signals from different brain regions to determine appropriate motor output for maintaining balance and stability.

   • Fractionated movement – isolate motor activity to a limited set of muscles;

   1 A smaller unit of organization of the cerebral cortex is the cortical column.  0 1 A column of cortex that goes through all six layers.  0 1 The idea of a cortical column might be  0 1 likened to the segmental motor center of the spinal cord.  0 1 All layers of the cortical column have a relation to a specific aspect of a function,  0 1 like a mini community for a role.  0 1 For all columns, the most superficial layers are  0 1 activated for more general effects of attention, focus and awareness.  o 1 The deeper layers, four to six,  0 1 have more specific effects.  0 1 These layers are involved with specific inputs and outputs.  - 1 As an overview, ascending information from  o 1 thalamic nuclei that do not project to primary areas of the cortex.  0 1 Horizontal intracortical communication pathways synapse first and the superficial layers.  0 1 Layers 1-3, and then they project to layer 4.  o 1 Ascending information from specific thalamic nuclei, the nuclei that projected primary cortical areas like primary visual cortex,  0 1 primary motor cortex synapse in layer 4.  o 1 Descending output information from the cortex originates in layers 5 and 6,  o 1 which also send feedback to layer 1.  o 1 This feedback is thought to be related to keeping  o 1 the cortical column engaged or aware of the output.

   1 The Cerebral cortex has essentially two main types of cells,  0 1 projection neurons and interneurons.  - 1 The projection neurons are pyramidal cells,  0 1 the output cells of the cortex.  0 1 The interneurons are stellate cells for local communication in the cortex.  0 1 The output of the cortex via the pyramidal cells is  o 1 from small pyramidal cells of layers 2 and 3,  o 1 and then the large pyramidal cells of layer 5.  o 1 The small pyramidal cells of layer 2 and 3 project to  o 1 other cortical areas for intracortical communication.  0 1 The large pyramidal cells of layer 5 project out of the cortex to subcortical structures, the brainstem and the spinal cord.  0 1 The projection neurons of layer 6,  o 1 have spindle-shaped and project either to the thalamus,  0 1 back to superficial layers of the cortex or  0 1 some other area of the cortex for intracortical communication.

.Cerebral cortex: organized for function
   • Interneurons are stellate cells (spiny, smooth, small, medium …); can be excitatory or 
   inhibitory
   • Stellate cells: 
   • All layers, mainly in layer 4
   • Multiple synaptic inputs to pyramidal neurons in layers 3 and 5
   • Basket cells (type of stellate)
   • Inhibit at the soma of pyramidal neurons in layers 2, 3, & 5;
   • ‘Horizontal or lateral inhibition’ (help focus or define the information)

   The stellate cells or interneurons,  0 1 communicate between layers of the cortical column,  0 1 and between cortical regions for intracortical communication.  0 1 There are several types of stellate cells,  0 1 and the stellate cell effect on other neurons can be excitatory or inhibitory.  0 1 All layers have stellate cells.  0 1 The stellate cells in layer 4 are generally larger and there are more of them. These stellate cells in layer 4 synapse onto  0 1 pyramidal neurons and the output layers, 3 and 5.  o 1 Basket cells are a special type of stellate cell.  0 1 As described for the cerebellum,  o 1 basket cells in the cortex generally provide  0 1 inhibitory projections to the cell body of the pyramidal neurons.  0 1 Specifically, they make inhibitory synapses  - 1 on the cell bodies of the pyramidal cells in layers 2,  o 1 3, and 5.  o 1 Their inhibitory function can be described as sharpening the output message,  0 1 suppressing other activity to enable a more focused output.

.Active Recall!
   • Name one source of input to the ventral lateral nucleus of the thalamus. Where do the axons from this nucleus project to?
      One source of input to the ventral lateral nucleus of the thalamus is the cerebellum. Axons from this nucleus project to the motor cortex for motor planning and motor adaptations to well-learned movements.

   • Name one source on input to the ventral posterolateral or ventral posteromedial nuclei. Where do axons from these nuclei project to?
      One source of input to the ventral posterolateral (VPL) or ventral posteromedial (VPM) nuclei of the thalamus is the somatosensory information related to all somatosensory modalities from the body (VPL) and from the head, neck, and face (VPM). Axons from these nuclei project to the primary somatosensory cortex.

.Summary/Key points
   • The organization of the cerebral cortex allows for extensive networks of neural connections for cortico-cortico communication, and cortical communication with brainstem and spinal structures.
   • The thalamus contains relay nuclei that convey information from the sensory systems, cerebellum, and basal ganglia (Module 8) to specific areas of the cerebral cortex.

.Human cerebral cortex: perception, behavior; willed movement - ‘movement for a reason’
   1. Which area of the brain is primarily responsible for generating ideas, thoughts, and intentions, and transforming them into actions?
      a) Cerebellum  
      b) Cerebral cortex  
      c) Brainstem  
      b) Cerebral cortex

      The cerebral cortex is involved in generating ideas, thoughts, intentions, and plans for action. It interprets the environment, influences it through communication, and plays a crucial role in goal-directed movement.

   2. What is the main function of fractionated movement?
      a) Initiating reflex actions  
      b) Isolating specific muscle contractions  
      c) Coordinating large muscle groups  

      b) Isolating specific muscle contractions
      Fractionated movement involves isolating movements to specific muscles, allowing for precise control over actions. This is often demonstrated in activities such as playing the piano or typing.

   3. Which process involves the acquisition of motor skills?
      a) Motor control  
      b) Motor learning
      c) Motor planning  

      b) Motor learning
      Motor learning is the process of acquiring motor skills through practice and experience. It involves the development of efficient movement patterns and the refinement of motor control.

   4. At what age does walking typically begin in humans?
      a) 3 months  
      b) 1 year  
      c) 3 years  

      b) 1 year
      Walking typically begins around one year of age, marking the initiation of a goal-directed sequence of movements that is learned and refined through practice.

   5. Which part of the brain is involved in abstract reasoning and conceptual thinking?
      a) Thalamus  
      b) Hippocampus  
      c) Cerebral cortex  

      c) Cerebral cortex
      The cerebral cortex is responsible for abstract reasoning and conceptual thinking, which are essential for planning and executing goal-directed actions.

   6. What is the characteristic feature of goal-directed movement?
      a) Random and uncoordinated actions  
      b) Unpredictable muscle contractions  
      c) Motivated and planned actions  

      c) Motivated and planned actions
      Goal-directed movement involves actions that are motivated, planned, and aimed at achieving a specific objective, reflecting the involvement of the cerebral cortex in generating and executing intentions.

   7. Which area of the brain is primarily responsible for motor control requirements such as speed, accuracy, and adaptability?
      a) Basal ganglia  
      b) Cerebellum  
      c) Cerebral cortex  

      c) Cerebral cortex
      The cerebral cortex plays a crucial role in motor control, including regulating factors such as speed, accuracy, and adaptability, to execute goal-directed movements effectively.

   8. What illustrates the exquisite specificity of some cerebral cortex neurons in carrying out isolated muscle contractions for a goal?
      a) Reflex arcs  
      b) Fractionated movement  
      c) Synergistic muscle actions  

      b) Fractionated movement
      Fractionated movement demonstrates the precise control and specificity of some cerebral cortex neurons, allowing for the isolation of muscle contractions to achieve particular goals, such as playing a musical instrument or typing.

.Cerebral cortex: motor control is not just top down but distributed at multiple levels of NS
   1. What term describes the distributed and interconnected nature of motor control across multiple levels of the nervous system?
      a) Hierarchical control  
      b) Heterarchical control  
      c) Homogeneous control  

      b) Heterarchical control
      Heterarchical control refers to the distributed and interconnected nature of motor control across multiple levels of the nervous system. It emphasizes that motor control involves coordination and interaction between various brain regions rather than a strict hierarchical order.

   2. Which part of the brain is responsible for receiving sensory information and providing motor copy about the status of segmental motor centers?
      a) Cerebral cortex  
      b) Brainstem  
      c) Cerebellum  

      b) Brainstem
      The brainstem receives sensory information and provides motor copy about the status of segmental motor centers. It plays a crucial role in coordinating and regulating basic motor functions.

   3. What does vertical information flow in motor control refer to?
      a) Flow of information within one level or segment  
      b) Flow of information from the cortex to the spinal cord and muscles  
      c) Flow of information from the periphery up to the cortex  

      c) Flow of information from the periphery up to the cortex
      Vertical information flow in motor control describes the flow of sensory information from the periphery up to the cortex. This flow allows the brain to receive input about the external environment and the body's position and state.

   4. What is the main function of the cerebellum in motor control?
      a) Generating movement plans  
      b) Executing motor actions  
      c) Monitoring and adapting movements  

      c) Monitoring and adapting movements
      The cerebellum plays a key role in monitoring and adapting movements by integrating sensory information and comparing it with motor commands. It helps to ensure smooth and coordinated movements.

   5. What is emphasized by the term "horizontal information flow" in motor control?
      a) Communication between different brain regions  
      b) Feedback from muscles to the spinal cord  
      c) Transmission of motor commands to the muscles  

      a) Communication between different brain regions
      Horizontal information flow in motor control refers to the communication between different brain regions at the same level or segment. It facilitates the coordination of motor functions and the integration of sensory and motor information.

   6. What is the significance of distributed control and organization in motor control?
      a) It relies solely on cerebral cortical activity  
      b) It ensures efficient motor coordination  
      c) It eliminates the need for sensory feedback  

      b) It ensures efficient motor coordination
      Distributed control and organization in motor control ensure efficient motor coordination by involving multiple control centers or hubs across the nervous system. This allows for the generation of movement plans, execution, monitoring, adaptation, and learning.

.Cerebral cortex has six layers; different layers expanded in specific regions relative to function (Memoritzar milllor amb mnemotècnia)(!!)
   1. Which layer of the cerebral cortex serves as the primary input layer, receiving inputs from specific thalamic nuclei?
      a) Molecular layer  
      b) External granular layer  
      c) Internal granular cell layer  

      c) Internal granular cell layer
      The internal granular cell layer (Layer 4) is the primary input layer of the cerebral cortex, receiving inputs from specific thalamic nuclei. This layer plays a crucial role in processing sensory information relayed from the thalamus.

   2. Which layer of the cerebral cortex contains small pyramidal cells and is involved in horizontal communication between cortical regions?
      a) External granular layer  
      b) External pyramidal cell layer  
      c) Internal granular cell layer  

      b) External pyramidal cell layer
      The external pyramidal cell layer (Layer 3) contains small pyramidal cells and is involved in horizontal communication between cortical regions. This layer facilitates intracortical networks and communication between adjacent cortical areas.

   3. Which layer of the cerebral cortex is primarily composed of dendrites of neurons?
      a) External granular layer  
      b) Molecular layer  
      c) Multiform layer  

      b) Molecular layer
      The molecular layer (Layer 1) of the cerebral cortex is predominantly composed of dendrites of neurons. It serves as a site for synaptic connections and processing of incoming signals.

   4. Which layer of the cerebral cortex serves as the primary output layer, sending projections to other areas of the nervous system, including the spinal cord?
      a) External granular layer  
      b) Internal pyramidal layer  
      c) Multiform layer  

      b) Internal pyramidal layer
      The internal pyramidal layer (Layer 5) serves as the primary output layer of the cerebral cortex. It contains large pyramidal cells, including Betz cells, which project to other areas of the nervous system, such as the spinal cord, via the corticospinal tract.

   5. Which stain is commonly used to visualize the structure of neurons and neural tissue?
      a) Golgi stain  
      b) Nissl stain  
      c) Weigert stain  

      b) Nissl stain
      Nissl stain is commonly used to visualize the structure of neurons and neural tissue by selectively staining cell bodies and their nuclei. It helps in identifying neuronal morphology and organization within brain tissue.

   6. What is the function of spindle-shaped cells in Layer 6 of the cerebral cortex?
      a) Processing sensory information  
      b) Filtering and reorganizing information from the thalamus  
      c) Generating motor commands  

      b) Filtering and reorganizing information from the thalamus
      Spindle-shaped cells in Layer 6 of the cerebral cortex project to the thalamus, facilitating reciprocal communication. They have the potential to filter, facilitate, and reorganize sensory information coming to the cortex from the thalamus, contributing to sensory processing and integration.

   7. Which layer of the cerebral cortex contains stellate cells and serves as the site for primary input?
      a) Molecular layer  
      b) External granular layer  
      c) Internal granular cell layer  

      c) Internal granular cell layer
      The internal granular cell layer (Layer 4) contains stellate cells and serves as the primary input layer of the cerebral cortex. It receives inputs from specific thalamic nuclei and plays a crucial role in sensory processing.

   8. What is the primary function of layers 2 and 3 of the cerebral cortex?
      a) Processing motor commands  
      b) Horizontal communication between cortical regions  
      c) Filtering sensory information  

      b) Horizontal communication between cortical regions
      Layers 2 and 3 of the cerebral cortex are involved in horizontal communication between cortical regions. They facilitate intracortical networks and communication between adjacent cortical areas, contributing to the integration and processing of sensory and motor information.

   9. Which type of cells are primarily found in Layer 5 of the cerebral cortex?
      a) Stellate cells  
      b) Large pyramidal cells  
      c) Small pyramidal cells  

      b) Large pyramidal cells
      Layer 5 of the cerebral cortex primarily contains large pyramidal cells, including Betz cells. These cells are the main output neurons of the cortex, sending projections to other areas of the nervous system, such as the spinal cord.

   10. What is the role of layer 1 (molecular layer) in the cerebral cortex?
      a) Initiating motor commands  
      b) Facilitating synaptic connections  
      c) Processing visual information  

      b) Facilitating synaptic connections
      Layer 1 (molecular layer) of the cerebral cortex facilitates synaptic connections and processing of incoming signals. It serves as a site for synaptic integration and modulation of neural activity within the cortex.

.Cerebral cortex: organized for function (Memoritzar milllor amb mnemotècnia)(!!)
   1. What is the main function of the superficial layers (1-3) of the cortical column?
      a) Specific sensory processing
