   distributed WITHOUT permission.

   Briefly, short-term memory includes a primary and a working short-term memory. Primary memory refers tojust holding or maintaining  information temporarily for a very short period of time.  An example might be holding a phone number in mind  as you enter the number into your context on your phone.  Working memory refers to the maintenance and  controlled manipulation of a limited amount of information before recall. Working memory is active and the processing occurring in  working memory is important for guiding decision-making and behavior. Long—term memory involves the storage and recall of  information over a long period of time.  There are several types of long-term memory that we will talk about. Episodic memory and semantic memory are  both types of declarative memory that wejust talked about.  Episodic memory and semantic memory are both types of declarative memory. Episodic memory is memory for events and  experiences and semantic memory is memory for facts and knowledge. Procedural memory, which we defined earlier,  is memory for task performance.  The MOCA, M—O—C—A,  which stands for Montreal Cognitive Assessment, is shown here.  It's a screening test for  short and long-term memory processes and also for executive function. Short-term working memory is assessed using delayed recall.  The person has to recall five items after a few minutes.  Here are the five items. You ask the person to repeat those words: Face,  velvet, church, daisy, red,  and then they do some other things then down here delayed recall,  they're asked to recall those five words.  There's also assessment of long-term memory.  Naming these animals requires long-term semantic memory.  In the abstraction task,  the person is asked the similarity between a train and a bicycle and a watch and a ruler. This requires use of long-term semantic memory to describe these associations. Age—related effects are more marked for those components of memory with the asterisk. We see most age-related decline in short-term  working memory and long-term episodic memory. Long-term procedural memory or memory for well—learned motor acts,  is generally considered unchanged by aging.

   In this figure, we see the major divisions of human memory  : Short-term memory and long-term memory.  Some people acknowledge a third sensory memory,  which refers to the very brief experience or impression of raw sensory data.  For example, a visual image flashed onto a screen or  sign can be held momentarily in memory even though the visual image may be gone. Similarly, we can hold sounds briefly in sensory memory.  Long-term memory is more complex and has sub-classification that we've already mentioned. Long-term memory can be classified as either explicit or implicit.  Explicit and implicit referred to classification of  memory based on mechanisms of recall of the memory.  Explicit memory is referred to as  conscious memory while implicit is referred to as unconscious memory.  Explicit memory is also known as declarative memory,  which is long-term memory for facts and events. Declarative memory can then be further subdivided into episodic and semantic memory. Episodic memory, again,  is the memory for events and experiences while  semantic long-term memory is memory for facts,  concepts, general knowledge about the world.  Procedural memory is one type of implicit, unconscious, memory.  Why is explicit declarative memory called conscious memory?  Because memory for facts and events can be  brought into consciousness and expressed overtly.  That is, we can recall, think about,  discuss, and declare our memories for events and experiences in general knowledge. Implicit memory or unconscious memory,  is typically manifested in  an automatic manner with little conscious processing on the part of the subject.  For example, tying your shoes is  a procedural memory that does not require the conscious retrieval of  past information and can be performed automatically with little or no awareness of the skill involved.

   Let's review what we know.  There are two types of long—term memory.  Explicit declarative memory that is conscious.  This declarative memory can be subdivided into semantic memory, our memory for general knowledge.  That's why you see the books there and episodic long—term memory, our memory for events and experiences.  For example, recalling your own wedding or the wedding of a friend. Implicit memory is non-declarative and unconscious.  Procedural memory which is right here.  Our memory for skills and habits is one type of implicit memory. There are other types of implicit memory,  as you can see here.  Habituation refers to a decrease in responsiveness to  a stimulus following repeated exposure to that stimulus.  For example, a dog will be active and alert when they hear a strange tone or sound. If the tone is played over and over,  the dog will eventually no longer be engaged by the tone.  We say that the dog has habituated to that sound.  This kind of learning makes sense.  It is not efficient for an animal or person to go on  responding to a stimulus that has no meaning or importance.  One example for us is that habituation happens with clothing.  Clothes touch us all the time.  The stimulation is repeated so much that the response is habituated.  Another example is that we become habituated to many common background noises. Again, habituation is learning to ignore  innocuous stimuli that have no meaning or immediate importance. In contrast, sensitization is an enhanced response to  many different stimuli after experiencing an intense or noxious stimulus.  For example, repetition of  a painful stimulus often makes one more responsive to a loud noise.  There are many different uses of the word sensitization.  For example, you may have heard of central sensitization,  which is a process implicated in chronic pain.  Here, nociceptive neurons in the dorsal horn of  the spinal cord become sensitized by peripheral tissue damage or inflammation, resulting in a stronger pain response.  Drug sensitization occurs in drug addiction and is  defined as an increased effect of the drug following repeated doses.  Suggested anatomical correlates of the various types of  implicit memory are provided in  this bottom row and it is likely that these regions are  involved in these various types of implicit memory.

.Short term/working memory: a multicomponent system used to manipulate information
   Working memory
   • Maintains current, transient goal relevant knowledge
   • Two subsystems: one for verbal information, one for visuospatial information
   • (Note: these are controlled by executive control processes, allocate attention 
   one way or the other)
   • Verbal: keeping speech-based information in awareness, e.g. rehearsing a 
   phone number
   oPhonological loop: store, articulatory processes
   • Visuospatial: retains mental images of visual objects and locations of objects 
   in space
   • Prefrontal cortex – heavily connected with parietal lobe/ visual input (see 
   upcoming Figure)

   Now that we have defined the major classifications and subdivisions of memory, let's go back and talk about short-term working memory.  Working memory is engaged memory using it at this moment.  It maintains the information in mind for the purpose of using it now,  as this information is relevant to the current action or additional learning. Baddeley et al originated the idea of two subsystems of working memory. There's an executive controller that directs — attention to one or the other of the subsystems.  The verbal subsystem also referred to as the articulatory or phonological loop, is a subsystem of working memory for language-based information.  An example is self talk,  as in recalling or rehearsing a phone number or recalling or rehearsing  a credit card number to reproduce it in writing or type it in an online form. The other subsystem and working memory  is the visuospatial subsystem,  also referred to as a visuospatial Sketchpad.  This subsystem retains mental images of objects and locations of objects in space. Working memory holds the what and where in mind.  This is particularly important for guidance of reaching movements.  The prefrontal cortex and its connections with  the parietal and visual association cortices are  very much involved in the short-term working memory component systems.

.Prefrontal cortex in working memory
   The role of prefrontal cortex in maintaining information 
   in working memory is often assessed using 
   electrophysiological methods in conjunction with a 
   delayed-match-tosample (DMS) task. In this type of 
   task, each trial begins when the monkey grabs a 
   response lever and visually fixates a small target at the 
   center of a computer screen. An initial visual stimulus 
   (the sample) is briefly presented and must be held in 
   working memory until the next stimulus (the match) 
   appears. In the task illustrated here, the monkey was 
   required to remember the sample (“what”) and its 
   location (“where”) and release the lever only in response 
   to stimuli that matched on both dimensions.

   This figure illustrates the role of the prefrontal cortex in working memory,  as in this description so I encourage you to read this at some point.  A monkey right here first fixates on the center of the screen.  A visual target with a specific shape at a specific location then briefly appears. Then there is a delay.  The stimulus, the original stimulus is removed during  the delay and then a match stimulus is presented.  The match stimulus could be the same as the original, as is shown here,  the same shape in the same location.  Or it could be a different object in  the same location or the same object in a different location.  This would be a match,  this would not be a match and this also would not be a match.  The monkey receives a reward only when it releases a lever  when the match stimulus matches the original target's shape and location. To do this task,  the monkey then has to keep in mind and short-term working memory, the original object shape, and location.  The prefrontal cortex is critical for keeping that image in  mind to figure out whether the match stimulus is correct or not.  B on the left here is the activity of  one prefrontal neuron in response to our preferred object,  to which the neuron responds robustly and to  a non-preferred object to which the neuron responds minimally. Activity is robust both when the monkey looks at  the preferred object and during the delay when the stimulus is removed. Interestingly, this neuron is active when a non-preferred object is first presented, but then the activity is significantly  reduced during the delay for a non-preferred object.  This sketch on the right,  you can see it's taking a little area of the prefrontal cortex and zooming in on it. The symbols represent recording sites  where certain neurons maintained each type of information.  There were neurons that were coding object,  neurons that were coding location,  and neurons that were coding both object and location. What is happening here  is similar to the population vector coding we talked about in the motor cortex.  Recall that neurons in the motor cortex were directionally tuned.  They had a preferred direction and fired more robustly in advance of  a movement made in that direction.  Here, neurons in the prefrontal cortex appear to have  preferred objects and preferred locations.  That is, a pre-frontal cortex neuron fires more frequently when a preferred object  or location needs to be held in working memory.

.Tasks that use working memory
   These are examples of cognitive tests that  likely require the prefrontal cortex to keep an image,  or location, or another characteristic that is key to the correct response in mind.  The upper left illustrates the digit span task, which is right here.  This is a task of how many numbers can be learned and recalled in orders.  Basically, an experimenter would say 6, 8, 2,  5 and the participant would have to recall the numbers in that order. . Then they increase the amount of numbers by one each time. The digit symbol test over here on the right matches a symbol with a number. . Up here you can see the coding, . one is this symbol, . two is this symbol, . three is this symbol and so on. i The participant is asked to fill in i the rows with the correct symbol as quickly as possible. ' Thus, the ability to keep the correct number symbol match in mind for i the next presentation of that number is . important and it enhances the speed of completion. . The flanker task seen over here in the lower left, . asks for responses that match the direction of the central arrow. . Despite changes in the directions of the other arrow. - Here, this would be a match. . The arrow is pointing this way and the other arrows match it. i This is a congruent response, and this is incongruent. Here you have to keep the rule in mind that you only respond when the arrow matches.  The arrow that is shown next matches the direction of the central arrow. ' The lower middle figure illustrates the trail making tests. . For trails B, which is pictured here, i the goal is to connect the numbers and letters in ascending order, ' but alternate between numbers and letters. They're asked to start at one, i and they would connect from one, I they would go to a, so 1a, then to two, i then to b, i then to three, then to c, and then so on. i This requires that the rules be kept in working memory, . and where you are in the sequence must be updated. . The information is processed and manipulated in working memory. . Lastly, in the Stroop Color word test, . the participant is instructed to say the color and not the word. ' Working memory must keep the rule in mind to say the color and inhibit saying the word. . Here, your response would be red. . Here, your response would be black, yellow, blue, green. . Hard to do.

.LTM: explicit processing, four distinct operations
   • Encoding = new information is attended to and linked with 
   existing information in memory
   • Consolidation = makes temporarily stored information 
   more stable, processes of LTP
   • Storage = neural mechanisms by which memory is 
   retained over time
   • Retrieval = when stored information is recalled

   Let's move on to long-term memory. . While we have discussed the subdivisions of long-term memory, explicit, declarative, . implicit procedural, let's now discuss the processes of long-term memory. . The processing to create long-term memory, which largely moves information from short-term memory to long-term memory, . is modeled as four main processes. . To create long-term memory, . it is important to encode, . consolidate, and then store and retrieve. . Encoding refers to attending to new information, i and linking that new information with existing information already in long—term memory. . Consolidation refers to making ' temporarily stored information more stable through processes of long—term potentiation. . Recall that long—term potentiation, or LTP, . occurs when there is correlated firing between a pre and . postsynaptic neuron that overtime induces - changes in the neuron to create a very stable synapse. . Storage refers to the mechanisms by which . memory is retained over longer periods of time, i and retrieval refers to the neural processes for recalling the information when needed. . Though great gains have been made in memory research. Much of the specifics and the mechanisms of  these neural processes is not currently well understood.

.Explicit memory: Anatomical correlates
   Recall that explicit long-term memory is declarative, . and sub-classified as either episodic or semantic long-term memory. ' What are the neural correlates for explicit episodic memory? ' Some anatomical locations of where i — explicit memory is stored or recalled are shown here and in the next few slides. ' In general, I explicit episodic memory involves the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe system. I The key structures are the hippocampus, . which is seen over here. i The intrarenal cortex, which is seen over here.  The perirhinal cortex and the parahippocampal cortex. . Both of those, the pair of rhino and parahippocampal cortex surround the hippocampus. . These regions of the medial temporal cortex are necessary for the processes of encoding, . consolidation, storage, and recall of explicit episodic long-term memory.

.Explicit memory: anatomical correlates
   • Association cortices: semantic knowledge distributed throughout association cortices (prefrontal cortex, 
   limbic, parieto-occipital-temporal) in bits and pieces; episodic knowledge stored in prefrontal cortex
   • Parahippocampal and perirhinal cortex: cortical areas that surround hippocampus
   o Perirhinal cortex particularly important encoding object recognition
   o Parahippocampal cortex important for encoding spatial context .
   • Entorhinal cortex: main input and output path to hippocampus
   • Hippocampus: converts declarative STM to LTM
   o Bind together spatial and object information from perirhinal and parahippocampus forming a unified 
   memory.
   o Processes for transferring to association cortices for storage
   o Involved in retrieval of long-term memories from association cortices
   • Same systems involved in imagination of future events

   That wejust talked about the key areas involved an explicit episodic memory. ' Understand that many other brain areas are involved. . That is, memory like motor control is distributed throughout the cortex. . Association cortices are involved, as you see here. . Prefrontal, limbic and parietal cortex all seemed to have a role in memory storage. . The parahippocampal, and perirhinal cortical areas surround the hippocampus. . The perirhinal cortex appears to support memory for - objects and factual knowledge about the world. i The parahippocampal area appears important for . encoding the spatial information about an object or scene. i The entorhinal cortex is the major input and output pathway to and from the hippocampus. . Lesions here do not take away memory, but new learning and use of memory are impaired. . The hippocampus is both part of working memory and long—term memory. . As this structure is critical, . it's necessary to convert explicit short-term memory to long-term memory. . It appears to bind together information from . perirhinal and parahippocampus areas to form a unified memory. . The hippocampus also appears important for processes related to . transferring information to the association cortices for storage. ' Finally, the hippocampus appears important and . retrieval of long—term memory from those association cortices.

Summary/Key points
   • Memory is classified by the time course of storage and the type of 
   information being stored.
   • Explicit (declarative) working memories are stored in several 
   different association areas; the hippocampus is critical 
   for encoding short term memory into long term memory, 
   particularly for episodic memory.
   • The prefrontal cortex is critical for short-term working memory 
   processes.

.Learning and memory
   1. What is the definition of learning in neuroscience?
      a) The process by which knowledge is encoded, stored, and retrieved.
      b) A change in behavior resulting from acquiring knowledge about the world.
      c) The retention of information available for retrieval when useful for future actions.
      Correct Answer: b) A change in behavior resulting from acquiring knowledge about the world.
      - The correct answer is b) A change in behavior resulting from acquiring knowledge about the world. Learning, in neuroscience, is defined as a behavioral change that occurs as a result of acquiring new knowledge or experiences.

   2. What is memory in neuroscience primarily concerned with?
      a) Encoding and retrieval of information.
      b) The process of learning new skills.
      c) The consistency of performance during practice sessions.
      Correct Answer: a) Encoding and retrieval of information.
      - The correct answer is a) Encoding and retrieval of information. Memory, in neuroscience, involves the process of encoding new information, storing it, and retrieving it when needed for future actions or tasks.

   3. According to the passage, how is learning typically assessed in rehabilitation?
      a) By the consistency of performance during practice sessions.
      b) By observing changes in behavior over time.
      c) By improvements in performance during sessions and consistency over retention intervals.
      Correct Answer: c) By improvements in performance during sessions and consistency over retention intervals.
      - The correct answer is c) By improvements in performance during sessions and consistency over retention intervals. In rehabilitation, learning is often assessed by observing improvements in performance during sessions and the consistency of performance over retention intervals.

   4. What does a retention interval refer to in the context of learning and memory?
      a) The duration of a therapy session.
      b) The time period between practice sessions.
      c) The time interval between the end of a practice session and the subsequent assessment.
      Correct Answer: c) The time interval between the end of a practice session and the subsequent assessment.
      - The correct answer is c) The time interval between the end of a practice session and the subsequent assessment. A retention interval is the period during which no practice occurs, allowing for the assessment of memory retention.

   5. What indicates that motor learning has occurred and memory for a skill has been encoded, stored, and recalled?
      a) Consistency of performance during therapy sessions.
      b) Improvement in performance during a single session.
      c) Maintenance of performance levels over a retention interval.
      Correct Answer: c) Maintenance of performance levels over a retention interval.
      - The correct answer is c) Maintenance of performance levels over a retention interval. When performance levels for a motor skill remain consistent over a retention interval, it indicates that motor learning has occurred and memory for the skill has been encoded, stored, and recalled.

   6. How is memory retention typically assessed in a rehabilitation setting?
      a) By observing improvements in performance during sessions.
      b) By evaluating the client's learning rate.
      c) By comparing performance levels across retention intervals.
      Correct Answer: c) By comparing performance levels across retention intervals.
      - The correct answer is c) By comparing performance levels across retention intervals. Memory retention in rehabilitation is often assessed by comparing the client's performance levels across different retention intervals to determine the extent of learning and memory consolidation.

   7. What is a longer retention interval in the context of memory assessment?
      a) The time period between consecutive therapy sessions.
      b) The duration of a single therapy session.
      c) The time interval between the end of a session and the client's return for further therapy.
      Correct Answer: c) The time interval between the end of a session and the client's return for further therapy.
      - The correct answer is c) The time interval between the end of a session and the client's return for further therapy. A longer retention interval refers to the time interval between the end of a session and the client's subsequent return for further therapy, allowing for a more extended period to assess memory retention and learning consolidation.

.Memory
   1. What are the two dimensions along which memory can be classified?
      a) Short-term and long-term memory, and declarative and procedural memory.
      b) Time course of storage and nature of information stored.
      c) Associative and dissociative memory, and implicit and explicit memory.
      Correct Answer: b) Time course of storage and nature of information stored.
      - The correct answer is b) Time course of storage and nature of information stored. Memory can be classified based on the time course of storage (short-term vs. long-term memory) and the nature of the information stored (declarative vs. procedural memory).

   2. Which type of memory is associated with memory for facts and events?
      a) Short-term memory.
      b) Long-term memory.
      c) Declarative memory.
      Correct Answer: c) Declarative memory.
      - The correct answer is c) Declarative memory. Declarative memory involves memory for facts and events, such as remembering historical dates or recalling specific experiences.

   3. What is procedural memory primarily associated with?
      a) Remembering historical events.
      b) Knowing how to perform tasks or skills.
      c) Recalling specific facts.
      Correct Answer: b) Knowing how to perform tasks or skills.
      - The correct answer is b) Knowing how to perform tasks or skills. Procedural memory involves memory for knowing how to do things, such as riding a bicycle or tying shoelaces.

   4. Which type of memory is particularly important for supporting motor behavior?
      a) Short-term memory.
      b) Long-term memory.
      c) Procedural memory.
      Correct Answer: c) Procedural memory.
      - The correct answer is c) Procedural memory. Procedural memory plays a crucial role in supporting motor behavior by encoding and recalling skills and actions, making it especially relevant for physical therapists.

   5. What distinguishes declarative memory from procedural memory?
      a) Declarative memory is short-term, while procedural memory is long-term.
      b) Declarative memory involves memory for facts and events, while procedural memory involves memory for knowing how to perform tasks or skills.
      c) Declarative memory is conscious, while procedural memory is unconscious.
      Correct Answer: b) Declarative memory involves memory for facts and events, while procedural memory involves memory for knowing how to perform tasks or skills.
      - The correct answer is b) Declarative memory involves memory for facts and events, while procedural memory involves memory for knowing how to perform tasks or skills. This distinction highlights the different types of information stored in each memory system: facts and events for declarative memory, and skills and procedures for procedural memory.

.Memory systems
   1. What does short-term memory primarily involve?
      a) Storing and recalling information over a long period.
      b) Temporary maintenance of information.
      c) Recalling events and experiences.
      Correct Answer: b) Temporary maintenance of information.
      - Short-term memory involves the temporary maintenance of information for a short period, such as remembering a phone number before dialing it.

   2. Which type of memory is episodic memory?
      a) Memory for facts and knowledge.
      b) Memory for events and experiences.
      c) Memory for task performance.
      Correct Answer: b) Memory for events and experiences.
      - Episodic memory involves remembering specific events and experiences, such as recalling a birthday party or a vacation.

   3. What is the primary function of working memory?
      a) Storing information over a long period.
      b) Active maintenance and manipulation of information.
      c) Recalling facts and knowledge.
      Correct Answer: b) Active maintenance and manipulation of information.
      - The primary function of working memory is to actively maintain and manipulate a limited amount of information before recall, aiding decision-making and behavior.

   4. Which memory type is relatively unchanged by aging?
      a) Short-term memory.
      b) Episodic memory.
      c) Procedural memory.
      Correct Answer: c) Procedural memory.
      - Procedural memory, which involves memory for well-learned motor acts, is generally considered unchanged by aging, unlike short-term and episodic memory.

   5. What does semantic memory primarily involve?
      a) Recalling events and experiences.
      b) Temporary maintenance of information.
      c) Memory for facts and knowledge.
      Correct Answer: c) Memory for facts and knowledge.
      - Semantic memory involves memory for facts and knowledge, such as recalling historical dates or understanding language meanings.

   6. Which memory type is assessed through delayed recall in the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA)?
      a) Short-term memory.
      b) Episodic memory.
      c) Procedural memory.
      Correct Answer: a) Short-term memory.
      - Short-term memory, specifically working memory, is assessed through delayed recall in the MoCA, where individuals are asked to recall items after a few minutes.

   7. What type of memory is crucial for recalling how to ride a bicycle or tie shoelaces?
      a) Episodic memory.
      b) Semantic memory.
      c) Procedural memory.
      Correct Answer: c) Procedural memory.
      - Procedural memory is crucial for recalling how to perform tasks or skills, such as riding a bicycle or tying shoelaces, as it involves memory for motor actions and procedures.

.Human memory
   1. What characterizes sensory memory?
      a) Retains information for a lifetime.
      b) Holds raw sensory data briefly after stimuli has ceased.
      c) Stores facts and events.
      Correct Answer: b) Holds raw sensory data briefly after stimuli has ceased.
      - Sensory memory briefly retains raw sensory data from the five senses for a very short duration, typically lasting only a fraction of a second after the stimulus has ended.

   2. What distinguishes short-term memory from long-term memory?
      a) Short-term memory holds information for a lifetime, while long-term memory retains it for a minute.
      b) Short-term memory involves unconscious recall, while long-term memory is conscious.
      c) Short-term memory stores information for a minute, while long-term memory retains it for a lifetime.
      Correct Answer: c) Short-term memory stores information for a minute, while long-term memory retains it for a lifetime.
      - Short-term memory holds information for a short period, typically around a minute, while long-term memory stores information over a lifetime.

   3. What type of memory is procedural memory?
      a) Implicit memory.
      b) Explicit memory.
      c) Sensory memory.
      Correct Answer: a) Implicit memory.
      - Procedural memory is an example of implicit memory, which is unconscious and automatic, involving memory for skills and tasks.

   4. How is explicit memory characterized?
      a) Stores sensory information briefly.
      b) Involves unconscious recall of information.
      c) Allows conscious recall of facts and events.
      Correct Answer: c) Allows conscious recall of facts and events.
      - Explicit memory, also known as declarative memory, allows for conscious recall and expression of facts and events, distinguishing it from implicit memory.

   5. Which type of memory includes memory for events and experiences?
      a) Sensory memory.
      b) Episodic memory.
      c) Procedural memory.
      Correct Answer: b) Episodic memory.
      - Episodic memory is a subtype of declarative memory and involves memory for specific events and experiences.

   6. What is the duration of sensory memory?
      a) Lasts for a lifetime.
      b) Retains information for about a minute.
      c) Holds raw sensory data briefly after stimuli has ceased.
      Correct Answer: c) Holds raw sensory data briefly after stimuli has ceased.
      - Sensory memory holds raw sensory data for a very short duration, typically lasting only for a fraction of a second after the stimulus has ended.

   7. Which type of memory is assessed through unconscious recall?
      a) Short-term memory.
      b) Explicit memory.
      c) Implicit memory.
      Correct Answer: c) Implicit memory.
      - Implicit memory involves unconscious recall and automatic processing, such as remembering how to ride a bicycle without conscious effort.

.Human long-term memory
   1. What characterizes explicit long-term memory?
      a) Unconscious recall of skills and habits.
      b) Memory for general knowledge and events.
      c) Enhanced response to repeated exposure to a stimulus.
      Correct Answer: b) Memory for general knowledge and events.
      - Explicit long-term memory, also known as declarative memory, involves conscious recall of facts (semantic memory) and events (episodic memory).

   2. What type of memory refers to a decrease in responsiveness to a repeated stimulus?
      a) Sensitization.
      b) Procedural memory.
      c) Habituation.
      Correct Answer: c) Habituation.
      - Habituation is a form of non-associative learning where there is a decrease in responsiveness to a stimulus after repeated exposure to it.

   3. What is an example of habituation in everyday life?
      a) Learning to play the piano.
      b) Becoming more responsive to a loud noise after experiencing a painful stimulus.
      c) Ignoring common background noises like traffic sounds.
      Correct Answer: c) Ignoring common background noises like traffic sounds.
      - Habituation occurs when we become accustomed to repeated, non-meaningful stimuli, such as background noises, leading to a decreased response.

   4. Which brain structure is implicated in sensitization related to chronic pain?
      a) Amygdala.
      b) Striatum.
      c) Dorsal horn of the spinal cord.
      Correct Answer: c) Dorsal horn of the spinal cord.
      - Sensitization related to chronic pain involves the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, where nociceptive neurons become sensitized by peripheral tissue damage or inflammation.

   5. What form of memory is unconscious and involves memory for skills and habits?
      a) Episodic memory.
      b) Procedural memory.
      c) Semantic memory.
      Correct Answer: b) Procedural memory.
      - Procedural memory is a type of implicit long-term memory that involves unconscious recall of skills and habits.

   6. In what type of learning does an individual become more responsive to various stimuli after experiencing an intense or noxious stimulus?
      a) Habituation.
      b) Sensitization.
      c) Semantic learning.
      Correct Answer: b) Sensitization.
      - Sensitization involves an enhanced response to various stimuli after exposure to an intense or noxious stimulus.

   7. Which memory type is conscious and involves memory for facts and general knowledge?
      a) Procedural memory.
      b) Implicit memory.
      c) Semantic memory.
      Correct Answer: c) Semantic memory.
      - Semantic memory, a form of explicit memory, involves conscious recall of facts and general knowledge about the world.

   8. What is the primary function of habituation in learning?
      a) Enhancing memory recall.
      b) Decreasing responsiveness to non-meaningful stimuli.
      c) Increasing sensitivity to repeated stimuli.
      Correct Answer: b) Decreasing responsiveness to non-meaningful stimuli.
      - Habituation reduces the response to repetitive, non-threatening stimuli, allowing individuals to focus on more relevant stimuli.

.Short term/working memory: a multicomponent system used to manipulate information
   1. What is the primary function of working memory?
      a) Storing long-term memories.
      b) Maintaining current, goal-relevant knowledge.
      c) Retrieving stored information from the past.
      Correct Answer: b) Maintaining current, goal-relevant knowledge.
      - Working memory allows individuals to hold and manipulate information in mind for immediate use, facilitating ongoing cognitive tasks.

   2. Which brain region is heavily involved in short-term working memory?
      a) Temporal lobe.
      b) Prefrontal cortex.
      c) Occipital lobe.
      Correct Answer: b) Prefrontal cortex.
      - The prefrontal cortex, along with its connections to the parietal and visual association cortices, plays a crucial role in short-term working memory.

   3. What term describes the subsystem of working memory responsible for retaining speech-based information?
      a) Phonological loop.
      b) Visuospatial Sketchpad.
      c) Semantic memory.
      Correct Answer: a) Phonological loop.
      - The phonological loop is the subsystem responsible for storing and rehearsing speech-based information, such as phone numbers or verbal instructions.

   4. Which subsystem of working memory retains mental images of visual objects and spatial locations?
      a) Phonological loop.
      b) Articulatory processes.
      c) Visuospatial Sketchpad.
      Correct Answer: c) Visuospatial Sketchpad.
      - The visuospatial Sketchpad is responsible for holding and manipulating visual and spatial information, such as mental images of objects and their spatial locations.

   5. How does working memory differ from long-term memory?
      a) Working memory retains transient information for immediate use, while long-term memory stores information over a lifetime.
      b) Long-term memory is involved in maintaining current, goal-relevant knowledge.
      c) Working memory is responsible for retrieving stored information from the past.
      Correct Answer: a) Working memory retains transient information for immediate use, while long-term memory stores information over a lifetime.
      - Working memory holds information temporarily for immediate use, while long-term memory stores information for longer periods, potentially over a lifetime.

   6. What is the role of the executive control processes in working memory?
      a) Maintaining verbal information.
      b) Directing attention to different subsystems of working memory.
      c) Retrieving stored memories.
      Correct Answer: b) Directing attention to different subsystems of working memory.
      - The executive control processes allocate attention to either the verbal or visuospatial subsystem of working memory based on task demands.

   7. Which subsystem of working memory is particularly important for guiding reaching movements?
      a) Phonological loop.
      b) Visuospatial Sketchpad.
      c) Semantic memory.
      Correct Answer: b) Visuospatial Sketchpad.
      - The visuospatial Sketchpad is crucial for retaining mental images of objects and their spatial locations, which is essential for guiding movements in space.

   8. How does the phonological loop contribute to working memory?
      a) By maintaining mental images of visual objects.
      b) By storing and rehearsing speech-based information.
      c) By directing attention to different subsystems of working memory.
      Correct Answer: b) By storing and rehearsing speech-based information.
      - The phonological loop is responsible for storing and rehearsing speech-based information, aiding in tasks such as recalling phone numbers or verbal instructions.

.Prefrontal cortex in working memory
   1. In a delayed-match-to-sample (DMS) task, what is the primary role of the prefrontal cortex?
      a) Identifying the reward stimuli.
      b) Maintaining information in working memory.
      c) Initiating the response lever.
      Correct Answer: b) Maintaining information in working memory.
      - In the DMS task, the prefrontal cortex is crucial for holding the original stimulus (sample) in working memory until the appearance of the matching stimulus (match).

   2. What is the purpose of the delayed period in the DMS task?
      a) To distract the monkey from the task.
      b) To allow time for the monkey to prepare its response.
      c) To test the monkey's ability to maintain information in working memory.
      Correct Answer: c) To test the monkey's ability to maintain information in working memory.
      - The delayed period between the presentation of the sample and match stimuli assesses the monkey's ability to retain the sample in working memory until the match appears.

   3. Which part of the brain is critical for keeping the original object shape and location in mind during the DMS task?
      a) Parietal lobe.
      b) Prefrontal cortex.
      c) Occipital lobe.
      Correct Answer: b) Prefrontal cortex.
      - The prefrontal cortex plays a crucial role in maintaining the sample stimulus in working memory during the delayed period of the DMS task.

   4. What happens when the match stimulus does not correspond to the original object shape and location?
      a) The monkey receives a reward.
      b) The monkey releases the response lever.
      c) The monkey does not receive a reward.
      Correct Answer: c) The monkey does not receive a reward.
      - The monkey only receives a reward when the match stimulus matches both the original object shape and location, indicating successful retention of information in working memory.

   5. How do neurons in the prefrontal cortex respond during the delay period for non-preferred objects in the DMS task?
      a) They show robust activity.
      b) They exhibit minimal activity.
      c) Their activity remains unchanged.
      Correct Answer: b) They exhibit minimal activity.
      - Neurons in the prefrontal cortex show reduced activity during the delay period for non-preferred objects, suggesting a decrease in the maintenance of non-relevant information.

   6. What do the recording sites in the prefrontal cortex of the monkey indicate during the DMS task?
      a) Neurons coding for reward stimuli.
      b) Neurons coding for motor responses.
      c) Neurons maintaining information about object and location.
      Correct Answer: c) Neurons maintaining information about object and location.
      - Recording sites in the prefrontal cortex reveal neurons that code for both object and location, highlighting their role in maintaining relevant information during the task.

   7. How does the DMS task help assess the function of the prefrontal cortex?
      a) By measuring visual acuity.
      b) By testing memory retention under cognitive load.
      c) By evaluating motor coordination.
      Correct Answer: b) By testing memory retention under cognitive load.
      - The DMS task evaluates the prefrontal cortex's ability to maintain information in working memory, providing insights into its cognitive function.

   8. Which component of working memory is primarily assessed in the DMS task?
      a) Retrieval.
      b) Maintenance.
      c) Encoding.
      Correct Answer: b) Maintenance.
      - The DMS task primarily assesses the maintenance component of working memory, as the monkey must retain the sample stimulus until the appearance of the match stimulus.

.Tasks that use working memory
   1. Which cognitive test involves recalling and repeating a sequence of numbers in the same order they were presented?
      a) Digit symbol test.
      b) Flanker task.
      c) Digit span task.
      Correct Answer: c) Digit span task.
      - The digit span task requires participants to recall and repeat a sequence of numbers in the same order they were presented, testing their working memory capacity.

   2. In the digit symbol test, participants are required to match symbols with:
      a) Letters.
      b) Colors.
      c) Numbers.
      Correct Answer: c) Numbers.
      - In the digit symbol test, participants match symbols with numbers based on a provided key, testing their ability to associate symbols with numerical values.

   3. Which cognitive task assesses the ability to respond based on the direction of a central arrow despite conflicting surrounding arrows?
      a) Digit span task.
      b) Flanker task.
      c) Stroop Color-Word test.
      Correct Answer: b) Flanker task.
      - The Flanker task requires participants to respond based on the direction of a central arrow while ignoring surrounding arrows, assessing their ability to maintain focus and inhibit distraction.

   4. What is the goal of the trail making test, specifically Trail B?
      a) Connecting numbers and letters in ascending order.
      b) Recalling a sequence of numbers.
      c) Matching symbols with numbers.
      Correct Answer: a) Connecting numbers and letters in ascending order.
      - In Trail B of the trail making test, participants are tasked with connecting numbers and letters in ascending order while alternating between them, testing their ability to maintain a sequence and update their location within it.

   5. What does the Stroop Color-Word test primarily assess?
      a) Color perception.
      b) Language comprehension.
      c) Inhibition and cognitive flexibility.
      Correct Answer: c) Inhibition and cognitive flexibility.
      - The Stroop Color-Word test primarily assesses the participant's ability to inhibit automatic responses and demonstrate cognitive flexibility by naming the color of the ink while ignoring the printed word.

   6. Why does the digit symbol test require working memory?
      a) To match symbols with colors.
      b) To recall and match symbols with numbers based on a key.
      c) To respond based on the direction of a central arrow.
      Correct Answer: b) To recall and match symbols with numbers based on a key.
      - The digit symbol test requires participants to remember the symbol-number associations provided in the key and match symbols with their corresponding numbers, necessitating the use of working memory for accurate performance.

.LTM: explicit processing, four distinct operations
   1. Which process involves attending to new information and linking it with existing memories?
      a) Storage.
      b) Encoding.
      c) Consolidation.
      Correct Answer: b) Encoding.
      - Encoding is the process of attending to new information and connecting it with existing memories, facilitating its entry into long-term memory.

   2. What process makes temporarily stored information more stable through mechanisms like long-term potentiation?
      a) Retrieval.
      b) Storage.
      c) Consolidation.
      Correct Answer: c) Consolidation.
      - Consolidation involves stabilizing temporarily stored information, often through mechanisms like long-term potentiation, to facilitate its transition into long-term memory.

   3. Which process involves retaining memory over time through neural mechanisms?
      a) Encoding.
      b) Storage.
      c) Retrieval.
      Correct Answer: b) Storage.
      - Storage refers to the mechanisms by which memories are retained over time, ensuring their availability for retrieval when needed.

   4. What is the term for recalling stored information when needed?
      a) Encoding.
      b) Retrieval.
      c) Consolidation.
      Correct Answer: b) Retrieval.
      - Retrieval is the process of recalling stored information from memory when it is needed for use, allowing individuals to access previously encoded and stored memories.

   5. Which process involves inducing changes in neurons to create stable synapses over time?
      a) Storage.
      b) Retrieval.
      c) Consolidation.
      Correct Answer: c) Consolidation.
      - Consolidation includes processes like long-term potentiation, which induce changes in neurons over time, leading to the creation of stable synapses and facilitating long-term memory formation.

   6. Despite advances in memory research, which aspect of these neural processes remains less understood?
      a) Encoding.
      b) Retrieval.
      c) Specific mechanisms.
      Correct Answer: c) Specific mechanisms.
      - While significant progress has been made in memory research, the detailed mechanisms underlying encoding, consolidation, storage, and retrieval processes remain less understood in neuroscience.

.Explicit memory: Anatomical correlates
   1. What neural structures are crucial for explicit episodic memory?
      a) Prefrontal cortex.
      b) Hippocampus and medial temporal lobe system.
      c) Cerebellum.
      Correct Answer: b) Hippocampus and medial temporal lobe system.
      - The hippocampus, along with the medial temporal lobe system including structures like the intrarenal cortex, perirhinal cortex, and parahippocampal cortex, are essential for encoding, consolidation, storage, and recall of explicit episodic long-term memory.

   2. Which area of the brain is primarily associated with encoding, consolidation, storage, and recall of explicit episodic memory?
      a) Prefrontal cortex.
      b) Cerebellum.
      c) Hippocampus.
      Correct Answer: c) Hippocampus.
      - The hippocampus plays a central role in explicit episodic memory, facilitating various processes such as encoding, consolidation, storage, and recall.

   3. What is the function of the perirhinal cortex and parahippocampal cortex in explicit episodic memory?
      a) Visual processing.
      b) Auditory processing.
      c) Encoding, consolidation, storage, and recall.
      Correct Answer: c) Encoding, consolidation, storage, and recall.
      - The perirhinal cortex and parahippocampal cortex, along with the hippocampus, contribute to encoding, consolidation, storage, and recall of explicit episodic long-term memory.

   4. Which lobe of the brain houses the key structures for explicit episodic memory?
      a) Parietal lobe.

   5. What distinguishes explicit episodic memory from other types of memory?
      a) Involvement of the prefrontal cortex.

      - Explicit episodic memory is characterized by its dependence on structures like the hippocampus and the broader medial temporal lobe system for encoding, consolidation, storage, and recall of episodic memories.

.Objectives for Part 2
   • Describe the integrative functions of the brain not localized to 
   specific structures alone: cognition, language, judgment, memory 
   and learning. Unit 5, Outcome 1.
   • Specific Objectives for Lesson 10b, part 2:

.Review: processing for explicit LTM - four distinct operations
   • Encoding = new information is attended to and linked with 
   existing information in memory
   • Consolidation = makes temporarily stored information 
   more stable, processes of LTP
   • Storage = neural mechanisms by which memory is 
   retained over time
   • Retrieval = when stored information is recalled

   This is review.  Recall that there are four distinct operations or stages of explicit long-term memory. The first stage is encoding,  where new information is attended to and linked with existing information in memory. The second stage is consolidation,  where temporarily stored information is made more stable through processes of LTP. The third operation is storage,  where memory is retained over time. The fourth operation is retrieval when stored information is recalled and used.

.Semantic memory: Does it use the same processes and cortical areas as episodic memory?
   • Semantic memory, like episodic memory, is a highly flexible, multimodal system
   • Semantic knowledge:
   oNot a static repository of information
   oIt grows and changes as we continuously acquire, integrate, and reinforce rich 
   representations of the relations between words, their referents, and their relations with 
   associated referents (Zettersten etal, 2018)
   oSemantic richness:
   ▪ Refers to the amount of information contained within or associated with a word or concept and it influences 
   the speed and accuracy of behavioral responses.
   ▪ Words and concepts that are richer, or associated with more information, are better remembered.
   • Like episodic memory, the hippocampus is critical to encoding and consolidation of semantic 
   memories
   oFollowing hippocampal damage, patients fail to show normal acquisition of new semantic 
   information

   Let's take a closer look at semantic memory.  Recall that semantic memory is explicit,  declarative, long-term memory for facts or general knowledge.  If you recall that semantic memory is a category of explicit declarative memory, then your own semantic memory is at work.  Semantic memory like episodic memory is a highly flexible multi—modal system. Semantic knowledge is notjust a static repository of information.  It isn't like a dictionary or somehow we look things up,  recall individual facts that are each stored separately.  Semantic memory grows and changes as we continuously acquire, integrate, and reinforce rich representations of the relations between words,  their referents, and their relations with associated referents.  Here, referent means the person, thing,  or idea, that a word or expression or symbol stands for.  For example, in the sentence,  the front door is open. We know the word door refers to a concrete object.  An object that has certain general properties.  It has four sides and it's something we can open or close.  Another example of a referent is when we  see a sign of a cigarette with a red X through it.  We have learned that this symbol means or stands for no smoking. — All this is part of semantic memory.  Semantic richness refers to the amount of information contained within or associated with a word or concept and it  influences the speed and accuracy of behavioral responses.  If we go back to the word door,  even though it seems simple, it has meaning. We can associate it with many things.  We know there are all kinds of doors,  wooden doors, metal doors, barn doors,  church doors, some are heavy and hard to open,  some you slide open.  We also know that the phrase,  the door is wide open,  often is a metaphor,  meaning an opportunity is available.  Words and concepts that are richer or  associated with more information are better remembered. Like episodic memory, the hippocampus is  critical to encoding and consolidation of semantic memories. Following hippocampal damage, patients fail to  show normal acquisition of new semantic information. That is, they don't have normal acquisition  for learning new words or gaining new knowledge.

.Understanding memory
   • H.M: '‘the best known single patient in the history of neuroscience’: bicycle accident age 7 
   years, developed epilepsy, age 27 unable to work, surgery removed the hippocampus, 
   amygdala, parts of temporal cortex (passed away in 2008, Henry Molaison)
   • COULD DO: Normal working memory (seconds/minutes), also had LTM for events prior to the 
   surgery (name, job, childhood ok, years immediately prior to sx not as robust), IQ unchanged, 
   vocabulary and ability to speak fine
   • COULD NOT DO: Transfer new information from STM into LTM, make new memories 
   (couldn’t recall people he met after surgery even after many encounters, couldn’t remember 
   new telephone numbers (even though he could repeat it back initially))…BUT..
   • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2649674/

   Much of what researchers know and understand about  memory comes from one single case study.  In 1955, scientists began setting  HM and used his initials in publications to protect his privacy.  We now know that H.M was Henry Molaison,  who passed away in 2008 at the age of 82.  H.M is referred to as the best-known single patient in the history of neuroscience. For roughly 10 years,  the 27—year—old H.M had suffered severe seizures.  They were so debilitating,  he can no longer hold down hisjob on an assembly line.  H.M underwent at the time  an experimental procedure to remove brain tissue to stop the seizures.  His surgeons removed a thumb-sized section of tissue from each side of his brain. The surgery worked.  The seizures abated but afterwards,  H.M was left with permanent and significant memory impairments. Here's what H.M could do.  He could hold things in working memory.  He also had long-term memory for his childhood,  his parents, and historical events that occurred before his surgery.  His IQ was unchanged and he could speak fine.  What could he not do? — He was unable to form new memories.  If he met someone who then left the room within minutes,  he had no recollection of that person or their meeting.  He also could not learn new vocabulary words or  new telephone numbers but there are  some interesting things that he could still do and we will get to that in a few minutes. This is a really interesting link if you want  to learn and understand more about the life of Henry Molaison.

.What HM lost
   The top figure on the left is to remind you of  the key components of the medial temporal lobe important for explicit memory. Here you see a sagittal view and a coronal view of  the entorhinal and perirhinal cortices and  the parahippocampal cortex and the parahippocampal cortex includes the hippocampus. In 8 over here there's a vertical series of sections,  these show you what HM lost,  what was removed during the surgery.  The surgery was bilateral but the figure shows you the lesion just on one side.  The lesion or what they removed is pictured in  black and the structures that were lost on the other side.  They removed most of the amygdala and the entorhinal cortex, as you can see here. The lesion was here that  involved removing the amygdala and most of the entorhinal cortex.  It also involves removing about half of the hippocampus. Portions of the ventral perirhinal cortex were  spared and portions of the parahippocampal cortex were also spared.  Recall that the entorhinal cortex is  the main input and output pathway for the hippocampus.  Even though part of the hippocampus remained from the surgery,  it effectively was denervated as it lost its input and output pathways.  C shows you an MRI scan of  a parasagittal section from the left side of  HMS brain and this was done later in his life.  The asterisk, which you can see right here in  the central area of the scan indicates the resected portion of the medial temporal lobe. The nearby arrowhead which is right here,  points to the remaining portion of the hippocampal formation.

.What HM was still able to do
   Here's the really interesting thing about what HM was able to do.  HM was taught to trace between two outlines of a star while viewing his hand in a mirror. This task is called mirror tracing.  Mirror learning reflects the formation of new associations between vision and arm movement.  The graph plots the number of times  during each attempt that he strayed outside the lines as he drew the star. They did this mirror tracing task with him over three days.  Here's his practice on day 1,  day 2 and day 3. — On the y-axis is the number of errors in  each attempt and you can see that over the three days,  he made less and less error,  to finally, he made very little error.  As with healthy subjects,  HM improved considerably with repeated attempts but interestingly, he had no recollection of performing the task,  he cannot verbalize the task or what he had learned.  Each day when the person came in to do the task with him,  it was like he had never seen this before,  he had no knowledge,  no recollection of doing it.  But when he actually went to do it,  his performance did improve over days.  HM could still learn skilled movement,  indicating his procedural implicit memory was still intact.  This led to the idea that the hippocampus and  medial temporal lobe system was not involved in procedural memory.  Recent evidence suggests that it's not quite that simple,  the hippocampus does seem to be involved in certain types of implicit learning. But we also know that other areas are much more engaged in implicit learning, the basal ganglia and cerebellum are highly involved in procedural learning and memory. Those structures, the basal ganglia, cerebellum and frontal areas were still intact,  they were still intact in HM.

.Neural substrates of procedural memory
   • BG
   • SMA
   • Cbm
   • Amygdala

   We will be talking more about this in  Module 11 when we talk about motor learning but again,  the neural substrates of procedural memory are not exactly the same as explicit memory. Procedural motor learning and procedural memory rely heavily on the basal ganglia, the SMA, the supplementary motor area and the cerebellum.

.Active Recall!
   • Name two things that H.M could do after his surgery.
      After his surgery, H.M. could still learn new motor skills through a process called procedural memory. This means he could improve at tasks like drawing a figure or tracing a maze, even though he couldn't remember ever doing them before. Additionally, he retained his ability to form implicit memories, such as classical conditioning, where he could associate certain stimuli with responses without consciously remembering the learning experience.
   • Name one thing that H.M could not do after his surgery.
      After his surgery, H.M. was unable to form new episodic memories or recall events and experiences that occurred after the surgery. This condition is known as anterograde amnesia.

.Summary/Key points
   • The hippocampus is critical to both semantic and episodic memory, 
   and like episodic memory, long term semantic memory is 
   distributed throughout association cortices.
   • The case study with H.M was invaluable to the understanding that 
   declarative memory and procedural memory use different neural 
   substrates.
   • The neural correlates of procedural memory are dependent on the 
   phase of learning, but heavily involve the basal ganglia and 
   cerebellum.

.Review: processing for explicit LTM - four distinct operations
   1. What is the primary function of encoding in explicit long-term memory?
      a) Making stored information more stable.

   2. Which process involves making temporarily stored information more stable?
      a) Encoding.
      b) Consolidation.
      c) Storage.
      Correct Answer: b) Consolidation.
      - Consolidation refers to the process of strengthening and stabilizing temporarily stored information, typically through mechanisms such as long-term potentiation (LTP), which enhances synaptic connectivity and durability.

   3. What is the role of storage in explicit long-term memory?
      a) Linking new information with existing memory.
      b) Retaining memory over time.
      c) Recalling stored information.
      Correct Answer: b) Retaining memory over time.
      - Storage involves the neural mechanisms responsible for retaining memory traces over extended periods, ensuring that information remains accessible for retrieval when needed.

   4. When does retrieval occur in the process of explicit long-term memory?
      a) During encoding.
      b) During consolidation.
      c) When stored information is recalled.
      Correct Answer: c) When stored information is recalled.

   5. What neural mechanism is associated with making temporarily stored information more stable?
      a) Long-term potentiation (LTP).
      b) Synaptic pruning.
      c) Short-term memory activation.
      Correct Answer: a) Long-term potentiation (LTP).
      - Long-term potentiation (LTP) is a process commonly associated with consolidation, involving the strengthening of synaptic connections, which enhances the stability and durability of memory traces.

   6. Which operation in explicit long-term memory involves attending to and linking new information with existing memory?
      a) Encoding.
      b) Consolidation.
      c) Storage.
      Correct Answer: a) Encoding.
      - Encoding is the initial stage of explicit long-term memory processing, where attention is directed towards incoming information, and connections are established with pre-existing memory representations, facilitating the integration of new knowledge.

.Semantic memory: Does it use the same processes and cortical areas as episodic memory?

   6. What happens to semantic memory following hippocampal damage?

   This should look familiar.  Again, two forms of long-term memory,  explicit declarative, which can be further divided into semantic and episodic memory. Episodic memory for events,  semantic memory for facts and knowledge.  Then we have the implicit non—declarative, also unconscious, memory. One type is procedural,  one type is non-associative habituation and sensitization,  which we already talked about.  Then there's two more, associative learning and then priming.  This lesson is focused on implicit memory,  which unlike explicit memory,  cannot be reported verbally.  An implicit memory,  the memory is expressed as a behavior without conscious awareness.

.Implicit Memory
   • Procedural: learning of skills/habits
   • Non-associative: single event learning
   • habituation - repeated stimuli; usually weak stimulus; ignore
   • Sensitization – exposed to strong stimulus; defensive reflex; avoid
   • Associative: paired stimuli learning
   • Classical conditioning: Stimulus/Response; cause and effect presumed 
   between events
   • Operant conditioning: a form of learning in which new behaviors develop in 
   terms of their consequences
   • Priming: an effect whereby exposure to certain stimuli influences 
   the response to subsequently presented stimuli

   Procedural learning refers to the classic View of motor learning.  In a sense here, you learn by doing.  The pattern and timing of muscles and movements in  a sequence are learned through repetition and practice and can be recalled and executed without conscious attention.  We already talked about non-associative learning,  again that's the habituation and sensitization.  Classical and operant conditioning are examples of associative implicit memory. The famous example of classical conditioning is Pavlov's dogs.  In that experiment, they rang a bell,  which was a neutral stimulus,  then fed the dog.  After repetitions of ringing and feeding,  the dog would salivate when they heard the bell in anticipation of the food. This is stimulus-response paired learning.  In contrast to classical conditioning,  operant conditioning involves encouraging or  discouraging a specific behavior using reinforcement.  While classical conditioning is training dogs to salivate to the sound of a bell, operant condition is training dogs to sit by giving them a treat when they do. An easy way to think about it is classical conditioning pairs a stimulus with a behavior.  Operant conditioning pairs a behavior with a reward or consequence.  Priming is a phenomenon whereby exposure to one stimulus influences  a response to a subsequent stimulus without conscious guidance or attention. For example, in word priming experiments,  the word "nurse" is recognized more quickly following — the word "doctor" than following the word "bread", for example.

.Implicit memory - anatomical correlates
   • Cortex
   • Striatum
   • Amygdala
   • Cerebellum
   • Sensory-motor reflex 
   pathways

   • Priming
   • Skills and habits
   • Associative: emotional 
   patterned responses
   • Associative: muscle patterned 
   responses
   • Non-associative

   As shown in the previous diagrams,  different regions of the CNS are linked more  highly to certain aspects of implicit memory.  Priming appears to involve the cerebral cortex.  Procedural learning involves the basal ganglia. Associative learning involves the amygdala and cerebellum,  the amygdala more with patterned emotionally-charged behavior,  the cerebellum with patterned muscle movement sequence performance. Non-associative learning is linked with sensory-motor pathways.

.Cellular mechanisms of memory
   1) Transient change but consistent
   2) Enduring plasticity (Hebb: relation of pre- and post-synaptic 
   elements, strengthens the connection)
   • Patterned activity at a synapse
   oTemporal and spatial summation
   • Changes in synaptic physiology
   oPresynaptic facilitation/axoaxonic synapses
   oConvergent inputs
   • Postsynaptic intracellular events
   oSecond messenger systems

   In prior modules, we have discussed some of what is  known about cellular mechanisms of memory.  There can be transient changes at a synapse due to changes in  extracellular ion concentrations or other synaptic inputs.  Some of these transient changes, when consistent,  can lead to more lasting structure and functional changes in the synapse.  For example, Hebb hypothesized that neurons that are paired at a synapse,  that frequently communicate with each other create a more stable, stronger synapse. They are undergoing plasticity.  This plasticity can be facilitated by several mechanisms that you are familiar with. First, temporal or spatial summation  makes it more likely the postsynaptic neuron will fire.  Presynaptic facilitation by axoaxonic synapses with the presynaptic neuron result in  more neurotransmitter released from the presynaptic neuron,  again, making it more likely the postsynaptic neuron will be brought to threshold. Lastly, the second messenger systems in  postsynaptic cells related to metabotropic receptors,  like the NMDA receptor we talked about,  leads to functional and structural changes in the neuron.

.Cellular mechanisms of memory
   • Structural changes in the synapse
   oNew synapse, enlarged; specialization of receptors, dendrites, 
   endplates
   oInvolves protein synthesis, even gene activation
   • Long-term changes in synaptic strength
   oBiochemical
   oAnatomical

   Structural changes can include changes in the synaptic membrane,  including more receptors and specialization of  receptors, and the synapse itself will become larger.  These changes become long-lasting as  the second messenger biochemical cascade influences the nucleus in the cell, resulting in DNA and RNA changes and  new protein synthesis that alters the cells future responses for long periods of time. The current theory is that activity-dependent synaptic plasticity is induced at appropriate synapses during memory formation and is both  necessary and sufficient for the encoding and storage of memory.

.Memory deficits in patients that physical therapists commonly treat
   .Declarative memory failure: amnesia
      • Retrograde = loss of memories for events that occurred 
      before trauma or disease that caused the condition
      • Anterograde = loss of memory for events following the 
      trauma or disease
      • Traumatic brain injury (TBI): may have severe declarative 
      memory deficits, but often retain procedural memory
      oPTA = post traumatic amnesia = length of time between the head 
      injury and the time at which the patient is able to consistently 
      remember ongoing events
      oPTA severity of injury and can predict recovery

      Let's talk briefly about memory deficits in patients that PTs commonly treat. Memory can be altered by disease or injury.  Amnesia refers to problems with declarative memory.  Amnesia can be retrograde or anterograde,  referring to whether the loss of declarative memory is for history,  so events prior to the injury, — or for events following or since the injury or disease.  Traumatic brain injury can be associated with severe amnesia, and the severity of the post-traumatic amnesia is an indicator of the potential for recovery. However, procedural memory is often  intact or less influenced by brain in traumatic brain injury.  That's good news for therapists. Retraining of motor skill involves procedural memory.  So even if a patient doesn't remember you from day to day,  just like HM. and the mirror tracing task,  motor learning may still be available.

   .Dementia
      • AD – cortical atrophy/neuron loss
      • plaques and neurofibrillary tangles
      • Tau/amyloid deposits
      • Starts in entorhinal and hippocampus, spreads to other temporal 
      areas, then parietal then frontal
      • Early AD – Declarative memory loss is episodic, semantic,
      • frontal lobe = deficits in short term memory and attention, 
      executive function
      • Procedural memory initially spared.

      Alzheimer's disease type dementia is a degenerative brain disease. Essentially, neurons die.  The neuron loss is associated with abnormal tissue changes of  plaques and neurofibrillary tangles with  amyloid and tau deposits that disrupt neural function.  The largest loss of neurons and  degeneration is in the medial temporal lobe of the cortex.  But there's evidence of changes in other cortical regions of the brain as well, particularly as the disease progresses.  In the early stages of AD,  the prominent problems are in declarative memory,  particularly problems with short-term working memory and memory for recent events. Attention deficits are common, as well as executive functions, such as the ability to select responses,  cognitive flexibility, and verbal fluency.  People with Alzheimer's disease are able to implicitly learn or  re-learn motor skills to a certain extent and under specific conditions.  Patients are capable of acquiring motor skills without awareness by  repeated exposure or practice, although  their performances will generally not reach normal levels.  Additionally, the extent of learning will differ depending on the task to be learned. It is not correct for therapists to think that a person would not benefit  from physical therapy, based solely on the diagnosis of Alzheimer's dementia.

.Active Recall!
   • What is the difference between habituation and sensitization?
      Habituation and sensitization are two forms of non-associative learning, but they have opposite effects on behavioral responses to stimuli. 

      Habituation refers to a decrease in response to a repeated stimulus that is not biologically significant. In other words, with repeated exposure to the same stimulus, the response decreases over time. For example, if you live near a train track, you might habituate to the sound of passing trains and eventually not notice them as much.

      Sensitization, on the other hand, is an increase in response to a stimulus following either a single intense exposure or repeated exposure to the stimulus. This heightened response can persist for some time after the stimulus is removed. An example of sensitization might be becoming more sensitive to loud noises after being exposed to a sudden, loud sound.

      In summary, habituation decreases the response to a repeated stimulus, while sensitization increases the response to a stimulus.

Summary/Key points
   • Associative, non-associative and priming are types of implicit, 
   unconscious memory.
   • Patients with declarative memory loss often exhibit intact 
   procedural memory, indicating that motor learning can be achieved 
   through practice.
