            ● Part 2
            ○ Explain the importance of Pyramidal Tract Neurons to motor control.
            ■ Pyramidal tract neurons (PTNs)
            ● LCST
            ● PTNs = Upper Motor Neurons!
            ● Lesion PTNs: loss of the ability to fractionate movements, mainly
            hand dexterity
            ● Initially lose more movement, over time all but fractionation may or
            can recover; perhaps because:
            ○ 75-80% of PTN output of layer 5 is to subcortical and
            brainstem nuclei, not the spinal cord (RN, Reticular
            formation nuclei, and vestibnular nuclei)
            ○ 50% of PTNs project to cervical, 25% to lumbosacral,
            15-20% to thoracic
            ● Movements served by these PTNs usually involve a synergy, and
            blended muscle activity; smooth and graceful


            ■ Fractionation served by cortical PTN projections to MNs, but also INs
            and synergists to the action
            ● Pyramidal tract neurons (PTNs) layer 5 output:
            ○ PTNs for LCST arise from primary motor, premotor,
            supplemental motor, cingulate motor, and somatosensory 1
            & 2, posterior parietal
            ● Projections to spinal cord:
            ○ S1 and S2 to dorsal horn neurons
            ○ Motor areas of cortex (Areas 4, 6) to ventral horn MNs, INs
            and short propriospinal neurons from
            ● Note the convergent/divergent nature of PTN connections with
            motorneurons and support of reciprocal inhibition via Ia
            interneurons
            ○ Define the terms ‘corticomotoneuronal cell’ and ‘upper motor neuron’.
            ■ Corticomotoneuronal (CM) cells are PTNs that have direct cortex to
            motorneuron connections
            ● Chandelier & basket cells inhibit the PTNs at axoaxonic and
            axosomatic synapses [GABA]
            ■ For voluntary movement, the upper motor neuron enables the ability to
            activate a specific muscle or muscles in isolation
            ○ Describe the pathway of the corticospinal tract.
            ■ Originates: Primary motor cortex
            ■ Travels through: corona radiata, PLIC, midbrain, pons, superior medulla
            oblongata
            ■ Crosses: inferior medulla oblongata
            ■ 90% of fibers: go down contralateral spinal cord to the lateral motor
            neurons
            ○ Describe the signs of upper motor neuron lesions.
            ■ Weakness, resistance to passive movement and abnormal reflexes are
            ‘the’ signs of UMN lesions
            ● Corticospinal fibers lesioned = body weakness (e.g. hemiparesis);
            specific loss is fractionated movement (associated with
            corticomotoneuronal neurons)
            ● Corticobulbar fibers lesioned = facial, tongue, eye movement
            weakness for examples …
            ● Deficits opposite side of lesion, except if lesioned in the spinal
            cord
            ● Weakness; paralysis or paresis (consider pattern?)
            ● Hyperreflexia (increased DTRs) and spasticity, a velocity
            dependent increased resistance to passive movement
            ● Abnormal reflexes: Babinski reflex; Hoffman
            ■ Alone the signs may not be UMN; combination of weakness plus
            abnormal reflexes, plus resistance to passive movement is key to UMN
            pattern


            ■ Imbalance of descending input and spinal/peripheral input influences on
            segmental motor centers
            ○ Explain the mechanisms underlying resistance to passive movement and
            abnormal motor control in upper motor neuron lesions.
            ■ Current perspective to account for spasticity and abnormal movement
            control:
            ● Pontomedullary reticular formation (PMRF) is a collection of
            reticular formation nuclei in the pons and medulla. Cortical
            connections to the PMRF part of specific medial and lateral paths
            to spinal motor neurons.
            ● Dorsal cortico-reticulo-spinal tract (dorsal CRST): Contralateral
            primary motor cortex (M1) to pontomedullary reticular formation
            (PMRF) activates dorsolateral reticulospinal tract (RST), typically
            inhibitory input to spinal motor neurons; [travels near the
            corticospinal tract].
            ● Medial cortico-reticulo-spinal tract (medial CRST): Ipsilateral
            premotor (PM) and supplementary motor area (SMA) input to
            pontomedullary reticular formation activates medial reticulospinal
            tract, typically excitatory input to spinal motor neurons
            ● With damage to cortex activity in dorsal CRST reduced; activity in
            medial CRST not opposed, and progressively is upregulated
            leading to hyperexcitability of spinal motor neurons
            ● Part 3
            ○ Describe the role of brainstem locomotor regions in the control of walking
            ■ Brainstem locomotor regions influence pattern of stepping in walking by
            input to spinal central pattern generator
            ● Neurons in locomotor regions at level of subthalamic nucleus,
            midbrain, pons communicate to spinal CPGs by way of brainstem
            descending paths; generate stepping patterns relative to force [not
            timing]
            ● Cerebellar connections with the brainstem nuclei (reticular
            formation) adjusting pattern and rhythm
            ● Descending input to propriospinal paths may communicate across
            spinal segments
            ● Feedback from SMCs about ongoing motor activity via
            ventrospinocerebellar tract; and spinoreticular tract to brainstem
            locomotor centers
            ■ Supraspinal control: Visually guided locomotion involves the motor cortex
            ● "Skilled walking”
            ● Lesion studies: cats with lesions in motor cortex can walk on a
            smooth floor, but they cannot step over obstacles, or walk on the
            rungs of a horizontal ladder – missing visuomotor coordination
            ○ Explain the role of motor cortex and posterior parietal cortex in the control
            of walking


            ■ Supraspinal control: planning of locomotion involves the posterior parietal
            cortex
            ● Path planning, obstacle negotiation adjust our steps to the
            obstacle
            ● PPC: critical role in helping to plan adjustments, obstacle
            negotiation
            ○ Record PPC: neurons increase firing in advance of the
            obstacle, and neurons increase firing during crossing
            ○ Cats lesion studies: misplace their paws on the approach,
            andcontact obstacle more
            ○ Describe the role of the cerebellum in the control of walking
            ■ https://youtube.com/watch?v=NVsrexn3pT8&feature=shares
            ■ Cerebellar connections with the brainstem nuclei (reticular formation)
            adjusting pattern and rhythm in response to incoming sensory and their
            respective motor responses to command. Information is sent from
            purkinje cells through the cereblllar cortex and into the motor cortex to
            adjust ongoing locomotion.
            ○ Explain a 'reflex reversal' in the context of walking
            ■ Reflex reversal: “The phenomenon, observed in the study of locomotion,
            by which a given stimulus can produce two different reflex actions in a
            limb depending on the location of the limb.”
            ■ PPC is used in the planning of locomotion, where it is used regardless of
            which foot is currently stepping. One incidence of activity may cause an
            advancement of an R limb, whereas another may cause an advancement
            of a L limb based on limb position.
            Basal Ganglia

            Part 1
            1. Describe the major components of the basal ganglia – cortical loops and the
            general function of each loop
            a. Functional Roles
            i. Input
            1. Striatum: Caudate, Putamen & Ventral striatum
            ii. Modulator
            1. Substantia nigra compacta
            iii. Output
            1. Globus pallidus: Internal and external segments
            2. Substantia nigra reticulata
            iv. Facilitator
            1. Subthalamic nucleus
            b. All cortical loops start AND end in the cortex. Modulated by dopamine
            i. Motor (skeletal motor loop)
            1. Action selection, execution, sequence, reinforcement learning
            ii. Oculomotor


            1. Gaze (motor control for action)
            iii. Prefrontal (associative/executive)
            1. Dorsolateral prefrontal (organization of behavior for
            problem-solving)
            2. Lateral orbitofrontal (socially appropriate behavior)
            iv. Limbic
            1. Emotion/motivation

            2. Describe the similarities and differences between the basal ganglia and
            cerebellum and cortex roles in actions
            a. Basal ganglia always ends on cortex, meaning there is always conscious
            awareness to the reward based outcomes. Extends to more ways of learning
            than motor.
            b. Both help with learning in motor actions

            Part 2
            1. Describe the direct and indirect pathways in the basal ganglia and how they
            contribute to motor control
            a. Direct
            i. Positive feedback will reduce GPi output
            1. GPi - inhibitory to the thalamus
            ii. Activated thalamocortical neurons
            iii. D1 receptor of SNc activates
            b. Indirect
            i. GPe
            ii. Negative feedback
            iii. Inhibits thalamocortical neurons
            iv. D2 receptor of SNc activates
            c. Hyperdirect
            i. WHOA
            2. Describe the clinical implications of basal ganglia dysfunction
            a. Hypokinetic BG disorders present as a loss of drive
            i. Parkinson’s Disease - reduced facilitation of striatum
            ii. Neither the direct nor indirect pathways are facilitated.
            b. Hyperkinetic BC disorders lose reduction of drive
            i. Huntington’s Chorea - reduced inhibitory GPi output
            1. Indirect path is lost, GPe inhibits GPi which eliminates inhibition of
            thalamus. Movement is facilitated
            ii. Hemiballism - reduced output of GPi
            1. Lose STN drive of GPi
            2. Movement facilitated
            Part 3
            1. Describe the roles of the cerebellum and basal ganglia in learning.
            a. BG - movement execution - Reinforcement/reward based learning


            b. Cerebellum - movement initiation - Supervised error detection learning
            2. Describe the connections between the cerebellum and basal ganglia and the
            impact of these connections on movement disorders.
            a. Deep cerebellar nuclei input to the thalamus which goes to the striatum. This
            input can then affect GPe/i excitation. GPi over excitation would cause
            hypokinetic issues and GPi inhibition would cause hyperkinetic issues.
            3. Describe the similarities and differences between the basal ganglia and
            cerebellum and cortex roles in actions
            a. Cerebral - Unsupervised learning
            b. Cerebellar - Supervised. Error detection and correction
            c. BG - Reinforcement. Selects skills and uses rewards to reinforce.

            Limbic Influences on Movement Control
            Part 1
            1. Describe how the hypothalamus influences physiological and behavioral actions
            a. Energy homeostasis sensed by hypothalamic neurons’ sensitivity to peripheral
            hormone, ghrelin, led to synaptic changes in hippocampus and ventral tegmental
            area; acute and long-term potentiation
            2. Describe the central autonomic network direct and integrated complex responses;
            relation of the response to the neural level of the response (e.g. medulla, midbrain,
            cortex)
            a. Visceral afferents reciprocally connected with suprasegmental structures of the
            network
            b. Direct connections for simple autonomic responses:
            i. To (medulla) nucleus of the solitary tract to
            1. Brainstem nuclei (e.g. vagal motor nucleus) – control of HR and
            stomach contractions
            2. Ventrolateral medullary reticular formation – modulate BP by
            altering blood flow in vascular beds
            c. Connections for integrative ANS, neuroendocrine and behavioral, ‘complex’,
            responses
            i. To (midbrain) parabrachial nucleus
            1. Behavioral responses to taste
            2. Relay of visceral sensory information to forebrain nuclei
            ii. To (midbrain) periaqueductal grey
            1. Behavioral patterns related to autonomic responses; example
            ‘fight or flight behavior’ related to the autonomic response of
            shunting blood to muscles and brain; involves connections from
            PAQ to medullary RF
            d. Connections for integrative ANS, neuroendocrine and behavioral, ‘complex’,
            responses
            i. To (subcortical limbic nuclei) amygdala: autonomic responses of
            patterned behavioral responses (usually emotion based):


            1. Example: fear or rage; physiologic reactions to chemotherapy
            occur upon entering treatment room
            ii. Hypothalamus
            iii. To (thalamus, cortex) visceral sensory thalamus and visceral sensory
            cortex: anterior insula and on to anterior cingulate conscious awareness
            visceral sensations:
            1. Hunger pains, full stomach, breath holding feeling; conscious
            awareness and reaction to feeling
            3. Explain sources of inputs and outputs by which the hypothalamus influences
            physiology of the body and behavior
            a. Emotional stress to sympathetic activity impacts cardiac function: amygdala,
            dorsal medial hypothalamus to raphe pallidus to heart
            b. ANS, “enteric”: organs can act without ANS; innervation for rapid adjustments,
            environmental responsiveness
            i. Two-neuron chains; dual innervation of organs
            ii. Sympathetic (thoraco-lumbar)
            1. Control of pupil dilation
            2. Lesions - Horner’s syndrome
            iii. Parasympathetic [cranio-sacral]
            1. Control of micturation
            2. Lesions – disruption of bladder function.
            4. Explain the integration of the three systems involved in the control of micturation
            at spinal, supraspinal [pontine] and cortical levels of the nervous system
            a. “Empty”
            i. Parasympathetic innervation:
            1. S2-4 spinal segment + detrussor muscle cholinergic system
            ii. Vesicoparasympathetic reflex:
            1. elimination; contracts bladder (detrussor); relaxes urethra
            b. “Fill”
            i. Sympathetic innervation:
            1. L1-3 segments - detrussor muscle (-adrenergic receptor) +
            internal sphinctor (-adrenergic receptor)
            ii. Vesicosympathetic reflex:
            1. filling; relaxes bladder (detrussor), tightens the urethra (internal
            sphinctor)
            c. “Help”
            i. Somatic motor innervation:
            1. S2-4 spinal segments; Onuf’s nucleus + external sphinctor muscle
            ii. Vesicopudendal reflex:
            1. voluntary control; inhibited during voiding; contracted during
            restraint (‘hold-it’)
            Part 2
            1. Explain negative feedback control of steroid hormones via the hypothalamus
            a. Negative feedback control


            i. Short loop:
            1. pituitary hormone inhibits at the hypothalamus (e.g. pituitary
            hormones)
            ii. Long loop:
            1. target organ/gland hormone inhibits at the hypothalamus (e.g.
            steroid hormones)
            iii. Higher centers:
            1. target organ/gland hormone inhibits at the hippocampus (cortex)
            then to hypothalamus (e.g. gluccocorticoids)]

            b.
            2. Understand a hypothalamic region, inputs, related path and main roles served;
            including pituitary connections for anterior and medial basal hypothalamus
            a. Detects information
            i. External environment: visual, cortical, hippocampal
            ii. Internal environment: visceral afferents, specialized neurons sensitive to
            physiological stimuli (e.g. osmoreceptors; gluccoreceptors)
            b. Compares “to a setpoint”
            i. Integrative nuclei; determine need for a response
            c. Output – effects a response
            i. ANS via brainstem
            ii. Endocrine via pituitary
            iii. Behavioral means via limbic system/cerebral cortex
            3. Recognize the interactions or collaboration of hypothalamus with the limbic
            system
            a. Hypothalamus acquires information about the internal and external environment,
            integrates the information and organizes responses via ANS and neuroendocrine
            control and collaboration with limbic system to regulate body physiology and
            meaningful behavior.
            Part 3


            1. Explain how the limbic system weights our decisions, flavors our experience,
            adds meaning and drive to our lives

            a.

            a. Some limbic structures beyond cingulate

            b. Some key thalamic nuclei with limbic connections:

      MODULE 3


      What are the differences 
      between active touch and 
      passive touch?

      Topic 1 - $100 Question

      Click to see answer


      Active touch = perception of the characteristics of an object through voluntary, intentional contact movement 
      (especially by the hands) that is self-initiated.
      - Driven by intent to gain information about the object
      - Top down approach
      - Sensory – motor interaction
      - ‘Motor gating’: the motor system pattern of descending commands to the spinal cord or subcortical 
      centers, ‘gates’ or inhibits some incoming sensory information, to enable you to focus on the sensory input 
      related to the task.
      o Movement attenuates the somatosensory information at multiple levels of the CNS – by activation 
      of inhibitory neurons, ‘motor gating’.
      o Experienced, motor skilled movers use this to acquire the most accurate or useful information and 
      suppress other information.
      Passive touch = sensory experiences that occur when the observer isn’t moving to intentionally acquire information.  In 
      passive touch, stimulation is imposed on the skin of the individual.
      - Driven by the peripheral sensory receptor activation
      - ‘Bottom up’ approach
      - Little to no gating, little to no activation of the motor system (if something very dangerous touches the 
      skin regardless of whether I am intentionally seeking the information, there is likely some mechanism of 
      gating that directs attention to managing the dangerous stimulation and ignoring other ongoing intents or 
      experiences)
      - Sensory experience competing with other stimuli

      Topic 1 - $100 Answer

      Click to return to Jeopardy Board

      you need to test first before doing an

      Topic 1 - $200 Question

      Click to see answer


      This would be active touch. Would need to perform a test of ‘passive touch’ first, to 
      ensure the integrity of the primary sensory pathway and primary somatosensory 
      cortex, including joint position sense and joint movement testing. If they couldn’t 
      appreciate peripheral touch, then they cannot accurately assess stereognosis.

      When in pain, it is common to 
      rub the area. Why might the 
      mechanical stimulus of 
      rubbing the region alter the 
      perceived pain from that 
      region?

      Topic 1 - $300 Question

      Click to see answer


      1) Painful site – rubbing effective in relief by a process of mechanoreceptor activation, signal from 
      rubbing/mechanoreceptors travel faster and get to cerebral cortex first which ‘gets the attention’; while 
      attending to the rubbing stimuli, the brain is less able to attend to the pain messages from the spinothalamic 
      tract to somatosensory cortex.   
      2) Rubbing activates the somatosensory cortex and could lead to ‘motor gating’ top down – meaning if the 
      brain decides to attend to the rubbing, the brain could send descending input to the dorsal horn to filter 
      [inhibit transmission of pain afferents centrally]. 
      3) At the same time, the nervous system has its own internal mechanism to try and stop transmission of the 
      pain signal. Recall the small fiber afferents are activated by nociceptors/pain stimulus can elicit SPA (stimulus 
      produced analgesia) from branches off the spinothalamic tract to midbrain, pons, medulla – raphe nucleus and 
      result in descending serotonergic projection to inhibit dorsal horn neurons and stop the message from being 
      transmitted up the spinothalamic tract.  
      All three could happen at the same time – and likely do. The difference is SPA elicited by pain 
      stimulus/nociceptors  and the rubbing activates mechanoreceptors (uses DCML system) which creates 
      ‘competition’ and we ‘feel the rubbing’ and not the pain.

      Describe the different types 
      of intrafusal fibers and their 
      innervation.

      Topic 4 - $100 Question

      Click to see answer


      There are 3 types of fibers in the muscle spindle. Nuclear chain, nuclear bag 
      which has static and dynamic nuclear bag. Nuclear chain and static nuclear 
      bag is sensitive to static length (i.e actual length) of the muscle fiber. Dynamic 
      nuclear bag is sensitive to quick stretch or rapid lengthening of muscle (rate of 
      change/velocity of muscle lengthening).

      - Primary (1 a) connected to all 3 fibers, but secondary (type 2 afferents) 
      connected to static nuclear bag and nuclear chain.

      Describe alpha-gamma

      Topic 4 - $300 Question

      Click to see answer

      voluntary, actively contracting muscle
      ■ Critical to keep the spindle sensitive and ready to sense stretch
      ■ If just alpha were active, muscle spindle would lose sensitivity in
      intrafusal muscle. Gamma activation causes this contraction of intrafusal
      muscle to keep the muscle spindle sensitive to the extrafusal muscle.

      elicits a response.

      Topic 5 - $400 Question

      Click to see answer


      ■ “Mexican Hat”
      ● If you were to not use surround inhibition, you could not pinpoint a
      stimulus. Any and all sensors in the region of the skin affected
      would fire the same and a “blob” of information would come in the

      Define interoception, 
      proprioception, 
      exteroception.

      Topic 5 - $500 Question

      Click to see answer


      Interoception is the sense of the internal world, psychological status, much of 
      interception takes place below our conscious awareness. Ex we aren’t aware of 
      signal that maintain blood sugar levels, or heart beat, physical and emotional 
      status

      Proprioception is the sensation from internal body tissues about our position, 
      motion and muscle contraction forces (detected by muscle and joint receptors).

      Exteroception is sensation from external stimuli (outside the body) and is 
      detected by exteroceptors including vision, hearing, touch, pressure, 
      temperature, pain and smell.

      .
      Module 2 Kahoot Questions

      Vision:

      1.    T/F: Fovea contains both rods and cones photoreceptors.
      False.

      Explanation: Fovea which is the region of most acute vision only contains cones (see color and acuity), whereas rodes are color blind, but they are better for detecting motion, rodes don’t code color. We move our head to best position the lens of the eye to get the light to focus on the fovea for best visual acuity!

      2.    Visual path to the visual cortex is a two neuron pathway. Select the correct pathway.
      a.    Retina>optic nerve>optic chiasm>LGN>optic radiations>visual cortex
      b.    Retina>optic chiasm>optic nerve>LGN>visual cortex
      c.    Retina>optic chiasm>optic nerve>optic radiations>LGN>visual cortex
      d.    None of the above

      Explanation: 1st neuron: ganglion cells in retina, Axons from the ganglion cells from the optic nerve travels to synapse on the 2nd neuron in the path and the LGN (lateral geniculate nucleus) of the thalamus project their axons to the primary visual cortex by way of option radiations. 

      3. T/F: Nasal retinal information are medial portions of the visual fields that cross at optic chiasm
      False
      Explanation: V1 is visual cortex
      Nasal retinal info are lateral portions of the visual field. They do cross at optic chiasm to go to contralateral V1. Whereas, temporal retinal information are medial portions of the visual field that DO NOT cross at the chiasm and continue ipsilaterally to V1. FOR EXAMPLE,  the left visual cortex receives retinal afferent axons with info about the right halves (opposite) of the visual field of each eye.

      4. The receptive field responsible for light/dark information is____

      Answer: center surround receptive fields

      Explanation: center surround receptive field sharpen key information by excitation of strongest visual input and suppression of neighboring light information

      5. Visual association cortex (V2,3 ) is responsible for

      a)    Recognition of edges and lines
      b)    Recognition of textures and contours
      c)    Perception of color and motion
      d)    All of the above
      Explanation: The other two options are mainly in visual cortex (V1). Edges and lines are from simple cells in visual cortex (V1), textures and contours are recognized when simple cells integrate with complex cells which recognize bars of lights in a specific orientation thus enabling recognition of corners and textures or surface changes.

      6. The visual stream responsible for action is______and for objection recognition is ______

      Answer: Dorsal (action), obj recognition (ventral).
      Explanation: 
      Discuss dorsal stream: WHERE AND HOW pathways
      -     Responsible for visual-guided reaching (where pathway) by translating visual info of obj location to reaching direction
      -     Responsible for visually-informed grasping (planning or how pathway) by translating visual information about object properties into successful grasping
      -     M cells (magnocellular)
      -     Preconscious path for quick action

      Ventral stream: WHAT pathway i.e what something is and what it means
      -     Major role is perception of object, ex: recognition of complex images such as faces
      -     Conscious slower path for integrated perception and thought
      -     P cells: parvicellular

      8. Choose the correct role coordinated by the prefrontal cortex
      a)    Motor planning
      b)    Modeling behavior
      c)    Allow for changes in behavior
      d)    All of the above

      Explanation: what about posterior parietal cortex? Recognition of self relative to world, international representation of body. Lesions in posterior parietal cortex is related to gaze disorders, disorientation, constructional apraxia (ex cannot arrange table or put on a sweater)


      7. Discuss feedforward and feedback control in regards to vision while catching a ball (Lesson 4B Pt 1) Refer slides
      No vision: uses feedback control, using muscle proprioceptors i.e feedback control from arm
      Vision: uses feedforward control, can anticipate ball trajectory if you can see


      8. Direction of gaze eye movement uses what type of movement
      a)    VOR
      b)    Saccades 
      c)    Smooth pursuit
      d)    Gaze stabilization
      e)    Both B&C
      f)    Both A&C

      Explanation: VOR and gaze stabilization is same, here helps keep the image stable when head is moving
      Saccades refers to reflexive movement (normal response, ex we use saccadic movements of eye while reading!), smooth pursuit is keeping image of moving target on the fovea 

      9. T/F: Saccadic movements are slower than smooth pursuit movements.

      False
      Explanation: saccadic movements are rapid, 900 deg/sec; whereas smooth pursuit movements are slower (max 100 deg/sec)

      10. Saccades that are triggered by a detection of motion in the field of view is an example of

      a)    Voluntary saccades
      b)    Rotatory saccades
      c)    Attention saccades
      d)    Reflexive saccades

      Explanation: Voluntary saccades are aka attention saccades and are driven by intent for ex reading (FIND). Reflexive saccades aka triggered saccades usually occurs when something unexpected or sudden that INVOLUNTARILY draws our gaze (DETECT)

      11. Fill in the blank: Horizontal gaze is coordinated from a pontine gaze center called the________

      Answer: PPRF: Parmedian pontine reticular formation.
       PPRF generates signal for eye muscle pattern for horizontal gaze (i.e saccades), responsible for gaze motor control

      12. The systems responsible for smooth pursuit eye movements are….

      Answer: Cerebellum and vestibular
      -     These two systems are involved in integrating speed of movement of the object of interest into the smooth pursuit eye movement

      13. T/F: Neurons in basal ganglia works to inhibit superior colliculus to suppress saccadic movements

      True

      14. Why does familiar size require high-level visual processing? Open ended!
      Explanation: Involves recall from memory, recall, discuss speed accuracy trade off: when moving to a target, size influences movement speed. 
      The larger the target, typically faster movement speed. The smaller the target, the slower the movement speed. This is called speed accuracy trade off because when we reach to grasp an obj, our grasp is unconsciously adapted to the size of the object. 

      15. Fill in the blank: The two types of dorsal stream information are ____ &____

      Answer: Tau and optical flow

      Describe each:
      Tau: provides” time to contact” info or when the object will arrive to us. Its predictive or feedforward mechanism. Tau is used when grasping an object

      Optical flow: visual info streaming past is. For example, when we are stationary and people/objects/cars are moving around us or when we are moving past objects or people the visual stream induces a sensation! For example, when you are in car that is stationary, but when the car next to you starts moving forward, you feel like you are moving backwards (optic flow effect)

      16. Tau cues impact balance and postural adjustments. T/F
      False
      Answer: Optical flow is responsible for posture and balance (moving room experiments)
      Whereas Tau is responsible for accurate and precise movements 




















      VESTIBULAR APPARATUS ANATOMY:
       

      External ear: aka pinna
      Middle ear: contains 3 bones which include the incus, malleus and stapes
      Inner ear: contain semicircular canals, otolith organs (utricle and saccule) and the cochlea

      Our focus is the vestibular apparatus which is located in the inner ear. Vestibular cochlear system has 2 fluid filled chambers. The outer chamber which consists of perilymph fluid and the inner chamber which consists of the endolymph and in the inner chamber is where  the VESTIBULAR APPARATUS and Cochlea are located!

      Semicircular canals: pairing of canals with opposite ear’s canal
      -     R horizontal with left horizontal
      -     R anterior vertical with L posterior vertical
      -     R posterior vertical with R anterior vertical



      2.5 Vestibular/Auditory System

      1.    What are the two components of cranial nerve VIII?
      a.    Vestibular division & cochlear division (OPEN ENDED)

      Explanation: These are separate systems but they share a common pathway! We use this info to know how we are in space and how our bodies are oriented in relation to our environment (working together). Everything that the vestibular system does is by the detection of motion and position and allowing us to keep ourselves upright


      2.    How many semicircular canals are there and what do they detect?
      a.    2 semicircular canals - detect linear acceleration
      b.    4 semicircular canals - detect head tilt
      c.    3 semicircular canals - detect linear acceleration and head tilt
      d.    3 semicircular canals - detect angular acceleration
      such as head rotation
      3.    What makes up the otoliths? What information do they provide?
      a.    Utricle and Macula - rotational movements
      b.    Saccule and Ampulla - head tilt and linear acceleration
      c.    Utricle and Saccule - head tilt and linear acceleration 
      d.    Macula and Ampulla - rotational movements
      4.    What does the Utricle detect?
      a.    Horizontal direction - like when accelerating in a car
      b.    Vertical direction - like when going up an elevator
      c.    Lateral direction - like dancing salsa
      d.    Rotation direction - like performing a ballerina step
      Explanation:

      5.    What does the Saccule detect?
      a.    Vertical direction -  like when going up an elevator
      b.    Lateral direction like dancing salsa
      c.    Rotation direction - like performing a ballerina step
      d.    Horizontal direction - like when accelerating in a car
      6.    The following happens when the cilia are deflected TOWARD the kinocilia. Select all that apply:
      a.    Hyperpolarization
      b.    Depolarization
      c.    Increased impulse frequency in the afferent nerve
      d.    Decreased impulse frequency in the afferent nerve

      Explanation: What info does kinocilia provide? provides Directional sensitivity and allows us to sense two different directions. If hair cells (cilia) move away it causes hyperpolarization. So as cilia deflect toward kinocilia, which depolarizes hair cell>increasing release of neurotransmitters and therefore increased firing in afferent nerve.

      7.    The striola enables sensitivity in all directions and allows some cells to depolarize and some to hyperpolarize.
      a.    True
      b.    False

      Explanation: Position of kinocilia relative to striola provides sensitivity in all directions…for ex: When flexing head forward, the otoconia gets displaced, depolarizing one side, but the opposite side of the striola are oriented in opposite direction so that the cilia are moving away from the kinocilia, so this results in hyperpolarization and inhibition of these efferent fibers. It provides the information that they're not moving in the opposite direction. Remember this is for acceleration and acceleration so if constant velocity movement then nerve would just fire at baseline rates.

      8.    The ampulla is for the semicircular canals like the Macula for the Otolith organs (utricle and saccule)
      a.    True
      b.    False 

       Inside the macula (part of the Otolith organs Utricle and Saccule) is a collection of hair cells located in the utricle and saccule, which are the otolith organs. Inside of each of these organs there is a macula, which is a collection of hair cells that are enclosed in a gelatinous mass, which is topped with calcium carbonate crystals called otoconia.
      9.    In left head rotation, the endolymph in the left ear moves against the cupula, causing deflection against the kinocilia, decreasing firing of the nerves.
      a.    True
      b.    False  
      Movement of fluid can deflect the cupula one way or other so as the head accelerates and moves to the left, the endolymph is moving towards the capula to deflect. This causes hair cells to bend towards kinocilia resulting in depolarization, thus causing increased firing in the left vestibular nerve and this tells us we are moving our head to the left. Whereas in the right ear, the endolymph is moving away from the cupula causing the deflection of cilia away from kinocilia resulting in hyperpolarization, decreased firing. So we need two indications for direction of turning (especially if there is a loss of function in one canal), because we get inputs from both canals!

       


      When rotating to the left, endolymph fluid in the left ear moves toward the cupula, causing a deflection toward the kinocilia, increases firing of the nerve. On the Right side ear happens the opposite.

      10.   Information about our head position by the hair cells is transmitted through efferent neurons to:
      a.    Vestibular ganglion (location of cell bodies)
      b.    Brainstem nuclei
      c.    Vestibular nuclei
      d.    Spinal cord
      through efferent neurons because the afferents are at the hair cells
      those vestibular ganglion cells have projections to the vestibular nuclei in the brainstem via cranial nerve VIII. 
      The vestibular nuclei have lots of different connections like the vestibular cerebellum, other brainstem nuclei for eye movement control, thalamus, up to the cortex, direct connections to spinal cord, and direct efferent inputs from vestibular ganglion to vestibulocerebellum.

      11.   The semicircular canals project information to which of the following nuclei?
      a.    Inferior
      b.    Superior
      c.    Medial 
      d.    Lateral 


      Explanation: there are 4 vestibular nuclei in brainstem: sup, med, inferior and lateral.  SCC project info to sup,med. Where do they output this information to? Medial Longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)
      -     SCC to med/sup>ascending projections to gaze centers and descending projections to cervical spinal cord for neck control via MLF
      -     What about otoliths? These project info to lat and inferior vestibular nucleir and output the info to lateral vestibulospinal tract (from lat vestibular nuclei) and inferior nuclei output to cerebellum, reticular formation and contralateral vestibular nuclei.
      -     Lateral vestibular spinal tracts inputs to lower portion of spinal cord and medial vestibular spinal tract inputs to cervical portion of spinal cord.

      12.   What is the function of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)
      a.    To send information from semicircular, ascending to eye movement control centers (gaze centers) and descending, to the spinal  cord for head/neck control)
      OPEN ENDED

      13.   In this reflex, with head rotation, eyes move opposite to head at the same speed and degree to stabilize the GAZE (image on the retina).
      a.    Vestibulo-ocular reflexes 
      b.    Rotational vestibular-ocular reflex
      c.    Translational vestibulo-ocular
      d.    Ocular counter-rolling response
      EXPLANATION: VOR responses help to stabilize eyes to keep image on the retina, these are the various types of VOR responses!
      -     Rotational vestibulo-ocular with head rotation, eyes move opposite to head at the same speed and degree to stabilize the GAZE (image on the retina) . 
      -     Translational vestibulo-ocular: helps stabilize gaze during translational movement. with visual image linear motion, close objects moving fast, far objects moving slower: otoliths stabilize eyes for far objects.
      -      Ocular counter-rolling response: stabilize eyes with head tilt. Otoliths stabilize eyes to correct for vertical offset. What happens if there is a loss of function of ocular counter rolling response? Results in skew deviation

      14.   The Position-vestibular pause (PVP) transmit info about passive head movement while floccular target neurons (FTN) modulate/cancel the VOR reflex with cerebellum input.
      a.    True
      b.    False
      15.   In this part of the ear sound is transformed to vibration and is a series of:
      a.    Outer ear; series of sound waves
      b.    Middle ear; series of 3 small bones (ossicles)
      c.    Inner ear; series of pressure waves
      d.    Middle ear; series of sound waves
      Stapes is the third bone in the middle ear and it rests on the oval window to the inner ear. The vibrations in middle ear cause stapes to move in and out of the oval window at the frequency of the sounds and establishes pressure waves in the perilymph at inner ear. This perilymph exist in two of the the three compartments of the inner ear and the cochlea, the scala tympani and scala vestibule. The pressure waves in these scala will deflect the scala media in which the organ for corti the place where sounds waves are transferred into neural signals lies. They will deflect the scale media at the frequency of the sound.

      What are the roles of the outer ear? To capture the sound.
      Summary: the outer and middle ear capture and transform sound waves and establish pressure waves in inner ears to activate the neurosensory receptors (which is the hair cells of the inner ear).
      16.   This bone in the middle ear moves in and out of the oval window at the frequency of sounds that establishes pressure waves in the perilymph at the inner ear.
      a.    Malleus
      b.    Stapes
      c.    Incus
      d.    Maya 
      17.   The low-frequency pressure difference in the perilymph off the two Scale (vestibuli and tympani) are shuttered through the:
      a.    Helicotrema (far end of cochlea, where low-frequency sounds are perceived) (SHORT ANSWER)
      Helicotrema (far end of cochlea) - where the two ducts communicate between the tympani and the vestibule Scales
      18.   Where is the organ Corti located and where specifically do high frequency sounds are perceived?
      a.    Scale tympani 
      b.    Scale Media 
      c.    Scale Media close to round window
      d.    Scale Media close to the Helicotrema
      because the basilar membrane near the oval window is STIFF therefore it capture HIGH frequency/high pitch sounds!
      Scale media close to the helicotrema captures LOW-FREQUENCY  - the basilar membrane near the helicotrema is more FLEXIBLE therefore allow lower sounds to be heard.
       

      19.   This membrane in the Organ of Corti, allows for depolarization and hyperpolarization at the frequency of the sound.
      a.    Tectorial membrane
      b.    Basilar membrane
      c.    Corti membrane
      d.    Hearing membrane
      20.   The dorsal cochlear nucleus pathway and the ventral cochlear nucleus are responsible for: (respectively)
      a.    Localizing sound in space; Hearing 
      b.    Hearing; afferent information
      c.    Hearing; localizing sounds in space
      d.    Localizing sounds in space; efferent information

      Explanation: These pathway share auditory info to other ear as well, therefore it is very rare and hard to lose complete hearing on one side of the ear. One sided earring loss is typically due to lesion of CN8 or inner ear itself. 
      Discuss Option A: Localizing sounds happens via ventral cochlear nucleus pathway. This pathway uses timing and intensity information about hearing for a sound heard from both ears. For ex, if sound is on left side, even the right side hears it but at a slightly different time and slightly diff intensity.
      -  WHERE IS THE timing and intensity of sound manipulated (structure?) SUPERIOR OLIVARY NUCLEUS. There are two : medial SON and lateral SON. medial is focused on detecting timing of sound and lateral is focused on determining Intensity of sound. 
      Excitation in ipsilateral cochlea is greater than inhibition from contralateral side b/c this can help us know the sound is localized to the excitation side thus intensity on that side is higher!

      21.   Primary auditory association areas are in the temporal lobe of the brain
      a.    True
      b.    False 



      How are they arranged? TONOTOPIC ARRANGEMENT THROUGHOUT

      .
      Module 2 Kahoot Questions

      Vision:

      1. T/F: Fovea contains both rods and cones photoreceptors.
      False.

      Explanation: Fovea which is the region of most acute vision only contains cones (see color and
      acuity)

      2. Visual path to the visual cortex is a two neuron pathway. Select the correct pathway.
      a. Retina>optic nerve>optic chiasm>LGN>optic radiations>visual cortex
      b. Retina>optic chiasm>optic nerve>LGN>visual cortex
      c. Retina>optic chiasm>optic nerve>optic radiations>LGN>visual cortex
      d. None of the above

      Explanation: 1st neuron: ganglion cells in retina, Axons from the ganglion cells from the optic
      nerve travels to synapse on the 2nd neuron in the path and the LGN (lateral geniculate nucleus)
      of the thalamus project their axons to the primary visual cortex by way of option radiations.

      3. T/F: Nasal retinal information are medial portions of the visual fields that cross at optic chiasm
      False
      Explanation: V1 is visual cortex
      Nasal retinal info are lateral portions of the visual field. They do cross at optic chiasm to go to
      contralateral V1. Whereas, temporal retinal information are medial portions of the visual field
      that DO NOT cross at the chiasm and continue ipsilaterally to V1. FOR EXAMPLE, the left
      visual cortex receives retinal afferent axons with info about the right halves (opposite) of the
      visual field of each eye.

      4. The receptive field responsible for light/dark information is____

      Answer: center surround receptive fields

      Explanation: center surround receptive field sharpen key information by excitation of strongest
      visual input and suppression of neighboring light information

      5. Visual association cortex (V2,3 ) is responsible for

      a) Recognition of edges and lines
      b) Recognition of textures and contours
      c) Perception of color and motion
      d) All of the above
      Explanation: The other two options are mainly in visual cortex (V1). Edges and lines are from
      simple cells in visual cortex (V1), textures and contours are recognized when simple cells


      integrate with complex cells which recognize bars of lights in a specific orientation thus enabling
      recognition of corners and textures or surface changes.

      6. The visual stream responsible for action is______and for objection recognition is ______

      Answer: Dorsal (action), obj recognition (ventral).
      Explanation:
      Discuss dorsal stream: WHERE AND HOW pathways
      - Responsible for visual-guided reaching (where pathway) by translating visual info of obj
      location to reaching direction
      - Responsible for visually-informed grasping (planning or how pathway) by translating
      visual information about object properties into successful grasping
      - M cells (magnocellular)
      - Preconscious path for quick action

      Ventral stream: WHAT pathway i.e what something is and what it means
      - Major role is perception of object, ex: recognition of complex images such as faces
      - Conscious slower path for integrated perception and thought
      - P cells: parvicellular

      8. Choose the correct role coordinated by the prefrontal cortex
      a) Motor planning
      b) Modeling behavior
      c) Allow for changes in behavior
      d) All of the above

      Explanation: what about posterior parietal cortex? Recognition of self relative to world,
      international representation of body. Lesions in posterior parietal cortex is related to gaze
      disorders, disorientation, constructional apraxia (ex cannot arrange table or put on a sweater)

      7. Discuss feedforward and feedback control in regards to vision while catching a ball (Lesson
      4B Pt 1) Refer slides
      No vision: uses feedback control, using muscle proprioceptors i.e feedback control from arm
      Vision: uses feedforward control, can anticipate ball trajectory if you can see

      8. Direction of gaze eye movement uses what type of movement
      a) VOR
      b) Saccades
      c) Smooth pursuit
      d) Gaze stabilization
      e) Both B&C
      f) Both A&C


      Explanation: VOR and gaze stabilization is same, here helps keep the image stable when head
      is moving
      Saccades refers to reflexive movement (normal response, ex we use saccadic movements of
      eye while reading!), smooth pursuit is keeping image of moving target on the fovea

      9. T/F: Saccadic movements are slower than smooth pursuit movements.

      False
      Explanation: saccadic movements are rapid, 900 deg/sec; whereas smooth pursuit movements
      are slower (max 100 deg/sec)

      10. Saccades that are triggered by a detection of motion in the field of view is an example of

      a) Voluntary saccades
      b) Rotatory saccades
      c) Attention saccades
      d) Reflexive saccades

      Explanation: Voluntary saccades are aka attention saccades and are driven by intent for ex
      reading (FIND). Reflexive saccades aka triggered saccades usually occurs when something
      unexpected or sudden that INVOLUNTARILY draws our gaze (DETECT)

      11. Fill in the blank: Horizontal gaze is coordinated from a pontine gaze center called
      the________

      Answer: PPRF: Parmedian pontine reticular formation.
      PPRF generates signal for eye muscle pattern for horizontal gaze (i.e saccades), responsible
      for gaze motor control

      12. The systems responsible for smooth pursuit eye movements are….

      Answer: Cerebellum and vestibular
      - These two systems are involved in integrating speed of movement of the object of
      interest into the smooth pursuit eye movement

      13. T/F: Neurons in basal ganglia works to inhibit superior colliculus to suppress saccadic
      movements

      True

      14. Why does familiar size require high-level visual processing? Open ended!

      The larger the target, typically faster movement speed. The smaller the target, the slower the

      15. Fill in the blank: The two types of dorsal stream information are ____ &____

      Answer: Tau and optical flow

      16. Tau cues impact balance and postural adjustments. T/F
      False
      Answer: Optical flow is responsible for posture and balance (moving room experiments)
      Whereas Tau is responsible for accurate and precise movements

      b. Superior
      c. Medial
      d. Lateral

      Explanation: there are 4 vestibular nuclei in brainstem: sup, med, inferior and lateral. SCC
      project info to sup,med. Where do they output this information to? Medial Longitudinal fasciculus
      (MLF)
      - SCC to med/sup>ascending projections to gaze centers and descending projections to
      cervical spinal cord for neck control via MLF
      - What about otoliths? These project info to lat and inferior vestibular nucleir and output
      the info to lateral vestibulospinal tract (from lat vestibular nuclei) and inferior nuclei
      output to cerebellum, reticular formation and contralateral vestibular nuclei.
      - Lateral vestibular spinal tracts inputs to lower portion of spinal cord and medial vestibular
      spinal tract inputs to cervical portion of spinal cord.

      12. What is the function of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)
      a. To send information from semicircular, ascending to eye movement control
      centers (gaze centers) and descending, to the spinal cord for head/neck control)
      OPEN ENDED

      13. In this reflex, with head rotation, eyes move opposite to head at the same speed and
      degree to stabilize the GAZE (image on the retina).
      a. Vestibulo-ocular reflexes
      b. Rotational vestibular-ocular reflex
      c. Translational vestibulo-ocular
      d. Ocular counter-rolling response
      EXPLANATION: VOR responses help to stabilize eyes to keep image on the retina, these are
      the various types of VOR responses!
      - Rotational vestibulo-ocular with head rotation, eyes move opposite to head at the same
      speed and degree to stabilize the GAZE (image on the retina) .


      - Translational vestibulo-ocular: helps stabilize gaze during translational movement. with
      visual image linear motion, close objects moving fast, far objects moving slower: otoliths
      stabilize eyes for far objects.
      - Ocular counter-rolling response: stabilize eyes with head tilt. Otoliths stabilize eyes to
      correct for vertical offset. What happens if there is a loss of function of ocular counter
      rolling response? Results in skew deviation

      14. The Position-vestibular pause (PVP) transmit info about passive head movement while
      floccular target neurons (FTN) modulate/cancel the VOR reflex with cerebellum input.
      a. True
      b. False
      15. In this part of the ear sound is transformed to vibration and is a series of:
      a. Outer ear; series of sound waves
      b. Middle ear; series of 3 small bones (ossicles)
      c. Inner ear; series of pressure waves
      d. Middle ear; series of sound waves

      16. This bone in the middle ear moves in and out of the oval window at the frequency of
      sounds that establishes pressure waves in the perilymph at the inner ear.
      a. Malleus
      b. Stapes
      c. Incus
      d. Maya
      17. The low-frequency pressure difference in the perilymph off the two Scale (vestibuli and
      tympani) are shuttered through the:
      a. Helicotrema (far end of cochlea, where low-frequency sounds are perceived)
      (SHORT ANSWER)
      Helicotrema (far end of cochlea) - where the two ducts communicate between the tympani and
      the vestibule Scales
      18. Where is the organ Corti located and where specifically do high frequency sounds are
      perceived?
      a. Scale tympani
      b. Scale Media
      c. Scale Media close to round window
      d. Scale Media close to the Helicotrema

      19. This membrane in the Organ of Corti, allows for depolarization and hyperpolarization at
      the frequency of the sound.
      a. Tectorial membrane
      b. Basilar membrane
      c. Corti membrane
      d. Hearing membrane
      20. The dorsal cochlear nucleus pathway and the ventral cochlear nucleus are responsible
      for: (respectively)


      a. Localizing sound in space; Hearing
      b. Hearing; afferent information
      c. Hearing; localizing sounds in space
      d. Localizing sounds in space; efferent information

      Explanation: These pathway share auditory info to other ear as well, therefore it is very rare and
      hard to lose complete hearing on one side of the ear. One sided earring loss is typically due to
      lesion of CN8 or inner ear itself.
      Discuss Option A: Localizing sounds happens via ventral cochlear nucleus pathway. This
      pathway uses timing and intensity information about hearing for a sound heard from both ears.
      For ex, if sound is on left side, even the right side hears it but at a slightly different time and
      slightly diff intensity.
      - WHERE IS THE timing and intensity of sound manipulated (structure?) SUPERIOR OLIVARY
      NUCLEUS. There are two : medial SON and lateral SON. medial is focused on detecting timing
      of sound and lateral is focused on determining Intensity of sound.
      Excitation in ipsilateral cochlea is greater than inhibition from contralateral side b/c this can help
      us know the sound is localized to the excitation side thus intensity on that side is higher!

      21. Primary auditory association areas are in the temporal lobe of the brain
      a. True
      b. False

      .
      Neuroscience Module 3:

      Lesson 1 & 2
      1. The sensory system is organized into three main categories: the sense of position and
      movement is_____
      a. Interoception
      b. Inception
      c. Proprioception
      d. Exteroception

      2. Which of the following is not a sensory receptor?
      a. Low threshold mechanoreceptors
      b. High threshold mechanoreceptors
      c. Baroreceptors
      d. Polymodal receptors
      e. Nociceptors
      f. All of the above are sensory receptors

      3. T/F: Polymodal receptors respond to discomfort, itch and hurt.
      True

      Explanation: polymodal receptors are a type of nociceptor that respond to high intensity
      mechanical, chemical and thermal stimuli

      Discuss the other types of receptors:
      1. Low threshold: discriminative touch, mechanoreceptors that respond to non-painful
      mechanical deformation of the receptor by touch, pressure, stretch or vibration
      2. High threshold: ouch, mechanoreceptors that respond to intense or painful mechanical
      stimulation such as pinching, cutting or stretching
      3. Thermal: warm and cool
      4. Nociceptors: noxious (painful) mechanical, chemical and thermal
      5. Proprioceptors: body and limb position, muscle stretch or muscle tension/force

      4. Open ended: What type of receptor is the pacinian corpuscle? What do they respond to?

      Answer: RA type 2 i.e fast adapting low threshold mechanoreceptors; Vibration


      Explanation: localize discriminative touch. These include the rapidly adapting, slowly adapting
      and pacinian corpuscle (respond to vibration). These receptors respond to non-painful
      mechanical deformation of the receptor by touch , pressure, stretch or vibration.

      5 T/F: Type 1 slow and fast adapting mechanoreceptors have large receptive fields, thus giving
      precise detail about the stimulus
      False

      Explanation: first statement is false here, SA and RA type 1 have small receptive fields, thus
      giving precise detail, large receptive fields give less detail about the stimulus due to less density
      of the receptors.
      Type 1: small receptive fields, and have greater density on skin of fingers, well defined fields
      therefore detect high acuity of touch and useful for detecting fine detail or texture of objects
      Type 2: large receptive fields

      RA: respond to when touch is initiated and when removed (on and off times only). It is not active
      when touch is maintained
      SA: responds maximally throughout the touch is maintained or as long as the stimulus is
      present.

      6. Which of the following are slow adapting receptors not known in humans?

      a. Merkel's disk
      b. Pacinian corpuscle
      c. Meissner corpuscle
      d. Ruffini endings

      7. T/F: RA type 1 fibers (meissner corpuscle) are most helpful in detecting the texture of objects
      and is sensitive to low frequency vibrations (30-50 Hz).

      True

      Explanation: How is RA 1 different from RA 2?

      8. T/F: Receptive fields tend to be smaller proximally and larger distally.
      FALSE

      Explanation: Receptive fields tend to be smaller distally and larger proximally. Distal areas like
      fingers have more density of receptors than proximal areas.


      9. Sensory system works together with motor system during active touch by ____

      a. Facilitation
      b. Filtering
      c. Used in feedforward and feedback mechanisms
      d. All of the above

      10. Describe pain (open ended)

      Explanation:
      - Goes beyond sensation thats why its hard to manage pain. Described as integrated
      physiologic, cognitive and motivational/emotional experience
      - Its a sensory experience that is unpleasant which can be evoked by stimulus that injure
      tissue or it can be an emotional experience
      - There are communicative and protective pain behaviors (communicative: facial
      expressions, verbal expressions such as sighing or moaning and protective: any action
      to reduce pain or probability of pain for ex we limp to alter weight distribution to minimize
      pain to injured limb,; muscle guarding).

      11. Fill in the blank: Pain and temperature is associated with ______ tract that is found in
      the_____horn

      Answer: Spinothalamic tract, dorsal horn.

      12. Peripheral pain afferents are small fibers which include___

      a. A delta fibers
      b. A alpha fibers
      c. C fibers
      d. All of the above
      e. Only A & C
      f. Only B & C

      13. The two types of muscle proprioceptors are _____&_______

      Answer: Muscle spindles & GTO

      14. Which of the following is true about Golgi tendon organ (GTO)?
      a. Within a contractile
      b. Within a tendon
      c. Sense muscle stretch causing muscle activation
      d. Sense tendon stretch causing muscle inhibition


      e. Sense stretch
      f. Sense tension in tendon as muscle contracts
      g. Monosynaptic reflex
      h. Autogenic inhibition
      i. Reciprocal inhibition

      15. The intrafusal fiber responsible for determining the actual length of the muscle is_____
      a. Nuclear chain
      b. Dynamic nuclear bag
      c. Static nuclear bag
      d. Both A & C
      e. Only C

      Explanation: There are 3 types of fibers in the muscle spindle. Nuclear chain, nuclear bag which
      has static and dynamic nuclear bag. Nuclear chain and static nuclear bag is sensitive to static
      length (i.e actual length) of the muscle fiber. Dynamic nuclear bag is sensitive to quick stretch or
      rapid lengthening of muscle (rate of change/velocity of muscle lengthening).

      - Discuss which afferents are connected to which fibers. Primary (1 a) connected to
      all 3 fibers, but secondary (type 2 afferents) connected to static nuclear bag and nuclear
      chain.

      15. Why is alpha-gamma coactivation important?
      - Critical to keep the muscle spindle sensitive and ready to sense stretch so we don’t
      injure ourselves
      - How does it work? Alpha motor neurons send efferent signal to contract extrafusal
      muscle fibers and at the SAME TIME, the gamma motor neurons are activated to
      contract the intrafusal muscle fibers and contraction of intrafusal muscle fibers at the
      polar ends keep the muscle spindle taut and sensitive. Remember this is a voluntary
      response!

      16. T/F: Monosynaptic stretch reflex is a voluntary reflex where alpha-gamma coactivation
      occurs.

      False

      Explanation: its a stretch reflex assessed during a neurological exam that is involuntary (patellar
      tendon reflex for ex), where gamma motor neuron are not activated therefore no alpha-gamma
      coactivation occurring here..---- elicited by H reflex

      REVIEW:


      - 17. Through what afferent fibers does the nuclear chain fiber convey its information to
      the spinal cord?
      Answer: Type 1 a and Type 11 a. Type 1 a conveys dynamic (nuclear bag) and static (nuclear
      chain and bag), whereas type 11a conveys only static (nuclear chain and static nuclear bag)

      - 18. What are the two different types of efferent fibers?
      Dynamic and static gamma motor neurons

      Lesson 6 Part A

      1. Study of control of movements and how the neuromuscular system functions to activate

      2. T/F: Motor unit is considered the final common pathway that transmits the descending CNS

      3. The sliding filament mechanism demonstrates that active force is greatest at the resting
      length of muscle due to:

      a. Resting length is 1.0
      b. Greater overlap of contractile proteins (actin & myosin)
      c. Resting length is little over 1.0
      d. Contribution of passive tension
      e. Both A & B
      f. Both B & C

      Expl:
      - Active force is greatest when resting length of muscle is 1.0, here there is greater
      opportunity for actin and myosin contractile proteins to form crossbridges. Note that
      passive tension does not contribute anything! And since overlap of filaments doesn’t
      allow for greater force productions, so active force keeps decreasing!
      - Total muscle force (i.e greatest total force production) occurs when both active and
      passive tension contribute. This happens at lengths slightly greater than resting length
      (i.e muscle is slightly stretched). This is why eccentric contractions where the muscle is
      under lengthening generally leads to greater force production.

      9. T/F: There are more type 1a afferent inputs to FF amd FR motor unit fibers than SO .

      False


      10. Open ended:
      Tension generated in SO fibers are potentiated, whereas tension generated in FF or FR are sag.
      Explain why?

      - SO twitch fibers have slow contractions times and form cross bridges slowly in
      comparison to FF or FR. Therefore SO crossbridge resists relaxation, this resistance to
      relaxation builds passive tension in the connective tissue such that together with slow
      relaxation times and with repeated stimulation, the tensions generated in slow twitch
      fibers is actually potentiated. Meaning there is an increase in tensions with repeated
      stimulation (passive tension builds ups).
      - - Now in FF and FR cross bridges are formed at a rapid rate, making these fivers LESS
      RESISTANT TO RELAXATION, meaning they can let go more easily.

      11. T/F; Higher fatigue index means greater resistance to fatigue.

      True

      Expl: FR: tension is 75% of initial tension after 5 mins of repeated stimulation. SO has 90% or
      more of initial tension after 60 mins of repeated stimulation!
      FF: 1 min <0.25, (fatigue index of less than 0.25), this means with FF tension is nearly gone
      after 1 min of repeated stimulus.
      FR: 2-5 mins, >0.75
      SO: 60 mins, >0.75, usually > 0.90

      42. Define balance in your own words:

      1. The cerebral cortex is involved in which of the following functions:
      a. Goal directed movements

      2. The ability to isolate movement to a limited set of muscles is called_______
      Answer: fractionated movement

      3. The motor control in the cerebral cortex is organized in a top down pattern. T/F?
      False
      Expl: Motor control in the cerebral cortex occurs at multiple levels (all levels) and the control of
      movement is hetarachial i.e distributed and interconnected (NOT HIERARCHICAL)

      4. Name the six layers of the cerebral cortex from the most superficial to the most deep
      cortex layer.
      Answer:
      1. Molecular, 2. External granular, 3. External pyramidal, 4. Internal granular, 5.
      Internal pyramidal, 6. Multiform
      Expl:
      - Superficial layers are layers 1-3, terminates in layer 4. These layers are involved in
      ascending and feedforward information
      - Deep layers are layers 5 and 6 and terminate in layers 1 and 6. Has descending and
      feedback information
      - Layer 4: receive direct thalamic projections and is thick for sensory cortex ex visual
      processing!

      remember that different cortical regions have diff thickness or expansions of the layers which is
      related to the function of that layer/cortex area
      - Discuss what is within each layer

      5. The layer within the primary visual cortex is:

      a. Layer 3: External pyramidal
      b. Layer 4: Internal granular
      c. Layer 5: Internal pyramidal
      d. Layer 6: Multiform

      Expl: Layer 4 is the primary somatosensory expansion layer


      what about motor cortex? Layer 5: Internal pyramidal, WHat about prefrontal cortex? Layer 3:
      external pyramidal, layer 3 has role in cognitive guidance of behavior, Layer 3 and 6 are parietal
      association areas.

      6. The primary output layer of the cerebral cortex?
      a. Layer 2: external granular
      b. Layer 3: external pyramidal
      c. Layer 4: Internal granular
      d. Layer 5: Internal pyramidal

      Expl:
      - Layer 2 and 3: i.e molecular and external granular layer are responsible for horizontal
      communication ( flow of info within one level or one segment, for ex dorsal visual stream
      info flows from occipital lobe to parietal and frontal lobes) between cortical regions
      - Layer 4: primary input layer of the cerebral cortex
      - Layer 5: primary output layer of the cerebral cortex. The pyramidal cells of layer 5 are
      the origin for pyramidal tract neurons that form the corticospinal tracts!
      - Layer 6: function is mystery!, but is considered to have reciprocal communication to
      thalamus from cortex with the potential to FILTER, FACILITATE AND ORGANIZE the
      info coming to the cortex from the thalamus. Layer 6 also has stellate cells which are
      interneurons for LOCAL communication within the column through the layers of the
      cortex.

      7. What are the two types of neurons in the cerebral cortex? Open-ended

      Answer: Projection neurons and Interneurons

      Expl: Projection neurons are pyramidal neurons. These are present in layers 2,3( have small
      pyramidal cells and involved in intra corticocortical communication i.e project to OTHER cortical
      areas), 5 (large pyramidal, these project to subcortical and brainstem regions).
      Whereas, interneurons are stellate cells which are present in all layers but mainly in 4. What
      are stellate cells responsible for? Local communication in the cortex!

      8. Basket cells , a special type of stellate cell have inhibitory effects. T/F?
      True

      Expl: stellate cells can be inhibitory or excitatory. However, basket cells have inhibitory
      projections. They inhibit at sima of pyramidal neurons in layers 2,3 and 5.
      9. What does the inhibitory effects of the basket cells aid in?

      Helps sharpen the output message (focus and define info), by suppressing other activity to
      enable a more focussed output


      10. The association area responsible for language is________

      a. Temporal association
      b. Sensory association
      c. Frontal association
      d. Visual Association

      Expl:
      - What are association cortices? These areas dominate the cortex in terms of space
      occupied but also likely dominate the functions of the cortex as most amount of
      processing and integration occur here
      - Association cortices INTEGRATE the info from multiple inputs. For ex, the integrate
      somatosensory info from visual and vestibular inputs and process this info to allow for
      creation of a motor plan!
      - frontal association includes: motor association and prefrontal cortex
      - Parietal association: includes sensory (posterior parietal cortex), visual association,
      temporal association
      11. All of the following are specific nuclei except:

      a. Ventral posterolateral
      b. Ventral posteromedial

      d. Lateral and medial geniculate

      Expl: pulvinar is considered association nuclei. Other association nuclei include lateral posterior,

      - Whereas the specific nuclei project to primary cortex (more superficial layers of the

      13. Lesion in the pyramidal tract neurons result in…

      14. The corticomotoneuronal cells, which are PTNs are kept silent by GABA input released

      15. LMN and UMN lesions can be distinguished by distinct signs which include…
      a. DTR responses
      b. Pathological reflexes
      c. Muscle weakness pattern
      d. All of the above
      e. Only A & C

      UMN:
      - DTR: hyperreflexia
      - Pathological reflexes are present: babinksi, hoffmans, clonus etc
      - Spasticty
      - The weakness tends to be more pronounced in flexor muscles (muscles that bend a
      joint) than in extensor muscles (muscles that straighten a joint). This pattern is known as
      the "pyramidal" or "corticospinal" pattern→ Weakness to one side of body known as
      hemiparesis
      - loss of fractionated movement
      - Common sites of UMN lesion: primary cortex, premotor cortex, posterior limb on internal
      capsule, corticospinal tracts: brainstem, spinal cord, corticobulbar lesions
      LMN:
      - More related to spinal nerve root or peripheral nerve root lesions
      - Hyporeflexia
      - Flaccid paralysis, weakness
      - Fasciculations
      - No pathological reflexes!

      - Supraspinal inputs provide voluntary initiation of locomotion, regulation of postural

      17. The term “skilled walking” requires:

      18. Planning of locomotion involves the posterior parietal cortex (PPC). What is the role of
      PPC?

      Answer: helps with planning adjustments, obstacle negotiation, storage of information regarding
      object ( for example when you see an object in front of your walking path, you step over it, now
      you remember the leg behind you also has to step over this object to allow for successful step
      over/obstacle negotiation therefore your PPC stores this info for the hind limb since you cannot
      see what your hind limb is doing)
      - Also helps with object location relative to body (termed limb state object coupling).

      Explanation: the Striatum formed by the caudate nucleus & putamen receive INPUT from the

      4. Explain how the BG circuits work using the following image. OPEN ENDED (NOT
      IN KAHOOT)


      ANSWER/EXPLANATION: Each circuit projects from cortex to the striatum; either to the
      putamen or caudate. Then these input areas project to the globus pallidus. Then the GPI
